en: The *Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra*, Scroll One.
The name of the translator is lost; it is now appended to the Qin Records.
The meaning of "Mātṛkā" shall now be explained: listen well to it, all of you!
Although the words herein are brief, they extensively encompass the meaning of the Vinaya.
Based on the primary matters, this exposition has been delivered;
the wise should know that the essential treasury of all sūtras is entirely contained within this.
The various meanings outside the Vinaya-piṭaka can be found within the Mātṛkā-sūtras;
the meaning of the Vinaya enters these sūtras like the many rivers flowing into the ocean.
The various meanings outside the Vinaya are likewise found within the Mātṛkā-sūtras.
The meanings of all the sūtras can be understood at will;
the Vinaya can extinguish doubt and confusion. As definitively taught in the various sūtras, all the precepts established by the Buddha are contained within this scripture.
Question: "For what reason is it called the *Mātṛkā-sūtra*?
The Wise One replied:

"This sutra can extinguish arrogance and untie the bonds of affliction; it can enable sentient beings to reach the end of all suffering and attain ultimate nirvana. Therefore, it is called the Mother Sutra."
*Vinaya* means "extinguishing"; it is called *vinaya* because it extinguishes all unwholesome dharmas.
Now I shall explain the meaning of the *Mātṛkā*.
As for the meaning of the *Mātṛkā*: that which can definitively resolve the established meanings and does not contradict what is taught in the various sūtras is called a *mātṛkā*.
Within this, two types of sūtras are explained:
first, the Bhikṣu Sūtra; second, the Bhikṣuṇī Sūtra. All the various aggregates shall be explained in detail later.
"The causal conditions for the establishment of the precepts for the initial group of ten persons, as well as the meanings from the *Ekottarika Āgama*, are all included within these sūtras."

By understanding the primary causes and conditions, one comes to know the primary matters and severs the doubts of others; thus, one will no longer be confused regarding the meanings within the various sūtras.

If a bhikṣu wishes to properly uphold the definitive understanding found in the *Vinayamātṛkā*, he can swiftly eliminate birth and death, which is superior even to overcoming the thief of transgressing the precepts.
"The meaning of receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*) shall now be explained.
Why is it called 'receiving full ordination'?
Because a wise person, having received full ordination, does not transgress and achieves what they seek; therefore, it is called 'receiving [ordination]' (*upasaṃpad*)."
The ability to accomplish the meaning [of the precepts] is called "receiving full ordination" (upasaṃpadā).
For this reason, the accomplishment of all virtues is termed "receiving full ordination.
Furthermore, because one is able to maintain the precepts with single-minded devotion, it is called "receiving full ordination."
Because it can bring about the meaning of being a śramaṇa, it is called "receiving full ordination" (upasaṃpadā).
Because it can cause a person to achieve the dharma of purity of mind, it is called "receiving full ordination.
Because it can accomplish the dharma of quiescence (nirvāṇa), it is called "receiving full ordination."
Furthermore, because one accomplishes the dharmas of a bhikṣu, it is called "receiving full ordination" (upasaṃpadā).
Within this Vinaya, knowing, seeing, penetrating, understanding, touching, and realizing is what is meant by "receiving full ordination."
“There are five ways by which a bhikṣu may achieve full ordination; these are called ‘receiving ordination.
What are the five?
First, one becomes a bhikṣu through the ‘Come hither’ formula and immediately attains full ordination.”
Second, one obtains full ordination through three utterances;
third, receiving the precepts through the ritual of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) is called obtaining full ordination;
fourth, by the Buddha’s command permitting the reception of full ordination, one immediately obtains full ordination.
Fifth is the "superior full ordination" (upasaṃpadā).
Why is it called the superior full ordination?

During the time when the Buddha was in the world, there were those who did not receive the precepts but instead attained arhatship by listening to the Dharma directly from the Buddha; this is called the superior full ordination.
These are called the five ways of receiving full ordination for a bhikṣu.
A bhikṣuṇī also has five ways of receiving full ordination:
first, practicing according to the teacher’s instructions is called receiving full ordination;
Second, receiving full ordination through the formal procedure of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*);
third, receiving full ordination by sending a messenger before the assembly;
fourth, receiving full ordination through the "Come hither" formula (*ehi-bhikṣu*).
Fifth is the higher ordination (*upasaṃpadā*).
Being able to accomplish the non-commitment of all evils is called receiving the full precepts.
Furthermore, because one is able to discern right from wrong within the Vinaya Piṭaka and can practice with faith, it is called receiving the full precepts.
Furthermore, being able to accomplish the method for severing the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*) is called receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*).

Being able to eliminate applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) is also called receiving full ordination; being able to relinquish attachment to the meditative mind (*dhyāna-citta*) is also called receiving full ordination. Because one is able to relinquish suffering, pleasure, grief, and joy, it is called receiving full ordination; because one is able to transcend the four formless absorptions (*catasra ārūpya-samāpattayaḥ*), it is also called receiving full ordination; and being able to know the cessation of all marks (*nimitta*) is also called receiving full ordination.

Furthermore, receiving the three refuges and the five precepts is also called "receiving full ordination" (upasampadā); receiving the eightfold fasting precepts is also called "receiving full ordination"; receiving the ten śrāmaṇera precepts is also called "receiving full ordination"; and receiving the precepts in stages is likewise called "receiving full ordination."

Furthermore, one who can contemplate white karma is also said to have received full ordination; because they have accomplished the stage of the lineage (gotrabhūmi), they are called "one who has received full ordination.
What is meant by the "stage of the lineage"?

It refers to a person who, while listening to the Dharma from the Buddha, is unwearied in body and mind and achieves realization in every thought-moment; by virtue of this mind, they suddenly awaken on their own and attain the fruit of Srotāpanna.
The *srotāpanna* is the seed-nature (*gotra*) of wholesome dharmas.

Those in the four fruits and four stages of approach, the eighth stage, the stage of seeing the truths, the stage of thinning [defilements], the stage of freedom from desire, the stage of having completed what was to be done, and even the teacherless solitary realizers (*pratyekabuddha*), are all called "fully ordained" (*upasampanna*).
The accomplishment of the six perfections is also called receiving full ordination; skillful speech is also called receiving full ordination.
From receiving full ordination through wisdom up to receiving full ordination through skillful speech, all are termed receiving full ordination.
Furthermore, if one wishes to explain in detail which persons should receive full ordination:
if there are sons or daughters of good family who are free from obstacles and pure, they shall all be able to receive full ordination.
There are three kinds of obstacles:
the obstacle of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*), the obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*), and the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

For those who are pure, one permits them to leave the household life, shave their hair and beards, don the dharma robes, receive the three refuges and the ten precepts, and even proceed through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* to receive full ordination.

One should cause those who have gone forth to know that the four *pārājika* dharmas must not be transgressed; they should rely upon the four supports (*niśraya*) for as long as life lasts, and by practicing even the affairs of the holy life (*brahmacarya*), they shall attain the dharma of going forth, realize the fruits of the dharma, experience bliss, and achieve great merit.
Regarding other matters, one should consult the upādhyāya and ācārya;

the upādhyāya and ācārya should instruct one on what ought and ought not to be done according to the Vinaya, and furthermore, they should exhort one to practice all wholesome dharmas together with fellow students and colleagues, never acting in opposition to one another.
"Why do you grant full ordination?
It is because you desire that they may attain the bliss of the five supernatural powers, see suffering without fear, possess few desires and be content, and achieve the awakening of a Great Man.
What is meant by 'achieving the awakening of a Great Man'? "
Because he practices the Vinaya as the Buddha has received it, he is called "Awakened" (Buddha).
What is meant by "desire" (chanda)?
It is like the Buddha’s diligent and tireless exertion; therefore, it is called "desire."
Furthermore, "desire" (chanda) refers to clearly maintaining mindfulness before one, no different from the awakening of a Buddha; for this reason, it is called desire.
Why is it called "contact" (sparśa)?
It is called contact because one attains meditative concentration (samādhi).
Experiencing the wholesome and experiencing the unwholesome are also termed "contact" (sparśa).
What is meant by "realization" (sākṣātkriyā)?
It is termed realization because of non-negligence (apramāda).
To testify that one knows the meaning is like the awakening of a Buddha.
"In this context, what constitutes the full ordination of a 'Come-hither' (ehi-bhikṣu)?
It is, for example, the case of the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya."

At that time, while the World-Honored One was traveling in Vārāṇasī, the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya had seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, realized the Dharma, and deeply understood the nature of phenomena. He immediately rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in salutation, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
“I only pray that the Tathāgata will grant me permission to leave the household life and practice the holy life.
The World-Honored One said to him,
“Welcome, bhikṣu.”
"I authorize you to practice the holy life within my Dharma to bring an end to suffering.
Thereupon, Ājñāta-Kauṇḍinya immediately went forth and immediately attained full ordination.

When the Tathāgata had finished speaking, the Brahmin robes he was wearing, as well as his beard and hair, all fell away; the dharma robes of a śramaṇa appeared naturally upon his body, and with dignified and orderly deportment, he held an alms-bowl in his hand, appearing like one who had studied the Dharma for twenty years.
The Venerable Ābhijit, Vāgīśa, Mahānāman, and others were also like Ājñātakauṇḍinya.
There were four companions of Yaśoda;
and there were fifty companions of Vimarati, Pūrṇaka, Gavāmpati, and the youth Yaśas.
Māṭhara and his companions were also fifty;
Nārada, Māṇava, Bhadra, and Bhārgava with their companions were fifty;
and Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, Nadī-Kāśyapa, and Gayā-Kāśyapa had a following of one thousand.
Upatiṣya and Kolita were their leaders, with a retinue of two hundred and fifty followers.
All such as these were of noble and wealthy lineage, having originally been renunciants of non-Buddhist paths.
The Buddha has already appeared in the world, and the time for realization has arrived; all have come to the Buddha seeking to leave the household life.
At the very end, Subhadra and those like him—all such as these—are "Come-hither" (Svāgata) bhikṣus.
The fruits they have attained are all those of the final body of one beyond training (aśaikṣa). Why is this?
Because it is thus that the Tathāgata has spoken from his own divine mouth; others cannot attain them.
He asked:
"Why did the World-Honored One not bestow his supernatural power upon Pāra-ga, Upapāra-ga, Puṣkara-sārī, and Upapuṣkara-sārī, so that they might come forth and leave the household life?"
He replied:
"The intention is this: because Pāṭaliputra possesses karma that obstructs the Path, he cannot receive the 'Come, monk' (ehi-bhikṣu) ordination.
As for Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta, because he has already attained the state of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) in this very life, he cannot receive the 'Come, monk' ordination."
For this reason, although they were all in the presence of the Buddha, they did not receive the "Welcome, come forth" (ehi-bhikṣu) ordination.
Regarding the "three-fold verbal acceptance" (tri-vācika-upasampadā): at that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying, "I have attained liberation from the net of humans and devas."
"You shall all be liberated from this net.
At that time, the evil Māra heard these words of the Buddha and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"You will not attain liberation from the net of humans and devas, nor will the bhikṣus attain liberation."
The Buddha then replied with a verse:
"Worldly people experience the five desires through the sixth consciousness;
I have already abandoned all desires, O Evil Māra—you shall fall by yourself."
When the Evil Māra heard these words, he realized that the Buddha knew he had not yet abandoned desire; filled with shame, sorrow, and distress, he suddenly vanished of his own accord.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Go each of you in pairs to various regions to teach and transform others; do not go alone.
The bhikṣus then departed.
When the people of that land heard the bhikṣu preaching the Dharma, they all came to the Buddha.
Along the way, some who felt regret immediately turned back and returned home.
For this reason, the bhikṣus came and informed the World-Honored One.
The Buddha immediately instructed them to receive the precepts through the threefold formula from that person, and said to the bhikṣus:
"Each of you should return to your respective places."

If there is anyone in that region who seeks to go forth from the household life, you should shave off their hair and beard, instruct them to don the Dharma robes, and confer upon them the threefold refuge precepts:
"I take refuge in the Buddha, I take refuge in the Dharma, I take refuge in the Saṃgha."
"The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is my teacher.
This is the method for receiving the precepts through three utterances.
At that time, the bhikṣus gave rise to doubt:
"How is it that three utterances constitute both going forth and full ordination?
The Buddha explained to him:
"Taking refuge in the Buddha, taking refuge in the Dharma, and taking refuge in the Sangha constitute going forth."

Having completed the second taking of refuge in the Buddha, having completed the taking of refuge in the Dharma, and having completed the taking of refuge in the Saṃgha, this is itself the reception of full ordination (*upasampadā*).
For this reason, the renunciation of the household life and the attainment of full ordination are accomplished.
Someone else again gave rise to doubt:

"For what reason do upāsakas receive the three refuges, and why is it that for śrāmaṇeras and even those who take the eight precepts, they all receive them through the three utterances, yet they are not called 'having received full ordination'?"
The Buddha said:
"These two meanings are distinct.
An upāsaka is not merely one who abides in the Three Refuges; it is only when he further adds the Five Precepts that he is first entitled to be called an upāsaka."
The same applies to śrāmaṇeras and even those who have received the eight precepts.
As for "receiving full ordination through three utterances," this constitutes the entirety; nothing further is added, and thus it is called "receiving full ordination."
The reason why nothing further is added is that there are two kinds of taking the Three Refuges:

first, one takes the Three Refuges for the purpose of receiving the five precepts, the ten precepts, or the eight fast-day observances, and even for the purpose of receiving the two hundred and fifty precepts, one takes the Three Refuges.
The second is to directly receive the three refuges.
The reason for this is that at that time, the Buddha had not yet established the two hundred and fifty precepts, nor even the eight precepts of the fast.
For this reason, it is taught that one may receive full ordination by simply reciting the Three Refuges.

After the Buddha established the prohibition against receiving the precepts through the three-fold formula, even if the three-fold formula is recited, it does not constitute a valid accomplishment of the ordination.
The reason the Buddha later established the ordination through the three utterances was because of a certain sick bhikṣu; it was for this reason that he abolished the previous method.

At that time, Ājñātakauṇḍinya rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"How may we know how to receive the full ordination through the three refuges and the three utterances?
The Buddha told Kauṇḍinya:
"If a person seeks to go forth from the household life, they should shave off their hair and beard, and you should instruct them to speak as follows:"
"I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha for as long as life lasts. ...
[and so on] ... "I now go forth under the Buddha; the Bhagavān is my teacher."
The Buddha told Kauṇḍinya:
“The ordination by three utterances is as I have explained and understood.

When the Venerable Kauṇḍinya heard the Buddha’s teaching on ordination by three utterances, his mind was opened and his understanding attained; he then withdrew from his seat, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed.
The Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya traveled to the country of Vṛji, and proceeding from there, he arrived at Vaiśālī.

In Vaiśālī there were men from Vṛji; these sons of noble families from the two countries gathered together in one place: first was Kakkaṭa, second Kālaṅga, third Vikkaṭa, fourth Kaṭissaha, fifth Cāla, sixth Belaṭṭha, seventh Bhadda, eighth Subhadda, ninth Paṇḍuka, tenth Yasas, eleventh Tissaka, and twelfth Ariṭṭha.
All these people thought to themselves:
"Ajñāta-Kauṇḍinya has gone forth to practice the holy life within the Dharma of the Great Śramaṇa.
Since even one of such great wisdom and insight was able to follow and learn from him, there must surely be a sublime Dharma."
"Why do we not go forth under him to study the sublime Dharma?
Whatever he practices, we shall practice together.
Having thus deliberated, the sons of noble family went together to where Kauṇḍinya was, prostrated with their heads at his feet, and standing to one side, addressed the Venerable One, saying:
"Venerable Sir, we pray that you grant us permission to go forth within the Dharma of the Tathāgata and practice the holy life.
Ājñātakauṇḍinya then accepted their words, granted them the going-forth, and for them he recited the threefold formula for receiving the precepts.
Having received the precepts, they immediately followed one another to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Venerable Kauṇḍinya then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"These sons of noble family desire to leave the household life; since they have received the precepts through the threefold formula, have they obtained the precepts or not?"
The Buddha told Kauṇḍinya:
"These people have received the precepts through the threefold formula; they have fully accomplished them and have properly attained the complete precepts. Why is this?"

The Buddhas of the past also conferred ordination through these three utterances; the Buddhas of the future shall likewise confer ordination through these three utterances; and I, now in the present, do the same as they.
For this reason, there are three ways of receiving the precepts through speech.

As for the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal motion followed by three proclamations), why must one receive full ordination (*upasampadā*) through a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* performed in the presence [of the Sangha]?
The commentary states:
At that time, the Buddha was residing in Rājagṛha.
Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa and his disciples had already completed their renunciation.
There was a sick bhikṣu who had no one to provide for him; his illness having become critical, he passed away.

When the other bhikṣus saw that this bhikṣu had died of his severe illness, finding that first, there was no one to tend to him in his sickness, and second, he had no disciples—suffering thus because both were absent—they went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha then assembled the community of bhikṣus and said:
"From this day forward, the formal act of three statements (trivācika-karman) is abolished.
Within a community of ten monks, the formal act of fourfold announcement (jñapti-caturtha-karman) shall be permitted for the conferral of full ordination."
"In this manner, each and every precept for receiving the vows should be understood as explained in detail above.

At that time, there was a wicked bhikṣu who ordained a person for renunciation; the one who had been ordained immediately gave rise to doubt toward his teacher and went to inform the World-Honored One."
The World-Honored One asked,
"Did you have doubts before you had received the precepts?
He replied:
"No," [he replied].
The Buddha said,
"You have already received full ordination."

Furthermore, there was another person who sought a teacher to leave the household life and receive full ordination (*upasampadā*). Having received the full ordination, doubt arose in his mind: "Is my preceptor pure? Have I truly obtained the precepts?"
They went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One asked them:
"Did you know beforehand that your teacher was impure?"
The candidate for ordination replied, "I do not know.
He was asked again:
"Did you previously know that you had not received the precepts from an impure teacher?
He replied, "I did not know."
The Buddha said, "You have thus obtained full ordination.
Furthermore, there was another person who sought a teacher to go forth; the teacher immediately conferred full ordination upon him.
Later, a doubt arose in his mind, and he went to inform the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One asked him:
"Did you previously know that your teacher had violated the precepts?"
He replied, "I know.
He was asked again:
"Did you previously know that you had received the precepts from an impure teacher and thus failed to obtain them?
He replied, "I knew it."
He asked again:
"Did you previously know whether your teacher obtained the precepts at the time he received them?
He replied:
"I do not know," [he replied].
The Buddha said,
"You have already received full ordination."
"Furthermore, another person sought a teacher to go forth from the household life, and the teacher immediately conferred the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon him.
Later, doubt arose in his mind, and he went to inform the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One asked:"
"Did you previously know that you were receiving the precepts from a teacher who was not pure, and thus would not obtain the precepts?
He replied,
"I knew it beforehand."
He asked again:
"Did you previously know that you would not receive the precepts when receiving them from your teacher's teacher?
He replied:
"I know them.
The Buddha said,
"Though you know all three matters, you may not receive the precepts."
For this reason, it is called the "White Fourfold Karmavācanā.
What is meant by "receiving full ordination through a formal proclamation"?
It refers to that very time.

The Buddha was staying in the city of Śrāvastī, in the upper hall of the Viśākhā-mṛgāramātṛ Garden. He questioned the śrāmaṇera Sudāya on the meaning [of the teachings], and the śrāmaṇera explained the meaning.
Because his explanation accorded with what the Buddha had understood and was in harmony with the Tathāgata’s intent, the Buddha immediately told him:
"From this day forward, if you have any doubts or confusion, feel free to come and ask me."

"Furthermore, one obtains full ordination (*upasampadā*) simultaneously with the conferral of the precepts; therefore, it is called 'receiving full ordination through a formal injunction' (*ājñā-śrāvita-upasampadā*).
What is 'superior reception of full ordination' (*uttara-upasampadā*)?

It is as when there is a person who has exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*), yet before reaching twenty years of age, receives full ordination and subsequently develops doubt within himself regarding the status of a bhikṣu."
The bhikṣus living with him, knowing that he had conceived doubts, went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said to this bhikṣu whose outflows were exhausted:
"Do you count the years spent in the womb, including even the intercalary months; is it complete?"
He replied, "It is not full.
The Buddha then questioned the bhikṣus:
"Has this bhikṣu attained arhatship?
The bhikṣus replied to the Buddha,
"He has attained arhatship."
The Buddha said:
"This is the superior method of receiving full ordination.
He further declared:
"Those who receive the precepts later are permitted to count the years spent in the womb.
"What are the five ways in which a bhikṣuṇī receives full ordination?
Practicing according to the teacher’s instructions is called receiving full ordination through the teacher’s dharma (śāstrīya-upasampadā)."
At that time, the Buddha was staying in the Śākya Grove.
Then Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, together with five hundred Śākya women, came to where the Buddha was. Having arrived, she prostrated herself with her head at the Buddha’s feet and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"May we women, within the Buddha-dharma, obtain the going forth?
The Buddha said,
"I do not wish to permit the going forth of women."
Having heard these words, she lowered her head, wept tears, and departed.
Later, when the World-Honored One traveled from the Śākya Grove toward the Jetavana Monastery in Śrāvastī, Gautamī and five hundred women heard that the Buddha was heading for the Jetavana Monastery.

Their hearts were filled with grief and distress as they lamented that they themselves were not included among the ranks of the Buddha’s disciples. Each shaved their heads, donned the dharma robes, and followed behind the Buddha.
Arriving at the Jetavana Monastery, they stood outside and saw the Venerable Ānanda.
Ānanda immediately asked the mother and the women:
"Upāsikās, why have you shaved your hair and put on the Dharma robes yourselves, appearing so haggard and unhappy?"
The mother and the women immediately replied:
"The reason we are unhappy is simply that the World-Honored One does not permit women to go forth; for this reason, we have such sorrowful countenances."
Ānanda said, "Wait a moment.
I shall inform the World-Honored One."
Ānanda immediately entered and addressed the World-Honored One:
"These upāsikās seek to leave the household life.
I pray that the World-Honored One will grant them permission."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The reason I do not permit women to leave the household life is that, just as in a worldly family where there are few men and many women, the family estate will surely go to ruin."
"In the Dharma of those who have left the household life, if there are women, they will surely cause the True Dharma to degenerate and it will not abide for long.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"Can women, within the Buddha’s Dharma, practice the holy life and attain the four fruits?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If one can cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya) with a resolve that does not regress, it may indeed be attained.
Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"May the World-Honored One grant permission for women to follow after the Buddha-Dharma.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If women are able to practice the Eight Rules of Respect, they shall be permitted to leave the household life; if they cannot, they shall not be permitted to enter the Path."

The reason for establishing the Eight Rules of Respect for women is like a person who wishes to cross water and first constructs a bridge or boat; later, even when great floods arise, they will certainly be able to cross.
"The Eight Rules of Respect are likewise; they were established merely because I feared that in the future the True Dharma would be destroyed.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Now that you have requested ordination for women, in the future the True Dharma of my five hundred-year period shall be diminished."

Upon hearing these words, Ānanda was filled with sorrow and distress; he immediately went outside and asked the upāsikās, "Can you all faithfully practice the Eight Rules of Respect that the Buddha has taught?"
Upon hearing these words, the women felt joy within their hearts and immediately requested Ānanda to return and inform the World-Honored One:
"Today we have received the Dharma bestowed by the World-Honored One; we shall practice it accordingly."
It is as if there were a person who has finished bathing in fragrant water and adorning themselves, and another person comes along to place a flower garland upon their head;
we today are just like this.
Ānanda reported these words to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"These individuals have already received full ordination."
This is called receiving full ordination through the teacher’s instruction (*ācārya-śāsana-upasampadā*).
Regarding receiving full ordination through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, it is as explained in the aforementioned *Bhikṣu-vyādhi-sūtra*.
Regarding receiving full ordination by sending a messenger, it is also as explained in the *Bhikṣuṇī-sūtra*.
"What is meant by 'the full ordination of a bhikṣuṇī through the words "Welcome, come" (ehi-bhikṣuṇī)?
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Śrāvastī.
The woman Mātaṅgī came to where the Buddha was, prostrated herself with her head at the ground to pay homage at the feet of the World-Honored One, and withdrew to sit to one side."
The Buddha then preached the Dharma for him.
He profoundly realized the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and attained the fruit of Srotāpanna; he then requested the Buddha’s permission to leave the household life.
The World-Honored One told him:
"I permit you to practice the holy life (brahmacarya) within my Dharma to bring an end to all suffering.

As soon as the Buddha had finished speaking, his hair fell away of its own accord; the Dharma robes and alms bowl suddenly appeared upon his person, and his dignified deportment was as orderly as that of one who had long been ordained in the Dharma.
Therefore, this is called "receiving full ordination by being welcomed.

Regarding "superior reception of full ordination": one who has exhausted all outflows (āsrava) and attained arhatship is so named because, like the aforementioned śrāmaṇeras, although they have not yet reached twenty years of age, they have nonetheless attained arhatship; thus it is called "superior reception of full ordination."
This bhikṣuṇī was also like this; this is called "receiving full ordination through the excellence of the Dharma.
Thus concludes the five ways of receiving full ordination for bhikṣuṇīs.

Regarding "receiving full ordination through the excellence of the Dharma": at that time, in the city of Rājagṛha, there was a brāhmaṇa named Nikumbha, whose wealth, treasures, and precious jewels were immeasurable, numbering in the hundreds of millions.
In this brahmin family, a son was born named Vipaśyan.
His parents were of pure lineage; he mastered all the scriptures of the brahmins without exception, and he was even able to penetrate the marks of a great man.
After the death of his father, this youth Vipaśyan had ninety-six *hu* of broken gold in his house, eighty billion *leṣa* of coins, and one hundred thousand *leṣa*.
He possessed a thousand villages of servants, slaves, and laborers.
His wife was named Bhadrā; her beauty was so extraordinary that she had no peer in the world. Therefore, he was able to sever his affection, cut off his greed, and abandon her to depart.
He silently formed this thought:
"If there were any true Arhats in the world, I would go forth under them and enter the forest of ascetic seers to cultivate the holy life."

Having formed this thought, he was thus able to sever his affection, cut off his craving, and depart from them. He went to the forest of ascetic seers and for twelve years practiced the holy life (*brahmacarya*), subsisting on vegetables and fruits and drinking from clear springs; he attained the various meditative states (*dhyāna*) and accomplished the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
At that time, the World-Honored One appeared in the world and, at the Deer Park, first turned the Wheel of Dharma; the Saṃgha was already established.

He was accompanied by a great assembly of one thousand bhikṣus, all of whom were venerable elders esteemed by the land, their faculties serene, and who had all attained liberation through the exhaustion of outflows.
The World-Honored One, traveling together with the bhikṣus from place to place, arrived at the kingdom of Magadha; he entered the Yaṣṭīvana grove and stayed beneath the king of trees, the Nyagrodha.

At that time, the World-Honored One surveyed the world with his Buddha-eye, [considering]: "Which beings, born into this world, have few afflictions and possess great supernormal power, such that they are capable of hearing and receiving the Dharma I teach?"
When the Tathāgata saw the youth Bīpālaya in the Uḍra forest, having seen him, he immediately formed this thought:
"This person is capable of receiving my True Dharma."

At that time, the World-Honored One, desiring to deliver the youth Vipaśyan, set out from the kingdom of Magadha with a thousand bhikṣus for the Many-Sons Stūpa; having arrived, he stayed there beneath a tree.
One day, within this grove, by the power of the Buddha’s spiritual authority, the light shone forth so that the trees blazed with brilliance and all became intensely bright.
It was like the autumn moon when the sun is free from the veil of clouds; the radiance of the Tathāgata was likewise so.
After twelve years had passed, this youth spontaneously conceived the desire to go to the Many-Sons Stūpa; traversing perilous mountains, valleys, and forests, he arrived at the Many-Sons Stūpa.
Having arrived, he saw that the radiance within this grove was exceptionally sublime and transcended all in the world; silently, he thought to himself:
"There must be various devas, Śakra, Brahmā, powerful ṛṣis, lion kings, and the like here; for this reason, this grove possesses such extraordinary auspicious signs."
The youth Bīpāraya proceeded forward by degrees; seeing that the footprints of the Tathāgata were clearly marked with the complete thousand-spoked wheel sign, he followed those tracks as he went on.

From afar he beheld the Tathāgata, whose faculties were clear and pure, whose countenance was extraordinary and endowed with all the marks of excellence, sitting in solemn stillness. At that moment, the hair on the youth’s body stood on end and faith arose within him; he thought silently to himself:
"This is exactly what I envisioned in my heart when I first left the household life."
The devas then proclaimed once more, saying:
"Do not harbor any doubt.
Upon seeing the bhikṣus again sitting in meditation with their minds focused, the boy conceived this thought:
"Finally, that which I have long sought, I now behold.
He went straight forward to the Buddha; having arrived, he prostrated himself with his head to the ground, rubbed the Buddha’s feet with both hands, and kissed them, saying to himself:
"My surname is Kāśyapa and my given name is Bīparaya-kumāra."
Thus he spoke three times.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"If there is one whose afflictions, fetters, and outflows are not yet exhausted, who is neither omniscient nor a teacher of men, yet accepts the prostrations of a person who has attained the Dharma of goodness, his head shall split into seven pieces."

"I am now truly one whose afflictions, fetters, and outflows are exhausted; I am the field of merit for all people; I am the one who has compassion for sentient beings, and I am also the All-Knowing One. For these reasons, I accept this prostration from the youth."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the youth, saying:
"You have now fully completed your offerings and perfected your faith; you may withdraw and sit to one side.
The youth, having received these instructions, prostrated at the Buddha's feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One skillfully expounded the various dharmas to the boy through many causes and conditions, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening him.
The boy immediately awakened to the Dharma and attained the Way, realizing the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
He immediately rose from his seat, joined his palms in salutation, and stepped forward to address the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, you are my teacher; I am your śrāvaka disciple.
The Buddha then spoke these words to the youth:
"One should cultivate and practice the four foundations of mindfulness;
this should be expanded upon in detail, up to and including the eightfold noble path.
The Buddha then said to the youth:

"When you enter the villages of the sons of good family, let your mind be free from attachment; just as the moon illuminates the world without being stained by it, so too should your mind be free from attachment when you enter the various villages."
Just as a bee gathers nectar from flowers, so too should you enter the various villages.
Young man!
Just as in the parable of the Candra youth, you should abandon the pride of lineage, wealth, and virtue, and enter the villages with humility.

Just as a great bull among a herd of cattle, relying on the sharpness of his horns, looks down upon the others, yet later, when his horns are cut off, his pride completely subsides; so too should it be with you when entering a village, remaining free from any defiled attachment.
The Buddha told the youth:
"Do not form conceptual attachments toward the six internal sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), for they bind and fetter the mind.

It is the same for the six external sense bases and even the six internal consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*). One should likewise not form conceptual attachments toward the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), and so on up to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*)."
The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, as well as the six external sense objects, should likewise not grasp at perceptions through the mental application of vitarka and vicāra;
they should be like drops of water in the air, following one another without any obstruction.
Observing the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, the five aggregates, and so forth, one does not grasp at them; that the mind is likewise free from obstruction is also thus.
Son of good family, you should train yourself in this manner.
The youth addressed the Buddha, saying,
"I shall follow the World-Honored One’s instruction.
At that time, having heard the Buddha, the World-Honored One, expound the Dharma through various analogies, the youth immediately attained awakening and understanding.
Having received the Dharma, the youth rose from his seat, circumambulated the Buddha three times, paid homage to him, and departed.

Arriving at the foot of a tree, he settled his body in upright posture and remained focused on the Dharma the Buddha had taught for seven days and seven nights. On the morning of the eighth day, all his taints were exhausted; he attained the three knowledges, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations, realizing the fruit of Arhatship.

Having attained the fruit of arhatship, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself with his head at the ground to pay homage to the Buddha, and sat down to one side. He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

Having previously heard the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, from the seventh day and night until the morning of the eighth day, my outflows were exhausted, my mind attained liberation, and I acquired the three knowledges and six supernormal powers, realizing the fruit of Arhatship.
For example, suppose someone were to say:
"There is an elephant seven cubits high, and there is a tree six and a half cubits high.
To claim that this tree could provide shade for that elephant is impossible.

"If there were anyone who had attained the fruit of Arhatship, possessing the three knowledges, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations, such that they could surpass me—that is impossible.
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa:
"Excellent, excellent!"
Kāśyapa! It is as you have said.
Through the various metaphors within the Dharma I have taught, you have profoundly realized non-arising and attained the fruit of arhatship.
This is precisely the full ordination (*upasampadā*).
At that time, for this reason, the World-Honored One assembled the bhikṣus and addressed them, saying:
"I have previously taught this Dharma to Kāśyapa; you all should now practice it."
The Buddha again addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I permit you to receive full ordination based upon established roots of goodness.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"All Buddhas of the past and all Buddhas of the future have received full ordination by establishing roots of goodness; I now do likewise.
This is called receiving full ordination by establishing roots of goodness.
At that time, the Venerable Kāśyapa rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in homage to the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Within the Dharma of the Tathāgata, in what dharmas do we abide?
What dharmas do we cultivate?
And what are the distinctions among those who practice the Dharma?
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent, Kāśyapa!"
Your inquiry is most excellent, emerging like a spring that can never be exhausted.
Regarding what you have asked concerning abiding, cultivation, and even their distinctions, your words and reasoning are unimpeded.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"The four noble lineages are the place of abiding; the twelve dhūtas are called the sphere of practice; and the exhaustion of all outflows is called the distinction."
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The four noble lineages, the twelve dhūtas, and even the liberation through the exhaustion of outflows—these I shall receive upon my head and practice accordingly.”
Suppose a householder or a householder’s son bathes in scented water, adorns himself with superior garments, and another person comes and ties a beautiful flower garland upon his head.
"We, too, shall do likewise, receiving upon our heads the Dharma thus commanded by the Tathāgata.
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa,
"How is it that you, moreover, abide within the four noble lineages?"
Kāśyapa said to the Buddha:
"First, one should regard whatever rag-robes (pāṃsukūla) one has previously obtained as sufficient;
second, upon seeing the rag-robes worn by others, one should likewise praise them."
Third, seeing for oneself that one wears rag-robes, one does not rely on this to disparage others;

fourth, regarding food and drink, even medicinal decoctions for illness and emaciation, one considers oneself satisfied with whatever is obtained and likewise does not rely on this to disparage others.
Furthermore, one does not give rise to this thought toward others:
"That person is superior to me," or "That person is inferior to me.
Nor does one think or say:
"He resembles me; this person does not resemble me.
Furthermore, one does not give rise to the thought:
"This person disparages me; that person does not disparage me."
Furthermore, he does not think:
"That person is superior to me; that person is not superior to me.
Worldly people all act contrary to what was described above, whereas I am as described above.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Kāśyapa, those who dwell in the four noble lineages should train in this manner."
"What, then, is the practice of the twelve dhūtas?
Kāśyapa replied to the Buddha:
"First, one should always personally dwell in secluded and quiet places, and one should also praise such secluded and quiet places."
Second, begging for food;
third, wearing rag-robes;
fourth, if anger arises, ceasing to eat until it has been extinguished, and only then eating.
Fifth, eating in a single sitting;
sixth, receiving food only once at a time;
seventh, constantly practicing the dwelling among tombs.
Eighth, sitting in the open air;
ninth, sitting at the foot of a tree;
tenth, always sitting and never lying down.
Eleventh, accepting bedding and seating as they are obtained;
twelfth, maintaining only the three robes.

Such dharmas as these should all be praised; furthermore, one should not rely on them to disparage others, but rather cultivate few desires, be content with one's requisites, and extensively demonstrate these requisites to others.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Excellent, excellent!
It is just as you have said; one who practices the twelve dhūtas should indeed act in this way."
The Buddha again addressed Kāśyapa:
"You may accompany me as I inspect the forests and thickets.
Kāśyapa replied:
"I obey the World-Honored One's command.
When the Buddha rose and departed, Kāśyapa immediately took his sitting mat, placed it upon his shoulder, and followed behind the World-Honored One.
Kāśyapa followed the Buddha like a lion cub following its great lion.
At that time, the World-Honored One proceeded along the road until he reached the foot of a tree, where he addressed Kāśyapa, saying:
"You should prepare a seat for me here beneath this tree."
Kāśyapa immediately followed the instructions, folding his saṃghāṭī robe into four layers and spreading it out as a seat.
The Tathāgata took his seat, and Kāśyapa prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.
The World-Honored One pressed down on the seat with his right hand and addressed Kāśyapa, saying:
"This seat is very soft.
Kāśyapa said,
"World-Honored One!..."
"This seat is truly soft and supple.

This robe was the one worn by my disciple when he first went forth; when it was new, its value was equal to the entire kingdom of Kāśī, but now its price has depreciated to half the kingdom. I only pray that the Tathāgata will accept this robe."
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Out of compassion for you, I have accepted this robe.
What do you intend to receive and uphold?"
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I shall seek out and accept the very lowest of the discarded *kāśika* grass rags.
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa:
“Excellent, excellent!
You who accept and maintain the kāśika-grass and refuse-rags (pāṃsukūla) will bring great benefit and great peace.

At that time, the World-Honored One, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, traveled through the kingdom of Magadha and sat beneath a well-established king of mango trees (mango-king) in a grove.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus were conversing together in a quiet room:

"Kāśyapa is not like Ājñātakauṇḍinya and the others who received full ordination through the 'Come, monk' formula; nor is he like the Bhikṣu Vatsagotra of Vaiśālī who received full ordination through the three statements; nor is he like the Bhikṣu Bharadvāja who received full ordination through the formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*. He has not received full ordination."
"How can one perform the *poṣadha* ritual together with the bhikṣus?
At that time, while the World-Honored One was beneath a tree, he heard with his divine ear the discussion taking place among the bhikṣus in a secluded place.
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa,
"Fetch me some water.
Kāśyapa immediately took his bowl and went toward the pond to fetch water.
When the group of six bhikṣus saw Kāśyapa approaching, they immediately addressed him, saying:

"You did not receive the full ordination through the 'Welcome' (ehi-bhikṣu) formula like the five men, Kauṇḍinya and the others; nor did you receive it through the 'Three Statements' (tri-vākya) like the son of Viśālā; nor did you receive it through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* like Upasena."
"You have not received full ordination; how then can you participate in the poṣadha and karmavācanā together with the bhikṣus?
Kāśyapa then replied to the bhikṣus, saying:
"The World-Honored One has established for me, at the Many-Sons Stūpa, the reception of full ordination through the 'Superiority of the Good Dharma' (Kuśaladharmottara)."
Having spoken these words, he immediately took water and went to where the Buddha was, offering the bowl of water to the Buddha.
After the Buddha had drunk, he gave the remainder to Kāśyapa.
Having received the water, Kāśyapa adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:
The group of six bhikṣus saw him and said to him:
"You did not receive full ordination by the 'Welcome' formula, nor did you receive it by the 'Threefold Declaration,' nor did you receive it by the formal ritual of *karmavācanā*."
"How may I participate in the communal legal affairs of the Saṃgha?
The disciple replied to the bhikṣus:
"The World-Honored One established me at the Bahuputraka Stūpa for the purpose of receiving full ordination (upasaṃpadā) through the *śrāmaṇeropasaṃpadā*."
"You all should go to the Buddha to inquire whether you may receive [the precepts] or not;
you should accept and practice them according to what the Buddha teaches.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to sever the future bhikṣus' hearts of slander and disparagement, addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Go to the city of Rājagṛha; when all the bhikṣus in that city have gathered together in the great saṃghārāma.
Ānanda immediately accepted the instruction and departed. Upon arriving there, he gathered all the bhikṣus in the great saṃghārāma.
Once the assembly of monks had gathered, they came and informed the Buddha:
"The Sangha has finished assembling;
World-Honored One, you yourself should know the proper time."
At that time, the World-Honored One proceeded to the monastery and, having settled himself calmly upon his seat, lay down on his right side like a royal elephant, gazing intently at Kāśyapa.
Then Kāśyapa rose from his seat, knelt with his right knee on the ground, bowed his head to the Buddha’s feet in salutation, and, kneeling with palms joined, addressed the World-Honored One:

"In my former life as a householder, after my father passed away, I possessed ninety-six measures of fine gold and eighty billion *leṣas* of gold coins; my wife was of such exquisite beauty that she was peerless in the world."
He reflected within himself:
"If there be any true Arhat, I shall receive ordination under him.
Having thus reflected, he immediately renounced his attachments, severed his cravings, and left the household life to seek the Way.
"If there is anyone in the world who is a teacher to disciples, it is only the Buddha.
How can the group of six slanderously claim that he did not receive full ordination?
He spoke further again:
"If there were any extraordinary forms or wondrous treasures in the world, they would not exist apart from what I already possess.
Since I have long since abandoned the craving for wealth and the gazing upon forms, how can I now be subject to such slander?"
Since going forth, he has remained in that forest for twelve years, attaining the four dhyānas and even the five supernormal powers, without a single thought of distraction arising before him.
Why is this? Because one perceives that these conditioned phenomena of birth and death are to be feared.
Furthermore, it says:
"While my father was alive, he provided me with two billion gold coins to take a wife.
Three times each day, I changed my garments according to the occasion, never lacking for anything.
Even regarding medical treatment for illness and emaciation, as well as the eight worldly dharmas, I never gave them a thought, relying instead on the nobility of our lineage."
"Although they took wives, each practiced the holy life (brahmacarya) without ever violating it.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
Because I gave food as an offering to a pratyekabuddha in a past life, from that time onward I have always delighted in leaving the household life to seek nirvāṇa and liberation.
The Buddha knows this for himself through his own realization.
For what reason?
Because in my heart I am constantly terrified of transmigrating through the five destinies and undergoing birth and death.
World-Honored One!
When I first arrived at the Bahuputraka Caitya Grove and beheld the Tathāgata, this thought immediately arose within me:
"This is indeed the teacher I sought when I first went forth into homelessness."
Why is this? Because the faith I have generated toward the Buddhas of the past is equal and no different from the faith I now generate upon seeing the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"If anyone whose afflictions, fetters, and outflows are not yet exhausted—who is neither omniscient nor a teacher of men—should receive this prostration of accomplishment from a Great Being, their head shall split into seven pieces."

I have indeed forever severed the afflictions, delusions, entanglements, and the dark obstructions of ignorance; I know all dharmas and act as a teacher for others. For this reason, I accept the prostrations of this person.
At that time, Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Although the bhikṣus slander me in this way, I feel no grief or distress.
And although the World-Honored One now praises my virtues in various ways, I do not feel any joy.”
Why is this? Because I observe that both the one who praises and the object of praise are empty of intrinsic nature. Why is this so?
Because I have attained the contemplation of the emptiness of all phenomena— being devoid of self and person—

from the time the World-Honored One taught me the parables of the moonlight and the water droplets at the Many-Sons Stūpa until now, my mind has been in continuous succession, constantly mindful of this Dharma and harboring no other thoughts.
The reason for this is that I constantly bind my mind to wholesome dharmas and do not follow after other thoughts.
World-Honored One!

Before I had seen the Buddha, for twelve years I constantly contemplated earth, water, fire, and wind, as well as the three realms, regarding them all as empty; how much less, on this day, having encountered the World-Honored One’s preaching of the Dharma, could I have any remaining thoughts?
Furthermore, there is no longer any seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing across the three periods of time; how could one harbor divergent thoughts regarding the six classes of beings?

Since the World-Honored One taught me the four noble lineages, I have no longer grasped at the perceptions of taste or touch; I view this aggregate-body as being like four venomous snakes, and while performing the four modes of deportment, my mind does not dwell together with them.
Why is this so? Because for a long time I have known that these are the root of all calamities.
Observing these five aggregates as arising and ceasing moment by moment, they are like five bandits with drawn swords.

One contemplates the arising and passing away of form, and the arising and passing away of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; one contemplates the six sense bases as an empty village with five bandits with drawn swords, and one contemplates non-self.
“World-Honored One!
When I contemplate this body, it is like a vessel filled with impurities that leak out from within; this is the contemplation of the body as the body, World-Honored One.”
I contemplate this mind as impermanent and swift, like a wild horse or a rushing wind; I observe the mind with the observation of the mind.
I contemplate feeling as suffering, arising and ceasing in succession like flowing water or the flame of a lamp; I observe feeling with the observation of feeling.
"I contemplate that phenomena are without self and are dependent upon various causes and conditions; this is the contemplation of phenomena according to phenomena.
World-Honored One!
Within the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, there is no error, and I shall receive it upon my head and practice it accordingly."
"World-Honored One!
At that time, among the twelve hundred and fifty monks in the city of Rājagṛha, I distributed voting tallies and proclaimed:
'Whoever is an Arhat may take this tally.'"
At that time, I immediately drew this tally.
Had I not encountered the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world, I would have attained the state of a Pratyekabuddha and entered nirvāṇa.
The reason for this is that I have long planted roots of goodness under various Buddhas.
At that time, while I was in the Piṇḍola Cave, I suddenly encountered a slight ailment, and the World-Honored One came specifically to inquire after my illness.
However, as the cave was small and my body large, I immediately used my hand to lift this cave and enlarge it.
The World-Honored One immediately entered and preached the Dharma of suffering and emptiness for me.

At that time, while I was in the Piṇḍola Cave absorbed in the Fire-Light Samādhi, Śakra and Brahmā came to pay homage at my feet; simultaneously, another person arrived brandishing a sword, intending to harm me.
"Having emerged from meditative concentration, I observe that these two persons are equal and without difference.
He further said:
"Whether I am among the great assembly or in a private chamber, my deportment is no different."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In your deportment and movements, you should be like Kāśyapa.
Although I heard these words, I was not pleased.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"Last night while I was walking in meditation, and at midday when I went begging for alms, the thought arose in my mind:
'The night is short and midday is drawing near.'"

I raised my eyes upward and saw that both the sun and the moon stood still and did not move; the various devas transformed themselves into human forms, surrounding me from front and back to make offerings to me.
At that time, amidst all these events, I felt no sense of joy or wonder whatsoever.
In the city of Rājagṛha, I was gathered together with one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus at one place, where we cast lots and proclaimed:
"After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, who will be able to uphold the Buddha-dharma?"
At that time, I immediately drew this tally.
The reason for doing so was that, within the debate, my eloquence was such that no one could restrain me; therefore, I drew the tally.
If someone were to ask correctly,
"Among those who indulge in the five desires, who is not deeply stained by them?
one should say, "It is I."
Why is this? Because they have attained excellent liberation within the three realms of existence.
If someone were to ask:
"Regarding the faculties, powers, factors of awakening, and the path—who is able to achieve them?
In this regard, I can let out a lion’s roar. Why is that?
Regarding all suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path leading to its transcendence, as well as the gratification and the peril therein, he sees them as they truly are.
He regards sensual desire as a pit of fire, even likening it to a trident; such is the danger and affliction of sensual desire.
I am free from craving and attachment, which have been forever severed.
My mind is directed toward liberation and nirvana, as swift as water cascading down a mountain peak; I abandon all that is tainted (āsrava) as one discards snot and spittle.

I have extensively cultivated the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; I enter and emerge with mastery from the eight liberations; and I am unimpeded and sovereign in my supernormal powers.
"Blessed One!
I am able to fully comprehend all the various minds of sentient beings, whether they are with outflows or without outflows; I know the immeasurable past lives of sentient beings."
“World-Honored One!
With the divine eye, which surpasses that of humans, I see beings being born there and dying here; I see them all.
I have exhausted all outflows (āsravas), and my mind has attained liberation through wisdom; I have attained liberation through insight.”
Kāśyapa said: "O bhikṣus and the rest of you, the group of six great virtuous ones!
Do not say that I am praising my own virtues."
He has already relinquished all merits, let alone other false and nominal things.
The reason he speaks thus is that he desires to benefit all sentient beings throughout the long night of saṃsāra.
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa:
"Excellent, excellent, Kāśyapa!"
Regarding the benefit you have brought about, with the single exception of myself, none of the other śrāvakas are capable of equaling it.
Out of compassion for the delusion of the group of six, you should grant them repentance.
At that time, Upāli rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in homage to the Buddha, and asked the World-Honored One:
"Do all Buddhas establish the full ordination by means of the formal procedure for receiving the precepts?"
The Buddha told Upāli:
"It is not the case that all Buddhas establish it.
The reason it is established is solely for the sake of establishing it for sentient beings in the five turbidities."

The five turbidities are: the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*), the turbidity of life (*āyuṣ-kaṣāya*), the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*), the turbidity of karma (*karma-kaṣāya*), and the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).
The Buddhas of the past and future were likewise thus.
"In this present age of the five turbidities and evil world, I have therefore established this rule.
Upāli asked the Buddha:
"In how many places may one establish the higher ordination (*upasaṃpadā*) so that the precepts of the superior Dharma are fulfilled?"
The Buddha told Upāli:
"Five factors must be fulfilled. What are these five?"
First, those in their final existence;
second, those from the Vāhīka country to the Bāluka country who have previously attained the fruit of stream-entry;
third, those following Sudāyin whose outflows are exhausted and whose minds have attained liberation.
The fourth was Nanda the cowherd;
the fifth is the present Kāśyapa.
It was to these that the Tathāgata conferred full ordination, and not to any other śrāvakas.
“Upāli! These five points establish the higher ordination through the excellence of the wholesome dharmas, whereby it becomes fulfilled.
“World-Honored One!”
"In how many places is the full ordination received through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* fulfilled?
The Buddha said,
"It is fulfilled in five places."
First, the preceptor (upādhyāya) must act in accordance with the Dharma;
second, the two ācāryas must act in accordance with the Dharma;
third, the seven-membered Saṃgha must be pure.
Fourth is the accomplishment of the *karmavācanā*;
fifth is the harmony of the Saṃgha and the granting of consent (*chanda*). Upāli!
If these five requirements are not fulfilled, it is not called "complete.

Within this context, there are four ways of receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), ranging from the "Come, Bhikṣu" (*ehi bhikṣu*) formula up to the formal motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).
“Bhikṣuṇīs also have four ways of receiving full ordination:
first, such as the case of the woman Maṅgura;
second, the method of the Teacher.”
Third is the "ordination by dispatching a messenger" (*dūta-upasampadā*);
fourth is the "ordination by *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.

The "ordination by imperial decree" (*ājñā-upasampadā*) and the "higher ordination" (*uttara-upasampadā*)—both of these are designated by the name "higher ordination established through the wholesome dharma" (*kuśala-dharma-vyavasthāpita-uttara-upasampadā*). The "higher ordination for bhikṣuṇīs" is likewise designated by the name "higher ordination established through the wholesome dharma."
This is called receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*).
One who does not receive it differs from the aforementioned reception of full ordination and is thus termed "one who has not received full ordination.
If a Śrāvaka bestows the precepts upon another by means of the "Come, O Bhikṣu" formula (*ehi-bhikṣu*), the reception of full ordination is not accomplished.
If one bestows the precepts upon another using only three utterances, that person may not receive full ordination.
If the proclamation of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal motion followed by three proclamations) is not accomplished, that person may not receive full ordination.
Furthermore, from an illegal Saṃgha, one may not receive full ordination.
What is called the "unlawful Saṃgha"?

Those who do not proceed to the ordination platform; those who perform the formal motion (*jñapti*) after the *karmavācanā*; and those who further perform other *karmas*—all such are called the unlawful Saṃgha.
If one receives full ordination apart from the Buddha, apart from the Dharma, and apart from the Vinaya, one does not obtain full ordination.
If one is less than twenty years of age, one may not receive full ordination; even if one does receive it, one does not obtain full ordination.
"If there is no preceptor, or if there are two preceptors, or three, or even many acting as preceptors, one may not receive full ordination.
'If the candidate for ordination or the preceptor remains hidden and does not appear, one may also not receive full ordination.'"
Even if the number of monks in the assembly reaches ten, if one is hidden and not present, or if the candidate for ordination is not present, the full ordination (upasampadā) cannot be conferred.
Furthermore, if no great boundary (mahā-sīmā) is established outside, but only a small boundary (kṣudra-sīmā) is established, the full ordination also cannot be conferred.

If the preceptor, the assembly of monks, and the candidate for ordination are situated on different sides of the boundary—either inside or outside—they likewise cannot confer full ordination (*upasampadā*).
There are thirteen types of persons who may not act as a preceptor or receive full ordination:

those who, while living as householders, have received the *upāsaka* (lay follower) precepts and have violated even one; those who have received the eightfold fast (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*) and violated one; or those who have received the ten precepts of a *śrāmaṇera* (novice) and violated one. Such individuals, even if they later leave the household life, will not obtain the precepts, nor may they act as a preceptor.
Second, if one has violated the pure conduct of a bhikṣuṇī, whether as a renunciant or a layperson, one may not serve as an upādhyāya.

Third, if for the sake of food or clothing, one shaves one's head, dons the kāṣāya, and falsely joins the Saṃgha to participate in the communal religious rites, such a person likewise may not serve as an upādhyāya.

Fourth, if there is a person from among the non-Buddhists who has gone forth within the Buddha-dharma, but later grows weary of the path and, without relinquishing the precepts, departs to return from among the non-Buddhists with the desire to remain within the Dharma—the Buddha does not permit such a person to be among the Saṃgha, nor may they act as an upādhyāya.
Fifth, a eunuch may not serve as an upādhyāya.
Sixth, one who has killed his father.
Seventh, one who has killed his mother.
Eighth, shedding the blood of a Buddha;
ninth, killing a true person, an Arhat;
tenth, causing a schism in the Saṃgha.
Eleventh, those who are non-humans (*amanuṣya*) that have transformed themselves into human form are called "non-humans.
Twelfth, those from the animal realm (*tiryagyoni*) that have transformed themselves into human form.
Thirteenth, those with dual sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*).
These thirteen types of persons are unfit to serve as preceptors. Why is this?
Because such individuals lack the precepts.
*Mātṛkā-vinaya* (The Vinaya-mother Sūtra), Fascicle One.
*Mātṛkā-vinaya*, Fascicle Two.
Translator’s name lost; now appended to the Qin Records.
Regarding the ordination of nuns through the dispatch of a messenger: during the Buddha’s lifetime, only one woman was permitted to receive it this way.

The reason she was permitted was that her appearance was so exceptionally outstanding that she had no peer in the world; he feared that if she were to go in person, wicked men might abduct her. For this reason, the Buddha granted permission.

In the present age, if there are such individuals as these, one may send a messenger to receive the precepts; for all others, it is essential that they be present in person to obtain full ordination, and it cannot be obtained if they are not present.

"Among those who receive full ordination through the *śāstṛ-dharma* (the teacher’s method), with the exception of the five hundred women headed by Gautamī, none of the others may receive it through the teacher’s method.

Among those who receive the 'superior' full ordination (*ūrdhva-saṃpādaka*), with the exception of the Venerable Mahākāśyapa Sautye, none of the others may establish the superior ordination of wholesome dharmas."
"If a man or woman is of a well-disciplined nature and possesses clear wisdom, and is free from obstacles, they may receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Furthermore, there are three types of persons who cannot receive full ordination:
first, those who do not state their own name;"
Second, not addressing the preceptor by name;
third, not requesting the precepts.
These three types of persons may not receive full ordination.
Contrary to this, one may obtain full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Furthermore, there are five types of persons who may receive full ordination:
first, one who has attained the status of a man (*puruṣa*);...
Second, not being in debt;
third, not being a slave to another person;
fourth, having reached the age of twenty.
There are five types of parents who permit their children to leave the household life;
these five kinds of persons may receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Furthermore, there are five locations where the reception of the precepts through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal motion followed by three proclamations) is perfected.
What are the five?
First, the upādhyāya;
second, the ācārya.
Third, the community of monks is complete;
fourth, their natures are harmonious and compliant;
fifth, their faculties are fully developed and free from all obstacles.
This is called the fulfillment of receiving the precepts through five conditions;
if one is contrary to these five persons, one cannot receive full ordination.
Furthermore, there are two other types of persons who are not permitted to receive full ordination:
First, there are those with karmic obstructions;
second, there are dragons who have transformed themselves into humans.
If one grants them the precepts without first knowing their status, and later discovers it, they should be expelled from the assembly.
One who possesses prior knowledge [of such marks] should not be granted the precepts.
As with the thirteen aforementioned analogies, this should be understood in detail.
Furthermore, there is another person who should not receive full ordination: on this body, white spots suddenly appear and, having appeared, vanish again.
If one knew [of the candidate's disqualifications] beforehand, one should not confer full ordination upon them.
If one did not know and has already completed the ordination, then even if one learns of it later, one should not expel them from the community.
"What constitutes an offense?"
There is karma of volition (*cetanā-karma*), karma of action (*kriyā-karma*), and karma that is the object of volition (*cetayitavya-karma*).

Thus, there is karma of volition that is not karma as an object of volition. There is karma to be experienced (*vedanīya-karma*) and karma not to be experienced; karma to be experienced little and karma to be experienced much; karma already experienced and karma not yet experienced; form-karma and non-form-karma; visible karma and invisible karma; resistant karma and non-resistant karma; noble karma (*ārya-karma*) and mundane karma (*laukika-karma*); karma to be experienced in the present life, karma to be experienced in the next birth, and karma to be experienced in subsequent lives; karma leading to the evil realms, karma leading to the heavenly realms, and karma leading to Nirvāṇa.
There are three types of karma, within which all karmas are subsumed:
white karma, white-second karma, and white-fourth karma.
Furthermore, there are four types of karma:
There is unrighteous action, righteous action, collective action, and action performed by a complete assembly.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of action:

the collective action of a group of bhikṣus; action performed by a complete assembly through an unrighteous *karmavācanā*; action performed by a group through an unrighteous *karmavācanā*; and action performed by a complete assembly through a righteous *karmavācanā*.

Regarding formal acts (*karmas*) performed according to ritual procedure: among these, acts that are contrary to the Dharma (*adharma-karman*) and acts performed by a faction (*gaṇa-karman*) should not be performed by the bhikṣus.
Furthermore, acts that are contrary to the Dharma and acts performed by a complete assembly (*sāmagrī-karman*): these two types of acts should not be performed.
One should not perform the karma of the Dharma nor the karma of the multitudes.
One should perform these two types of karma—the karma of the Dharma and the karma of communal assembly—as these are what I have authorized.
In this regard, three types [of karma] should be known:
first, white karma;
second, karma of expulsion and punishment; and third, black karma.
Third, there are actions that are neither white nor subject to formal censure.
What is called "white action"?

Having made a formal announcement (*jñapti*), one shaves the hair and receives the śrāmaṇera precepts; likewise, even for the full bhikṣu precepts, one first makes the announcement and then receives them.
If it is not permitted, one may not receive the dharma of a bhikṣu.
All matters are like this.

Whatever action is to be performed must be announced to the Saṃgha; if permission is granted, it may be done, but if not granted, it may not be done. Therefore, this is called the *jñapti-karman* (the formal act of announcement).
What is called the formal act of banishment (nissāraṇīya-kamma)?

If there is a bhikṣu who does not comply with the Buddha’s words, whether he himself informs the Saṃgha or another informs the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha assembles and, according to the gravity of his offense, the community reprimands him and expels him.

If there are those who have been subjected to the penalty of banishment, yet having not completed their transgression, commit it again, the community of monks shall likewise reprimand them more severely.
All such cases as these are termed the karmic act of banishment.
What is meant by "neither being formally authorized (*jñapti*) nor being subject to expulsion (*pravāsanīya*)"?
If there is a bhikṣu who is appointed by the Saṃgha to manage dwellings, this activity is neither a formal authorization nor an act of expulsion.

Furthermore, suppose this person was originally appointed by the Saṃgha through a formal motion (karma) to serve as a supervisor for building dwellings; this too is neither a formal announcement (jñapti) nor an act of suspension (pravāsanīya).
This procedure is termed "neither a formal announcement nor an act of suspension."
Furthermore, the *karmavācanā* (formal procedures) are not uniform.

For example, the *karmavācanā* for distributing the belongings of a deceased bhikṣu is neither a *jñapti* (motion) nor a formal act of censure or punishment; therefore, it is distinct [from other procedures].
The *karmavācanā* for receiving the *guṇavat-cīvara* is also like this.

Just as with the *karmavācanā* for establishing a great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) or the *karmavācanā* for purifying the ground (*śuddha-bhūmi*), such matters do not fall under the *karmavācanā* for formal announcements, censures, or penalties.
"Furthermore, there are two kinds of *karmavācanā*:
first, that which is for persons;
second, that which is for the Dharma."
What is the *dharmakarma* (legal action according to the Dharma)? It is as follows:

having performed the formal announcement (*jñapti*), the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* precepts, and the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*); leveling the grounds of the monastic quarters; appointing an official for administrative affairs; appointing an official for the distribution of robes and bowls; and [procedures] such as receiving the *kaṭhina* robe, relinquishing the *kaṭhina*, establishing boundaries (*sīmābandha*), relinquishing boundaries, and staying overnight separated from one's robes.
Regarding those who entered the rains retreat after the preceding *poṣadha*: there were donors who invited monks to enter the rains retreat.
When the days of the retreat were completed, the bhikṣuṇīs did not leave because the food and drink were delicious; consequently, the donors became weary and dissatisfied.
The bhikṣus immediately went to inform the Buddha.
The Buddha then established this rule:
"If, at the conclusion of the rainy season retreat, a bhikṣuṇī remains for even one day beyond the appointed time, it is a pāyattika offense."
If it were a great bhikṣu, it would be a duṣkṛta offense.
When they assembled for the *pravāraṇā*, those who asked about the Dharma answered regarding the Dharma, and those who asked about the Vinaya answered regarding the Vinaya.
The one who asked about the Dharma was Kāśyapa; the one who answered regarding the Dharma was Ānanda.
Kāśyapa is the one who asks about the *vinaya*, and Upāli is the one who answers regarding the *vinaya*.
Both are said to perform legal acts (*karmavācanā*) in reliance upon the Dharma.
What is meant by performing legal acts in reliance upon a person?
As in the procedure for ordaining a śrāmaṇera, one first makes a formal announcement, and afterwards shaves the hair and receives the precepts.

If, while undergoing *parivāsa*, one commits another offense before the days are completed, one must again perform the original practice; likewise for those undergoing *mānatva* or *ābhāṣaṇa*. [The Buddha] granted the *pratyakṣa-vinaya* (face-to-face settlement) and the *smṛti-vinaya* (settlement by recollection).
Because the son of a Gandharva, Māra-putra, was slandered, the Buddha established the *smṛti-vinaya* (the discipline of recollection).
Because the bhikṣu Nandika had originally received the precepts with a pure mind, yet through the loss of his mental faculties he acted in violation of the *vinaya*.
Later, when he regained his original mind, the bhikṣus slandered him, saying he had committed an offense.
This bhikṣu said of himself:
