"When I first lost my mind, I was neither conscious nor aware of what I did."
The Buddha said:
"What is done by one whose mind is deluded or insane does not constitute an offense.
For this reason, this bhikṣu requested the *amūḍha-vinaya* (the legal procedure for those who were not deluded) from the Saṃgha.
"What is meant by a bhikṣu who knows himself?
When the Buddha was in the world, he would regularly recite the precepts himself.

Once, when the day for the recitation of the precepts arrived and the time for the recitation had come, the bhikṣus requested the Buddha to recite the precepts during the first and middle watches of the night; yet the Buddha remained silent and did not speak."
With his divine eye, Maudgalyāyana surveyed the assembly to see who was impure, as the Buddha had not yet spoken on the matter.
He saw that one bhikṣu was impure.
Maudgalyāyana immediately rose, seized him by the arm, and dragged him out.
The Buddha then addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying:
"Why did you not examine them?
Question them all."
"The bhikṣus should know for themselves that the reason the Buddha did not speak during the first watch and the middle watch was because there were evil bandits outside.
At that time, the bhikṣus of Śrāvastī were quarreling and disputing; this [conflict] should be extinguished.
How is it to be settled?
Among the assembly, a *tripiṭaka* bhikṣu shall take up their words and settle the matter through reconciliation.

There was a bhikṣu named Hade who, because his mind was disturbed by wind and heat disorders, engaged in debate with various non-Buddhists; his speech was confused and inconsistent from beginning to end, leading him to be ridiculed by the non-Buddhists.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha.
The Buddha called that bhikṣu to his presence and said to him:
"Do not engage in debate with others while your mind is distracted."
"One should speak with certainty and truth.
He rebuked them face-to-face and extinguished the dispute face-to-face.
At that time, the bhikṣus of Śrāvastī were engaged in a legal dispute, and the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Each shall face the others and prostrate themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, like grass laid upon the earth to extinguish the dispute; after committing an offense, one must subsequently repent to eliminate it.
From the *karma* of censure (*pratikāśana-karman*) up to the *karma* for appointing a person to manage various miscellaneous items—these are the *karman*s based on persons.

"There are cases where the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is accomplished but the matter is not; there are cases where the matter is accomplished but the *karmavācanā* is not; there are cases where both are accomplished; and there are cases where neither is accomplished.
The *karmavācanā* refers to the Dharma."
The "matter" refers to the person.
What is meant by a *karmavācanā* (formal act) being accomplished through the matter but not accomplished [in its formal procedure]?
It is when this person is pure and entirely free from all obstacles; this is called accomplishment through the matter.
What constitutes an invalid *karmavācanā*? It is when the speech is incomplete, or when it is spoken out of sequence, or not clearly articulated;
this is called an invalid *karmavācanā*. What is meant by a valid *karmavācanā* but an invalid act?

When the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is accomplished, it means that the speech is complete, the sequence of before and after is correctly articulated, and the meaning is clear; this is called the accomplishment of the *karmavācanā*.
When the matter is not accomplished, it refers to cases where a person lacks the necessary faculties or has other obstacles; this is called the non-accomplishment of the matter.
Furthermore, regarding "accomplishment through both": this refers to the case where both the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) and the person [performing it] are complete;

hence, it is called accomplishment through both. Regarding "non-accomplishment through both": this refers to the case where both the ritual procedure and the person are deficient; this is termed non-accomplishment through both.

Regarding a *karmavācanā* that ought to be suspended: all the bhikṣus have assembled, yet the procedure is not performed according to the Dharma; that which requires a formal *karman* is performed without a *karman*, and that which requires a formal motion (*jñapti*) is performed without a motion. Among the assembly, one who upholds the Vinaya and practices purity says:
"This is neither Dharma nor Vinaya; this should not be done."
To immediately cease and not perform [the action] is called *sthitikarma* (the act of suspension).

That which should not be suspended by *sthitikarma* is when the community of monks has assembled in full, the proceedings are entirely in accordance with the Dharma, and there is no one in the assembly who censures or finds fault; this is called that which should not be suspended by *sthitikarma*.
These two chapters are the detailed exposition from the *Pārivāsikavastu* (The Chapter on Those Undergoing Exclusion).
*Pāri* is the name of a country.
"There are two types of formal acts (*karmavācanā*) for expulsion:"
First, permanent banishment;
second, banishment for the sake of discipline. Regarding "discipline":
during the interval before repentance, one may not participate in any monastic communal activities—whether eating, drinking, sitting, rising, or speaking—and this is termed "banishment."

Regarding the *karman* of subjugation: if this person is stubborn and never reforms or feels regret, they shall not be permitted to participate in the communal affairs of the Saṃgha for the remainder of this life.
Venerable Upāli then rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, joined his palms in prostration to the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"If there is a bhikṣu who is not deficient in his duties toward the Saṃgha, yet he is forcibly expelled— how is this matter to be understood?
The Buddha said,
"There are two kinds of expulsion:"
First is the virtuous expulsion;
second is the unvirtuous expulsion.
For example, the expulsion of the thirteen kinds of persons is called a virtuous expulsion.
That which is contrary to this is called an "evil suspension.
This is termed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of expulsion.
Furthermore, there is the formal act of the Saṃgha for permitting one to enter the assembly through repentance in due order.

If a bhikṣu has been expelled for the sake of discipline, and at a later time this person repents and seeks from the Saṃgha the removal of his offense, and if he complies with whatever instructions the Saṃgha gives him, not daring to disobey, and is able to cause the assembly of monks to be of one mind and joyful, the Saṃgha shall then assemble and perform the *karmavācanā* for revoking the expulsion, subsequently performing the *karmavācanā* for permitting re-entry; this is called the *karmavācanā* for permitting re-entry into the Saṃgha.
Upāli asked the Buddha,
"Regarding the act of being expelled and then repenting, how should this matter be handled?
The Buddha said:
"For those who are to be disciplined, one permits them to perform repentance;
for those who are to be permanently expelled, one does not permit repentance.
"What is called the *karma* of censure?"

There was a person who was habitually combative and contentious within the Saṃgha; in all matters concerning the Saṃgha’s Dharma, he acted contrary to the Dharma, and was consequently subjected to various forms of censure in their presence, even up to being expelled.
This matter of censure is explained in detail within the *Kṣudraka-vastu* (Section on Censure).
Regarding those who deserve censure: if a bhikṣu performs various kinds of improper acts, the Saṃgha says to him, "Venerable sir!..."
"You have committed an unrighteous act.
This person then replies to the Saṃgha, saying:
"I neither know nor see what kind of act I have committed."
The Saṃgha should reprimand him with various forms of censure and expel him; this is called the *karma* of reprimand (*tarjanīya-karman*).
The method of admonition should involve admonishing in three ways:
regarding [allegations of] breaking the precepts, breaking right view, or breaking proper conduct, based on what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
There are five conditions for one who offers admonition:
first, knowing the proper time;
second, being beneficial to the person before them.
Third, sincerity of mind;
fourth, harmonious speech;
fifth, refraining from coarse or malicious speech.
Furthermore, there are five internal reasons for which one should offer admonition:
first, for their benefit;
second, for their well-being; [and so forth].
Third, the mind of loving-kindness;
fourth, the mind of compassion;
fifth, the desire to cause one to quickly depart from transgressions.
This is called the method of admonition regarding the causal matter.
What is meant by "causal matter"? It refers to either the cause or the condition.
From what does this first arise?
This should be understood in detail from the *Bhadrapāla-bhikṣu-sūtra*.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Śrāvastī and eating a single meal while remaining seated.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Since I have practiced eating but one meal a day, my body has been harmonious and well-adjusted, free from all ailments and suffering; you, too, should eat but one meal.
Having heard this instruction, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The bhikṣu Bhadrapāla did not comply with the Buddha’s instruction, saying, "I am unable to eat but one meal.
Why is this? I have always eaten many times, and this has been my practice."
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
"If you are able to eat much, beg for food in large quantities before midday and eat it while remaining seated.
He spoke further:
"No. The Buddha again wished to travel through various kingdoms and towns, and Ānanda was sewing robes for the Buddha.
This bhikṣu went to where Ānanda was and asked:
"What are you doing? Ānanda replied, "The World-Honored One wishes to travel through various kingdoms and towns; therefore, I am sewing robes for the Buddha."
"It would be of no benefit for you to remain here.
Having heard these words, he went immediately to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"You should perform repentance on behalf of the disciple.
The Buddha said,
"Repentance will be of no benefit."
"All śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas know that you are practicing what is not the Dharma.
If you follow my words, then the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments, the various supernormal powers, and liberation can all be attained."
"Those who do not follow my words shall not attain these various virtues.
He then again earnestly entreated the World-Honored One three times; only then did the World-Honored One accept his repentance and further preach the Dharma for him, saying:
"If a person who has committed evil is able to reform and repent, they will bring great benefit within the Buddha-dharma."
Thus it was explained at length.
This bhikṣu, Bhadrapāla, repeatedly committed offenses; when the other bhikṣus saw this, they admonished him.
Yet, upon hearing their words of admonition, he did not take them to heart, but instead replied with other words.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣu Bhadrapāla, saying:
"There was a bhikṣu who committed various offenses.
When the other bhikṣus saw this, they admonished him in accordance with the Dharma."
"This bhikṣu answered with further different words and again gave rise to anger.
The Buddha said,
"Even though this bhikṣu does not accept the admonition, he should still be admonished."
"The reason for this is that I wish to make it widely known to all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, and also so that they may experience suffering for a long night in their present bodies.
The Buddha said: "There are three kinds of methods for subduing: [the subduing of the mind, the subduing of speech, and the subduing of the body]."
First, reprimand;
second, allow them to stay separately;
third, cause them to rely upon those who possess wisdom, or even expel them.

This person, through this matter, becomes disciplined; their mind becomes supple and they act in accordance with the Dharma of the Sangha, thereby able to bring joy to the great assembly. This is called the method of discipline.
“*Śamatha* means ‘cessation’ in the language of Qin. What matters should a bhikṣu cease?
If there is a bhikṣu who follows the wholesome dharmas, he can eliminate the four types of grasping (*upādāna*):
first, the grasping of sensual desire;”
Second is the grasping of views;
third is the grasping of precepts and observances;
fourth is the grasping of a self.

To be able to eliminate these four types of sensation, to practice in accordance with the Dharma of renunciation, to increase in goodness moment by moment, and to abandon what is evil—this is called cessation.

Furthermore, regarding "extinguishing": from *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence) up to *tṛṇastāraka* (covering with grass), the extinguishing of these seven types of disputes is also termed "extinguishing.
Regarding "that which should not be extinguished": if a bhikṣu possesses five qualities that give rise to matters of contention:
first, he constantly delights in living as a householder; [and so forth].
Second, they constantly delight in relying upon kings and ministers;
third, they do not delight in relying upon the Saṃgha;
fourth, they likewise do not rely upon the Dharma.
Fifth, they do not comply with whatever matters the Saṃgha undertakes.
If a bhikṣu is accomplished in these five kinds of matters, any dispute involving him should not be settled.
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who accomplishes five qualities by which a dispute that has arisen should be extinguished.
What are these five?
They are the opposites of the aforementioned five matters; these are the five.
Having accomplished these five dharmas, all matters of dispute should be extinguished.

Furthermore, as for "extinguishing," it means that one follows the Dharma practiced by the Saṃgha and accords with it; thus, all wholesome dharmas increase day by day, and one constantly provides explanations regarding the practices undertaken.
If there is any matter that causes the Saṃgha joy, and one practices it without weariness, this is called the "Dharma of Extinction.
The Dharma of Renouncing the Precepts:

If a bhikṣu is sorrowful and unhappy, taking no pleasure in the holy life (brahmacarya), desiring to return home and finding no joy in the bhikṣu-dharma, and if he conceives a sense of shame and remorse regarding this dharma, intending to fulfill the dharma of a householder—[this constitutes the renunciation of the precepts].
"The way of the renunciant is of no benefit to me; the way of the householder is very beneficial to me.
Intending to abandon the dharma of a bhikṣu and return home, he speaks these words:
"I renounce the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha; I renounce my upādhyāya and ācārya, the holy life (brahmacarya), the Vinaya, and the Prātimokṣa precepts."
Thus it is explained in detail; one should know that this constitutes the relinquishing of the precepts.
As for those who do not relinquish the precepts: if one is insane, mentally deranged, or even mute and unable to speak, this is not termed relinquishing the precepts.
It should be understood that this is explained in detail in this manner.

Regarding "weakness in the precepts" (*śīla-kaśāya*): when a bhikṣu conceives the thought that he does not delight in the holy life (*brahmacarya*) but delights in being among the followers of external paths (*tīrthika*), or even as a *saṃgha-bhūta*, this is called weakness in the precepts.

Regarding the matter of weakness in the precepts, it is as explained in the preceding text. "The method for reciting the precepts (*poṣadha*) is that the Saṃgha should assemble according to the Dharma;

once the Saṃgha has assembled, one should perform a *jñapti-karman* (a formal motion), and not a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a motion followed by three proclamations) or a *jñapti-tri-karman* (a motion followed by two proclamations)."
When the Saṃgha performs formal acts (karmas) and receives the consent (chanda) in accordance with the Dharma, all should remain silent and not obstruct it.
If the Saṃgha is incomplete, the precepts should not be recited; if the Saṃgha is complete, the precepts should be recited in full detail.
"The time was not appropriate; this is a brief explanation.
'Time' refers to that which is free from obstacles.
At that time, the World-Honored One was dwelling in a quiet chamber, reflecting thus in his mind:"
"I have established the precepts for the bhikṣus and taught the Prātimokṣa, which can lead people to attain the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
The Prātimokṣa is the locus for the practice and maintenance of the Vinaya; this is the meaning of 'Prātimokṣa.'"
At that time, the bhikṣus recited the precepts using a melodic chant.
The Buddha said:
"One should not recite the precepts with a loud voice or in a manner that is overly distinct."
There are five faults in chanting the precepts with a melodic tone:
first, the mind becomes stained by attachment to this sound;
second, one is disparaged by worldly people.
Third, they are no different from worldly people;
fourth, they obstruct and cause one to abandon the practice of the Path;
fifth, they obstruct entry into meditative concentration.
"These are called the five faults.
When the Buddha was in the world, the bhikṣus recited the precepts every day, and the assembly of monks all grew weary of it.
Upon hearing this, the Buddha immediately established the rule that the precepts should be recited once every fifteen days.
At that time, the *poṣadha* was being recited at a single residence. As the monastic quarters were vast, those bhikṣus who were far away could not hear it.
For this reason, the Tathāgata established a rule for the bhikṣus:

"If the assembly of monks is large and the monastic hall is also large, one should arrange seats in the center; the reciter of the *poṣadha* shall sit upon these seats and recite clearly with a loud voice so that everyone may hear it."
At that time, there were monks residing in a certain location; although the community was large, there was no one to recite the precepts, and thus the Dharma-rituals could not be accomplished.
Having heard this, the World-Honored One addressed the monks:
"From this day forward, any who have left the household life and reached five years of seniority must recite the precepts until they are proficient."
If one has dull faculties, they should recite it even if they have been a monk for as long as a hundred years.
If they still do not recite it, or if they previously recited it but later forgot it, or if they are of dull faculties and cannot attain it—these three types of persons have four kinds of faults:
first, they are not permitted to keep disciples;...
Second, one may not be separated from one's preceptor;
third, one may not act as an upādhyāya;
fourth, one may not act as an ācārya.
"This is called the offense of one who does not recite the precepts.
"There are eight kinds of difficulties that permit the abbreviated recitation of the precepts:
first, the difficulty of kings;..."
Second, the peril of bandits;
third, the peril of water;
fourth, the peril of fire.
Fifth, the difficulty of illness;
sixth, the difficulty of humans;
seventh, the difficulty of non-humans.
Eighth is the danger of venomous snakes.
When these eight kinds of dangers exist, the *saṃkṣipta-śīla* (abbreviated precepts) may be recited.
There are five such abbreviated [occasions]:
First, having recited the introduction to the precepts, one announces by name, saying:
"The four *pārājika* offenses, you have heard them repeatedly.
This is to be said in the same manner up to the *śaikṣa* rules.
The second abbreviated version: from the preface of the precepts, one recites up to the four matters; thereafter, the names are called out as before. The third abbreviated version:
from the preface of the precepts, one recites up to the thirteen matters; thereafter, the names are called out as in the previous two cases.
The fourth abbreviated version begins from the preface of the precepts and extends up to the two *aniyata* (undetermined) rules; the remainder is referred to by name, as in the previous three cases.

The fifth abbreviated version begins from the preface of the precepts and extends up to the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (forfeiture) rules; the latter portion is referred to by name, as in the previous four cases.

At that time, there were many bhikṣus staying in one place; they were all dull-witted and lacked understanding. Because of the threat of bandits, they were unable to go to another monastery to recite the precepts, and thus their religious rites could not be completed.
Having heard this, the Buddha instructed the bhikṣus:
"You should recite the precepts in brief:
'Commit no evil, practice all that is good, purify your own mind—this is the teaching of the Buddhas.'"
"This is called the brief exposition of the precepts.
"There are four ways in which the recitation of the precepts is not valid:
if a group recites the precepts together in an unlawful manner, it is not called a recitation of the precepts;..."
An illegal assembly is not called a recitation of the precepts;
a gathering of a crowd is likewise not a valid recitation;
and where one proclamation should be made, making two proclamations likewise does not constitute a valid recitation of the precepts.

If there are bhikṣus who, during the recitation of the precepts, engage in private discussions in groups of three or four, giving rise to a sense of arrogance, and because of these discussions on the meaning of the precepts, give birth to disputes and litigation—such a recitation of the precepts does not constitute a valid recitation of the precepts.
There are two kinds of failure:
first, the recitation of the precepts fails due to quarreling;
second, afflictions increase due to a malicious mind.
In both these cases, the recitation of the precepts is not valid.
This matter should be understood in detail within the *Poṣadha-khandhaka*.
It ought to be explained in that section.
What is this? If a bhikṣu, while not yet having committed an offense, conceives this thought in his mind:
"How can I avoid committing various evils and instead give rise to wholesome states?"
He immediately went to those who uphold the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkā-piṭaka and asked them:
"Venerable ones,
what is the Dharma?"
What is non-dharma?
What can be spoken?
What cannot be spoken?
Upon hearing these words, that teacher immediately explained them in successive order: he spoke of what is Dharma as Dharma, and what is not Dharma as not Dharma;
he spoke of what is Vinaya as Vinaya, and what is not Vinaya as not Vinaya;
he spoke of what is light as light, and what is heavy as heavy; and he spoke of harsh speech as harsh speech.
To speak what is not harsh speech as if it were not harsh speech; to speak of an offense as an offense, and to speak of no offense as no offense;
to speak of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* as a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, and to speak of what is not a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* as not a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;

to speak of what is appropriate as appropriate, and to speak of what is inappropriate as inappropriate; to speak of what is prescribed as prescribed, and to speak of what is not prescribed as not prescribed.
The teaching is proclaimed such that what is spoken is as it was spoken; as it was not spoken, so it is as it was not spoken;

as it is measured, so it is spoken according to its measure; as it is not measured, so it is spoken according to its lack of measure; as it is differentiated, so it is spoken according to its differentiation;
as it is not differentiated, so it is spoken according to its lack of differentiation.
"The rule for bhikṣus is this:
when food is within the boundary, it must not be eaten unless there is a purified kitchen. Why is this? "
While the Buddha was traveling through various villages, he saw some bhikṣus quarreling with one another.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus,
"What matter are you disputing over?"
The bhikṣu said to the Buddha:
"Yesterday, after we had finished our meal, there was leftover food; for this reason, we quarreled over it.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, one must not eat food stored overnight or food consumed within the great boundary (sīmā) unless there is a designated pure kitchen (viśuddha-maṇḍapa).

When first establishing a monastery at a site where the Saṃgha resides, the entire assembly of monks should gather and first perform the formal ritual (karmavācanā) to designate the pure kitchen area; only thereafter should they perform the ritual to designate the living quarters for the monks."

If at that time one forgets or errs and does not perform the *karmavācanā* to designate a pure kitchen area, and later remembers it, one should first dissolve the great boundary (*mahāsīma*), then dissolve the small boundary (*khuḍḍakasīma*), and subsequently perform the *karmavācanā* for the pure kitchen area.
The Method for Establishing Boundaries (*Sīmā-bandhana*): First establish the small boundary (*kṣudra-sīmā*), and afterwards establish the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*).

Regarding food kept overnight (*sāṃghika-śeṣa-rātri-bhakta*) and leftover food kept overnight (*paryuṣita-śeṣa-rātri-bhakta*), as well as food prepared within the small boundary of the Saṃgha and food prepared by the monks' own hands—if the Saṃgha encounters a time of famine, they may eat it; at other times, they must not eat it.
Having finished eating, if a donor invites them to a meal, they should eat only what is sufficient for that occasion and should redistribute the remaining food to other monks.
Once those monks have received it, they should consume it after performing the ritual of leftover food (*kṛtapiṇḍapāta*).

Furthermore, there were certain great masters who were highly esteemed by the sovereign and invited for a meal. Having eaten their fill among them, they brought back the leftovers to offer to the monks residing together with them.
The monks, fearing [the food], would not eat it.
The Buddha said, "I permit you to consume it by performing the *kṛtapiṇḍaka* (leftover food) rite; there is no fault in this.

A certain bhikṣu obtained some fruit from outside and gave it to a lay donor who had been purified for receiving it. Because the world was suffering from famine, the donor did not return the fruit to its original owner.
The Buddha thereupon established this precept:
"From this day forward, in times of famine, one may store and eat [these fruits] oneself.
This applies to all fruits from within a pond as well."
"Regarding the rules for possessing bowls:
with the exception of iron bowls and clay bowls, one must not possess any other kind of bowl whatsoever.
One must not possess robes of the highest quality among those of superior color."
Why? Because garments such as those with brocade patterns, garlands, and flowers are not fit to be kept.
"That which should be explained is this: there was a bhikṣu who gave rise to this thought:"
"How does one cultivate all wholesome dharmas?
He went to where the wise were and asked:
"What is called an offense?"
What constitutes non-offense?
What constitutes repentance?
On account of what matter does one commit an offense?
That teacher, in accordance with the Vinaya, explains for him what constitutes an offense and what does not; this should be understood in detail.

Once the questioner has heard the teacher’s explanation, his mind is no longer burdened by anxiety or suffering. He follows the teacher’s instruction and acts in accordance with the Vinaya; his mind attains purity, conforms to wholesome dharmas, and harbors no further distracting thoughts. This is called "that which should be explained."
Furthermore, regarding what should be explained: a bhikṣu gives rise to this thought:
"I am weary of birth and death; how may I transcend them by practicing the path to attain nirvāṇa?
Having given rise to this thought, he goes to the side of a wise person and asks him.
"Venerable Sir! How does one cultivate the four dhyānas up to the four fruits?
That teacher explained it to him in sequence, up to the fruit of arhatship; this is called "that which should be explained."
What is called "speaking what is not the Dharma"?

That teacher, for the sake of the questioner, speaks of the Dharma as non-Dharma and speaks of non-Dharma as Dharma; even to the point that what is spoken is called "not spoken" and what is not spoken is called "spoken"; he treats the limited as unlimited and the unlimited as limited; he treats discrimination as non-discrimination and non-discrimination as discrimination; and this applies likewise to everything from the alms bowl to the drinking water.
Furthermore, regarding that which should not be spoken: suppose a bhikṣu asks a wise person, "How does one attain the first dhyāna up to the fourth fruit?
and the wise person explains it for him as follows:
"If you have attained superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) as you claim,
you have committed a pārājika offense.
This is called what should not be said.
In the past, there was a bhikṣu named Nandika who had lost his mental faculties.
On the days of the Saṃgha’s poṣadha ceremony, he would sometimes remember and sometimes not; when he remembered, he would come, but when he did not remember, he would not come.
The bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
The Buddha told them:
"Simply perform the formal act of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* for this bhikṣu to declare him as one who has lost his sanity."
"Although he did not come, the Dharma-rite was accomplished.
This is explained in detail within the *Poṣadha-vastu*.
When this bhikṣu returned to his original state of mind, doubt arose in his heart: "Should the *jñapti-karman* for the loss of one's nature (*unmattaka-karman*) be revoked or not?"
He went and informed the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Those who have attained the mind may discard it."
The bhikṣus again had doubts:
"Later, he lost his mind once more; what does this mean?
The Buddha said:
"Perform the *karma* for one who has lost their sanity, and later, when they regain their original mind, perform the *karma* for relinquishing it.
"When a bhikṣu receives offerings from others, if he does so improperly, he falls because of those offerings."
There are two kinds of falling away:
first, consuming the offerings of others while failing to cultivate the Path according to the Dharma, becoming lax and dissolute so that no wholesome merit can be recorded;
second, giving what has been bestowed upon oneself to others in a manner that does not accord with the Dharma.
Therefore, in these two cases, one shall fall into the three miserable realms.

If there were no retribution to be received in those three realms, this body would immediately decompose in the belly with its food expelled, and the clothing one wears would instantly detach from the body.

"Regarding those who should receive gifts: if one's parents are poor and suffering, one should first bestow upon them the Three Refuges, the Five Precepts, and the Ten Wholesome Actions, and only then provide them with gifts.
If they are not poor, even if they have received the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts, it is not appropriate to give them gifts."
Furthermore, there are other recipients of offerings:
first, those who repair stupas;
second, those who serve the Sangha.
Third, those who manage the monastic quarters;
fourth, those suffering from illness;
fifth, infants.
Sixth, women who are pregnant;
seventh, those imprisoned in jail;
eighth, beggars who come to the monastic quarters to solicit alms.
Regarding such persons, one may give them a fair amount or not;
however, for those who repair stupas, serve the Sangha, or maintain monastic dwellings, their labor must be compensated at its proper value.
If one gives them more than this, it constitutes a downfall through over-generosity.
When giving food to the sick, one should cultivate a mind of loving-kindness and bestow it according to what is appropriate for the patient.
If one provides food erroneously due to negligence, one falls into the fault of improper giving.

To infants, those bound in prison, and those who are pregnant—one should give to such persons with a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), without expecting any recompense for their entry or exit; one should do so for the sake of the Buddha-dharma and not create obstacles.
If one gives with such a mind in accordance with the Dharma, it is proper; otherwise, one falls into the fault of giving.
When begging at a monastic dwelling, if one already possesses provisions, there is no need to give; for the giver to give in such a case is to fall into the fault of giving.
However, if one lacks food and provisions, there is no fault in giving.

If a bhikṣu does not practice meditation, does not recite the sūtras, and does not attend to the affairs of the Buddha, Dharma, or Saṅgha, yet accepts offerings from others, he falls because of those offerings.
If he possesses the three types of wholesome action, there is no fault in his receiving offerings.
If the person before one lacks the three types of karmic action, yet one knowingly transfers the gift to them, both the recipient and the donor fall into the fault of giving.
If a bhikṣu eats the offerings of a donor with contentment as his limit, yet forces himself to eat and drink when already full, he falls into the fault of giving.
If a bhikṣu eats and drinks with a mind of arrogance, he falls away from the gift.
Why is this? Because for a long night, the World-Honored One has constantly praised moderation in eating.
Finally, even down to the case of giving to one who upholds the precepts, such a person is able to receive the gift and is able to digest it.
As the Buddha said:
"The fruit and retribution of giving to one who upholds the precepts are greatly beneficial; the fruit and retribution obtained from giving to one who breaks the precepts are very slight."
As the Buddha said in a verse:
"It would be better to swallow a red-hot iron ball and die than to eat the faithful offerings of others without observing the precepts.

If one eats beyond satiety and forces oneself to eat more, it will not increase one's physical appearance or strength, but will only increase one's ailments; therefore, one should not eat without moderation.
"Regarding *karmas*, there are four causes and conditions by which a *karman* is successfully accomplished:
first, it must be in accordance with the Dharma;
second, the Saṃgha must be fully assembled."

Third, in a place where a single *jñapti* is required, one performs only a single *jñapti*, and so on up to a place where four *jñaptis* are required, where one does not perform three, two, or one *jñapti* instead;
fourth, those members of the Saṃgha who do not attend must give their consent (*chanda*), and there must be no one in the assembly to raise an objection.
When these four factors are fulfilled, it is called a formal act (*karmavācanā*) performed in accordance with the Dharma.
This matter should be understood in detail within the *Kṣudraka-vastu* (Minor Matters).
That which is not a formal act consists of four cases where the procedure is not accomplished and thus is not designated as a formal act.

“Regarding the Vinaya, there are various kinds of Vinaya: the Vinaya of offenses, the Vinaya of disputes, the Vinaya of afflictions, the Vinaya for bhikṣus, the Vinaya for bhikṣuṇīs, the partial Vinaya, the universal Vinaya, the Vinaya concerning the commission of offenses, and the Vinaya for the expiation of guilt.”
Furthermore, *vinaya* is so called because it can extinguish unwholesome roots, extinguish obstructive dharmas, and extinguish the evil conduct of the five hindrances; thus it is named *vinaya*.
There is also *vinaya* which can lead to confession and compliant practice, and which involves abandoning evil and following good; thus it is named *vinaya*.
What is meant by "confession"?
To confess without concealment whatever transgressions have been committed, speaking of them fully to others, is called confession.
This matter is explained in detail in the *Kṣudraka-vastu* (Section on the Extinction of Offenses).
"Conformity" means to conform to what the preceptor has said, to conform to what the ācārya has said, and even to not contradict anything said by the Saṃgha; this is called conformity.
What is meant by "cessation" (nirodha)?
It is called cessation because it can extinguish strife and contention.
What is meant by "severance" (prahāṇa)?
Just as the severing of afflictions is called "severance," one should understand this in detail within the *Vinaya of Afflictions* and the *Vinaya of Severing Afflictions*.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu said:
"According to what I know and see, desire cannot obstruct the Path.
Other bhikṣus admonished him, saying:
"Do not speak such words; desire is the very root that obstructs the Path."
We know this because the World-Honored One has employed various analogies for the sake of those with desires, such as the analogy of fire-pits and even the analogy of knives.
How can you say that they do not constitute an obstruction?
"You should abandon this view.
When the bhikṣus offer such admonition, it is well if the person accepts the advice.

If they do not accept it, the bhikṣus shall perform the formal ritual of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the motion followed by three proclamations) to cause them to remember [their transgression]; this is called the "reproach for the improper speech of a bhikṣu who holds an evil view and refuses to relinquish it."

When the bhikṣus assemble to perform a formal act (karmavācanā), if it is not performed according to the Dharma and there are those within the assembly who perceive this, the Saṃgha’s performance of the formal act is not accomplished.
If this person has two, three, four, or five companions, they may offer him admonition.
If there is only one person, there is no need for admonition.
Why is this? Because the power of the great assembly is great; they might expel him, which would be of no benefit to the Dharma and would only result in his own suffering.
For this reason, one should remain silent and say nothing.
If one enters the midst of the Saṃgha, one should maintain five virtues:
first, always give rise to a mind of loving-kindness, as in the analogy of the broom—regarding good and evil with equanimity, desiring that all may attain what is wholesome.
Second, one should always give rise to a mind of reverence and humility toward all seniors and must not be arrogant.
Third, one must not engage in conversation or socialize with those who are juniors.
Fourth, when the Saṃgha assembles to perform formal acts (karmavācanā), the great assembly should request one who knows the Dharma to preach the Dharma.
Fifth, if the assembly does not request it, one should address the assembly and urge them to request someone who knows the Dharma to preach.
Śāriputra also accomplished these five aforementioned methods for entering the Saṃgha.
"What is called 'the white'? [He said: 'Kāśyapa!'"
"Because the assembly has granted its consent by remaining silent as the bhikṣu spoke, this is called the 'motion' (jñapti).

A single motion is sufficient, such as when one first ordains a śrāmaṇera or receives full ordination (upasampadā), where one makes a motion to the Saṃgha; having made the motion to the Saṃgha, a teacher of instruction is appointed, who then leads the candidate to a secluded place to inquire regarding the obstructing factors (antarāyika-dharma)."
When he was about to recite the Prātimokṣa, or perform the Pravāraṇā ceremony, or receive a new alms bowl because the old one had broken,
there was a bhikṣu named Chanda who was on the verge of violating the precepts.
When the other bhikṣus learned of this, they admonished him.
That bhikṣu said to the other bhikṣus: "What are you saying?"
With whom do you speak?
Who is the one who commits the offense?
And what is meant by "committing an offense"?
Having spoken such heterodox words,
the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Perform the *nānāvāsa-pārivāsika-karman* (the formal act of separate residence for speaking differently) against this bhikṣu.
Later, the bhikṣu Chanda again began to mock the other bhikṣus;
when the bhikṣus told him not to sit, he sat; when they told him not to rise, he rose; when they told him not to speak, he spoke; and when they told him not to come, he came.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Perform a formal act of one motion (jñapti-karman) for the purpose of making him subject to ridicule."
"Such cases as these, and others whose names have not yet been listed, are all termed *jñapti-karman* (a motion with one announcement).
What is termed *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a motion with one announcement and one subsequent motion)?
The announcement (*jñapti*) is: 'Venerable Saṃgha, listen!'"
The dwelling of [Name] has fallen into ruin.

If the Saṃgha deems it the right time, may the Saṃgha, being pleased to grant its consent, bestow this dwelling upon [Name] to have it repaired by a certain donor and to entrust it to a bhikṣu in charge of construction.
The motion is as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!
Such-and-such a dwelling and such-and-such a dwelling have no patrons and are dilapidated."
The Saṃgha now grants this dwelling to a certain donor for the purpose of repair and to the *karmadāna* bhikṣu.
If the Saṃgha approves of granting this dwelling to the donor for repair and to the *karmadāna* bhikṣu, let those who approve remain silent;
those who do not approve may speak.
The Sangha has already consented to bestow such-and-such a dwelling upon such-and-such a donor and the bhikṣu in charge of construction.
Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.

The person managing monastic affairs shall divide the robes and bowls of a deceased bhikṣu; receive the *kaṭhina* robe and relinquish the *kaṭhina*; perform all procedures regarding the non-separation from one's robes while within a defined boundary (*sīmā*); first establish the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) and subsequently establish the boundary for not losing one's robes (*acīvarāpattisīmā*), and first relinquish the boundary for not losing one's robes and subsequently relinquish the great boundary; and provide instruction to the bhikṣuṇīs regarding the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*).
In such numerous cases as these, the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation) is employed.

As for the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations): having made the motion, there are three proclamations; this is called the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.
First is reprimand.

Second, when a bhikṣu fights with a layperson, the Saṃgha exhorts him to confess to the donor; [the procedures include] formal suspension (pārājika), temporary exclusion (nigarhaṇīya), probation (parivāsa), reconciliation (mūlāpakarṣa), the practice of mānatva, the practice of ābhāṣanā, and even the seven methods for settling disputes.
There was a monk of great virtue who was highly esteemed by a wealthy and faithful lay donor; having invited him for many years, the donor provided him with whatever he required.
Bystanders said, "This elder is immensely wealthy, yet because of this bhikṣu, his wealth has been greatly diminished.
A foolish and depraved bhikṣuṇī, having received the precepts, came before the Saṃgha to request the formal ordination.

For matters concerning the violation of precepts, the overturning of the alms bowl, and silent censure—such as these and others not yet enumerated—all are performed by the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations).
There are two kinds of *parivāsa* (probation).

If any non-Buddhist comes to enter the Buddha-dharma seeking to go forth as a monk, the Sangha should grant him the formal act of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for a four-month period of separate residence (*parivāsa*).

Furthermore, regarding this separate residence: if one has committed any one of the thirteen types of offenses within the category of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, and has failed to disclose them while concealing them; [one must undergo this probation].
At a later time, having confessed his offense, the Saṃgha grants him *parivāsa* (probation) through a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.
For what reason is it called "separate dwelling"?
Because he must dwell in a separate room and may not occupy the same place as the Saṃgha.
All members of the great Saṃgha must sit on lower seats and are not permitted to eat while sitting upon continuous grass.

Furthermore, all the members of the Saṃgha must perform manual labor, such as sweeping the stūpas and the monastic quarters, and even attending to the places where the monks walk and relieve themselves.
Furthermore, although one has entered among the Saṃgha, one is not permitted to engage in conversation with the Saṃgha, nor may one answer if someone questions them.
For this reason, it is called "living separately" (praticchanna-vāsa).

Regarding the *yadbhūyaḥ* (original matter): while the period of *parivāsa* has not yet been completed, one commits another offense and again requests *parivāsa* from the Sangha; the Sangha then grants him the original number of days for concealment through a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, and is therefore called *yadbhūyaḥ*.
What is meant by *mānatva*?

As for *mānatva*, it consists of living apart and performing menial service no differently than during the previous period of probation; the only slight difference lies in the limitation of its duration in days.
If one confesses immediately upon committing an offense, one must likewise practice the *mānatva* for six days and six nights.

*Mānatva* is translated in the Qin language as "joy of mind" (*yìxǐ*); whereas previously it was merely the joy within one's own mind, now one also gives rise to shame and remorse, and causes the community of monks to rejoice.
Because of the preceding joy, he is granted a short period of time; because of this short period, he first receives the name "joyful.
Regarding the joy of the Saṃgha, they observe that the person’s practice of the Dharma will not be transgressed again. Regarding the praise of the Saṃgha, they say:
"This person, having reformed through repentance, shall no longer give rise to afflictions and will become a pure person."
Therefore, he rejoices.
Regarding *ābhāṣaṇā*: it arises from pure precepts and attains pure liberation.
Within these precepts, one is pure and without transgression; having maintained them well, one departs. This is the meaning of *ābhāṣaṇā*.
"There are offenses and non-offenses. Regarding those who commit offenses, there are three types of persons who offend:
first, those who are not insane;
second, those whose minds are not distracted."
Third, not being oppressed by pain;
this is called an offense.
Furthermore, regarding those who commit offenses, whether they be light or heavy, one should understand them extensively according to the rules established by that Buddha.
The same applies to those who do not commit an offense.
One should understand in detail, according to whichever section explains them, what is clarified therein.
Regarding the determination of the meaning of what constitutes an offense and what does not, all such matters should be investigated within the Vinaya.

From not knowing whether the initial dharma is legal or illegal, up to not knowing whether a confession has been made or not, these twenty-two types of cases constitute an offense when conferring full ordination upon others.
If one wishes to resolve all cases of non-offenses, one should investigate them within the Vinaya.
If there is one who can fulfill twenty-two dharmas, they should confer full ordination upon another; this is called a non-offense.

“There are offenses committed by a bhikṣu that are not committed by a bhikṣuṇī; there are offenses committed by a bhikṣuṇī that are not committed by a bhikṣu; there are offenses committed by both a bhikṣu and a bhikṣuṇī that are not committed by a śikṣamāṇā; and there are offenses committed by both a bhikṣu and a bhikṣuṇī that are not committed by a śrāmaṇera or a śrāmaṇerī.”
There are cases where the five groups of monastics commit an offense while the male and female lay followers (upāsaka and upāsikā) do not;
there are also cases where all seven groups commit it.
What is meant by an offense committed by a bhikṣu but not by a bhikṣuṇī?
Regarding the practices to be observed at forest hermitages (*āraṇyaka-śayanāsana*), if a bhikṣuṇī does not perform them, it is an offense for the bhikṣu but not for the bhikṣuṇī.
There was once a bhikṣu living in a forest hermitage who was indolent; he was unable to store water in a jar, nor did he have any food.
Later, some bandits arrived; when they asked for water and food, they received neither, and in their rage, they beat this bhikṣu.
Having known this, the Tathāgata subsequently established a precept:
"Those who dwell in forest hermitages (āraṇyaka) should all keep water in a jar and set aside a small amount of leftover food; when bandits arrive and ask for it, they may give it to them."
All such matters as these are the rules for bhikṣus, not rules to be practiced by bhikṣuṇīs.
What are those offenses committed by bhikṣuṇīs that are not offenses committed by bhikṣus?

If a bhikṣuṇī crosses water alone, enters a village alone, or stays overnight apart from the community; or if she travels along a road alone, sends a man to shave her hair alone, walks in a place where bhikṣus practice walking meditation alone, or sits in the full lotus posture alone—such offenses as these are committed by bhikṣuṇīs but are not offenses committed by bhikṣus.
"What is meant by 'an offense for bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, but not an offense for śikṣamāṇās'?
If a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī eats food that has not been formally received, it is an offense for the bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī, but not an offense for the śikṣamāṇā."
"What are the offenses committed by the three assemblies but not by śrāmaṇeras or śrāmaṇerīs?
With the exception of the śrāmaṇera and śrāmaṇerī precepts, those who commit other precepts are offenders among the three assemblies but not among śrāmaṇeras or śrāmaṇerīs."
"What constitutes an offense for the five assemblies but not for the male and female lay followers?
With the exception of the five precepts, committing any other violation constitutes an offense for the five assemblies, but not for the two assemblies."
"What is meant by 'the seven assemblies all committing offenses'?
The seven assemblies all uphold the five precepts; if the seven assemblies violate these five precepts, they all commit the same offense.

There are those who commit offenses in winter but not in spring or summer; there are those who commit offenses in spring but not in summer or winter; and there are those who commit offenses in summer but not in winter or spring."
What is it that exists in winter but not in spring or summer?
When the four months of winter have been completed, one should relinquish the *kaṭhina* robe.
If one does not relinquish it and a day passes, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This offense occurs in winter and not in spring or summer.
Why is it that an offense committed in spring does not occur in summer or winter?
Because during the final month of spring, one ought to request a rain-bath robe.

If one begs for [robes] after a month has passed, or if one obtains them by begging for more than the permitted length, or if having obtained them one does not use them within fifteen days—these three matters all constitute an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
What is it that exists in summer but not in winter or spring?
It is the rule for bhikṣus to observe the summer rains retreat (varṣā).
There are two kinds of retreats:
The "before" and "after.

If one does not observe the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) and furthermore does not perform the *pravāraṇā* (ceremony of mutual invitation), this constitutes an offense during the summer, but not during winter or spring.
Therefore, regarding these three types of offenses, each occurs according to its respective season; this is what is meant by "offense" and "non-offense."
"What is light? An offense of *pāyattika* (pāratideśanīya) is a light offense; it can be extinguished by confessing it before a single person or by reflecting upon it within one's own mind."
Regarding "one's own species" (*svajātīya*): if a bhikṣu keeps leather sandals made from human skin or eats human flesh, should he keep or eat them, it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
As for "species," because the flesh and the skin are the very body of a human being, they are called "one's own species."
Regarding *dukkaṭa*: failing to maintain bodily decorum constitutes *dukkaṭa*. Regarding *pāruṣya* (harsh speech):
to say, "You are a craftsman, a son of an artisan, or one with deficient faculties"—to speak in such a manner constitutes a *pāyattika*; this is called the minor offense of harsh speech.
"Regarding 'heavy': the *pārājika* and the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
The *sthūlātyaya* incurred at these two extremes is heavy.
Furthermore, there are offenses that are heavy for a bhikṣu but light for a bhikṣuṇī."
There are some offenses that are grave for a bhikṣuṇī but light for a bhikṣu.
Regarding those that are grave for a bhikṣu: if one intentionally emits semen, the bhikṣu incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, whereas the bhikṣuṇī incurs a pāyattika offense.
Regarding the gravity of offenses for bhikṣuṇīs: when a bhikṣuṇī’s lustful desire is intense, she rubs her hand against a man in a secluded place;
the man likewise rubs her in a secluded place;
both experience the pleasure of touch.
If a bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense;
or if a bhikṣuṇī knows that another bhikṣuṇī has committed a grave offense,
yet conceals it and does not speak of it to even one bhikṣuṇī;
One also incurs a *pārājika* offense if a bhikṣu does not comply with the legal procedures of the Saṃgha,
and the Saṃgha accordingly grants him a *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure).
Furthermore, a bhikṣuṇī says:
"This bhikṣu accords with the Dharma of the Saṃgha," speaking in various ways so as to be of one mind with the bhikṣu.
The bhikṣuṇīs admonished them, saying,
"There is no need to exchange words and provide mutual assistance.
But they did not accept the admonition of the bhikṣuṇīs, continuing to exchange words and provide mutual assistance without ceasing.
If a nun performs the formal act of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* [on behalf of another],
this nun incurs a *pārājika* offense.
Furthermore, there are eight matters by which a bhikṣuṇī incurs a *pārājika* offense:
First, a nun and a man grasp each other's hands;
second, they further grasp each other's robes;
third, they sit together with a man in a secluded and private place.
Fourth, conversing together in a secluded place;
fifth, physical contact in a secluded place;
sixth, traveling alone on a road with a man.
Seventh, to have physical contact while naked on the road;
eighth, to go together to a place where impurity is practiced as previously agreed upon.
If a nun commits the first seven matters, she incurs a *sthūlātyaya*; if all eight matters are fulfilled, she incurs a *pārājika*.
This refers to cases where a bhikṣuṇī commits a grave offense while a bhikṣu commits a light one;

or where there is a grave offense with a light retribution; or where there is a light offense with a grave retribution; or where there is a grave offense with a grave retribution; or where there is a light offense with a light retribution.

There are cases where the offense is grave but the retribution is light: for instance, if a bhikṣu acts as a go-between to bring together a man and a woman, he incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense if they are united, but a sthūlātyaya offense if they are not.

If a bhikṣu privately constructs a dwelling without informing the Saṃgha and requesting *karmavācanā*, he commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense before it is completed; once it is completed, he commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
This is called a heavy offense with a light retribution.

Regarding offenses that are light in nature but result in heavy retribution: if a bhikṣu, with a mind of anger, strikes an arhat; or, with a lustful mind, touches an arhat and gives rise to defiled attachment; or even strikes the Buddha while giving rise to a mind of defiled desire toward the Buddha; or if one uses harsh speech to revile an arhat or the Buddha, disparaging them as being deformed, crippled, or lacking sense organs—this constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. This is called an offense that is light in nature but results in heavy retribution.

Regarding those who commit grave offenses and receive grave retribution: for a *pārājika* offense, as well as the two cases of groundless slander against an *arhat* or an ordinary person, one incurs the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
As for the "two groundless [slanders]":
once, out of a mind of anger, a bhikṣu sent his younger sister, the bhikṣuṇī Maitrī, to slander the *arhat* Dharmaruci, saying:
"Venerable sir, engage in sexual intercourse with me.
This constitutes slandering another bhikṣu.
While traveling along the road, he sees two rams engaging in sexual intercourse, and a thought arises in his mind:
"Since my previous slander was false, today I shall take this ewe as the nun Maitreyī and this ram as the monk Dharmaruci.
Having formed this thought, he went to the monastery and said to the assembly of monks:
"My former account was untrue; today I have seen it for myself."
The bhikṣus then admonished him, saying:
"This one is an arhat; do not slander him with evil words.
He replied:
"It is indeed so.
Listen to what I shall say.
The bhikṣus listened.
He said:
"As I was traveling along the road earlier, I saw two sheep engaging in sexual intercourse.
The male sheep was the son of Dharmaruci, and the female sheep was the nun Maitrī."
When the bhikṣus heard these words, they immediately began to discuss them. These two cases both lack a basis;
this is called the two types of groundless slander. First, defiling another's family;

second, the means of breaking the Saṃgha that maintains the Wheel of Dharma; third, following the assembly of those who break the Saṃgha that maintains the Wheel of Dharma; fourth, being of evil character and refusing to accept admonition from others—these incur the saṃghāvaśeṣa offense. This is a grave transgression, and the retribution for it is likewise grave.

Regarding offenses that are light and whose retribution is also light: if a bhikṣu enters a village and fails to maintain mindfulness regarding the four dignities of the body and the four faults of speech, and thus commits an offense through forgetfulness or error, he should confess a *pāyattika* and a *dukkaṭa* before a single person.

If a bhikṣuṇī has committed an offense but initially forgot it and did not disclose it, and only remembers it at the time of the poṣadha, she may, fearing that disclosing it would disturb the assembly listening to the precepts, think silently in her mind:
"I shall confess it after the recitation of the precepts is finished."
"In cases such as these, both the offense and the retribution are minor.
There are three types of offenses:
first, those where the matter is grave but the intent is light."
Second, the matter is light while the mind is heavy;
third, both the matter and the mind are heavy.

Regarding the case where the matter is heavy and the mind is light: if a bhikṣu preaches the Dharma to a bhikṣuṇī in a nunnery after sunset, yet in his mind he harbors the doubt that the sun has not set while he is preaching, this is an instance where the matter is heavy and the mind is light.

Regarding "the matter is light but the mind is heavy": when a bhikṣu preaches the Dharma in a nunnery, if the sun has not yet set but he thinks it has already set while preaching, this is a case where the matter is light but the mind is heavy.

Regarding those cases where both the intention and the action are grave: when a bhikṣu preaches the Dharma in a nunnery and the sun has already set, yet he perceives it as not having set—this is a case where both the intention and the action are grave.
In the two other cases—where the intention is light but the action is grave, or where the intention is grave but the action is light—one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense in both instances.
If both the intention and the act are grave, one incurs a *pāyattika*.
Although the names of the offenses, such as *pārājika*, are the same, their karmic retributions differ. Why is this so?
Just as the objects of sexual misconduct are not limited to one, they include both animals and humans.
Among humans, there are those who have left the household life and those who have not.
Furthermore, among those who have not left the household life, there are two types: those who maintain the precepts and those who do not.
Among those who have left the household life, there are five types, including those who maintain the precepts, those who do not maintain them, and even sages.
Because there are such distinctions, although the name "offense" is the same, the retributive results differ.
Regarding the second *pārājika*: the places from which theft is committed are not limited to one; they include both those in the ordained community and those in the lay community.

Among laypeople, there are distinctions in the theft of another's property; among the ordained, there are likewise distinctions in theft; and within the Three Jewels, there are also distinctions in theft.
Therefore, although the name "pārājika" is the same, the retributive results differ.
Regarding the third pārājika: whether it be devas, humans, or even noble ones (ārya), if one such as these has their life-faculty severed, one incurs a pārājika offense.
Although the names of these abandonments are the same, their retributive fruits also differ.

Regarding the fourth *pārājika*, there is likewise a distinction: it is grave to claim to have attained superhuman states (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*) when speaking to laypeople, whereas it is light when speaking to those who have left the household life.
"Therefore, although the names of the offenses incurred are the same, their karmic retributions differ.
*Vinayamātṛkā Sūtra*, Fascicle II;
*Vinayamātṛkā Sūtra*, Fascicle III.
The translator's name is lost; it is now appended to the Qin Records.
"What is meant by 'residual' (saṃghāvaśeṣa)? Because the offense can be removed, it is therefore called 'residual. What is meant by 'without residual' (anavaśeṣa)?"
The four *pārājika* offenses cannot be remedied; therefore, they are called "without remainder" (*anavaśeṣa*).
What is meant by "gross and evil transgression"?

It is when a person intends to commit one of the four *pārājika* acts, and whether through bodily action or verbal expression, lacks shame and dread of blame; because of these two factors, the *pārājika* act is inevitably accomplished—this is called "gross and evil."
Furthermore, there is one case that is turbid and grave: when a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense is nearly completed through its preliminary effort (*prayoga*), this constitutes it.
These two types of *sthūlātyaya* are called turbid and grave offenses.
What is not coarse, turbid, or heavy?

The *pāyattika*, the *pratideśanīya*, the natural *sthūlātyaya*, and the *duṣkṛta*—these are likewise unwholesome actions of body and speech, yet they do not constitute the preparatory means for a major offense; for this reason, they are not coarse, evil, turbid, or heavy.
If a śrāmaṇera or śrāmaṇerī commits a pārājika offense, they incur a duṣkṛta, which cannot be expiated through confession.
"There are offenses that require a formal ritual (karmavācanā) and those that do not."
Regarding offenses that require a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*): such as the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* down to harsh speech, these offenses can be removed through a formal ritual.
Those that do not require a formal ritual are the three *pārājika* offenses.
There is one *pārājika* offense that may be removed through a formal act (*karmavācanā*). Which one?
For example, the bhikṣu Nandika was constantly sitting in meditation in a secluded and quiet place, when a celestial Māra transformed himself into the form of a woman and appeared before him.
Nanda’s lustful mind was so intense that he pursued this woman.
Māra immediately concealed his form, and Nanda saw a dead horse with whom he committed an act of impurity.
Having done so, he immediately felt remorse; he took off his *kāṣāya* robe, embraced it to his chest, wept, and raising his hands, cried out to heaven:
"I am neither a śramaṇa nor a son of the Śākya.
Having gone to the World-Honored One, he confessed his transgression to the Buddha exactly as it had occurred.

Knowing that this bhikṣu’s intention in confessing was sincere and that he would not commit the offense again, the Buddha immediately assembled the bhikṣus and performed the formal ritual of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the motion followed by three proclamations) to restore his status and grant him the precepts.
The reason one obtains the precepts is twofold: first, this person has seen the Buddha; second, their resolve to confess is profound. Thus, they obtain the precepts.
Although they have regained the precepts, they must sit below all great practitioners of the Way, and they may not participate equally in any monastic ritual acts.
This is called "having need" and "not having need.
The Venerable Sarvāstivādin said:

"If a bhikṣu attains worldly concentration and arises from the fourth dhyāna, and the celestial Māra assumes the form of a woman to delude his mind, this bhikṣu then engages in impure conduct with her."

Having committed the offense, he immediately regrets it with a mind free from concealment; his remorse continues in an uninterrupted succession of moments without a single thought of hiding it, yet he does not take pleasure in abandoning the dharma-robes within his heart.
Such a person should request from the Saṃgha the *karma* for the removal of the *pārājika* offense.
The Saṃgha shall perform for this person the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) for the removal of the *pārājika* offense.

Once this person has received the precepts, they must follow all the instructions of the Saṃgha throughout their life. They are not permitted to act as an *upādhyāya* or an *ācārya*, nor may they act as a teacher (*śikṣamāṇā-ācārya*) for nuns. When the Saṃgha assembles, they are not permitted to recite the *Prātimokṣa*. While they are permitted to listen to all Dharma activities, they must sit below the great monks; they are not permitted to share the same seating row with the Saṃgha for meals.
As the Venerable Vaśa said:

"If a bhikṣu attains mundane concentration (*laukika-samādhi*), and having arisen from that concentration, his mind becomes deluded and distracted, or he is driven by sorcery, or even possessed by spirits, he may consequently engage in unchaste conduct."

Having committed the offense, one immediately regrets it and confesses it with a mind free from concealment; furthermore, not wishing to discard the dharma-robes, one should request from the Saṃgha the *karman* for the removal of the *pārājika* offense.

In accordance with the Sangha’s decree, for as long as life lasts, you shall not act as an upādhyāya or ācārya; you shall not serve as a preceptor for bhikṣuṇīs; when the great assembly gathers, you shall not recite the precepts, nor shall you perform *karmavācanā* on behalf of others; you shall sit below all fully ordained monks (*bhikṣu*) and above the novices (*śrāmaṇera*); and you shall not eat from the same grass mat as the Sangha.
There was a bhikṣu named Śāṇakavāsin who was practicing dhyāna-concentration in a secluded place.
Various donors sent him food every day, and there were no men present in between.
There was a woman who regularly brought him food; she came repeatedly and incessantly until she conceived a lustful mind and committed an act of impurity with him.
Having done so, she immediately felt remorse, stripped off her three robes and placed them on her shoulders, fled with her body exposed, and cried out, "Thief! Thief!"
A person from the borderlands asked him,
"What kind of bandits are there?
He replied:
"Plundered and exhausted by the thieves of the afflictions," he confessed before the donors and the assembly of monks with a heart free from concealment.
A wise person among the Sangha said to him:
"There is the Venerable Paśya, who is well-versed in the Vinaya and can remove your offense.
That bhikṣu then went to Paśya’s place and recounted his transgression to him exactly as it had occurred.
Vāsava said, "If you wish to eliminate your offense, can you follow my instructions?
He replied:
"Never! Vatsa sent someone to construct a great fire pit filled with blazing flames and said:
"If you wish to eliminate your sin, you may throw yourself into this pit."
Pakṣa had previously discussed with the other bhikṣus:
"If a bhikṣu enters the pit directly, you must seize him.
This bhikṣu, following Pakṣa’s words, was about to enter the pit directly when those nearby seized him.

Vaspa, knowing that this bhikṣu’s mind was sincere, immediately performed the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal procedure consisting of one motion and three proclamations) to remove his *pārājika* offense.
From this point forward, having received the *karman*, this bhikṣu shall be known as one who maintains the precepts with purity.

However, with this single body, one cannot transcend birth and death to realize the four fruits of the path, nor can one attain untainted merit; yet, such a person is merely shielded from entering hell.
It is as impossible as fallen tree leaves growing back upon that same tree;
likewise, it is impossible for one who has committed an offense against the first category of precepts to realize the four fruits of the path and attain untainted merit.
Although this person is in the same place as the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha is separated from him by ten thousand paths.
As stated above, there are seven kinds of offenses for violating the precepts:
first, the pārājika;
2. Saṃghāvaśeṣa; 3. Naiḥsargika-pāyattika; 4. Pāyattika.
Five sthūlātyaya; six prādeśanīya;
seven duṣkṛta.
Regarding a *pārājika* offense: it does not give rise to wholesome roots and can never be expiated; furthermore, there is no *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) by which the offense may be removed.
There are also *sthūlātyaya* offenses that cannot have their guilt removed through *karmavācanā*.
What is it? It is, for example, Devadatta shedding the Buddha’s blood.
This *sthūlātyaya* offense never allows the arising of untainted (*anāsrava*) roots of goodness, nor can the sin be removed through ritual action (*karma*).
There are *pāyattika* offenses for which no roots of goodness can arise and for which no *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) can effect the removal of the guilt. Why?
For example, if a bhikṣu, out of a mind of hatred, intends to take the life of the Buddha and strikes him, he incurs a *pāyattika*, which cannot be expiated through confession.
There is a *duṣkṛta* offense, yet it does not give rise to wholesome roots, nor is there a formal ritual (*karman*) for its removal. Why?
If a *śrāmaṇera*, *śrāmaṇerī*, or *śikṣamāṇā* commits even one of the four *pārājika* offenses, this transgression cannot be expiated.
Therefore, there are offenses for which a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) is required and those for which it is not, as explained above.
That which requires a *karmavācanā* followed by another *karmavācanā* refers to the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offenses requiring suspension).
Regarding "having performed the *karmavācanā* and not performing it again," this refers to the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*, the ninety-two *pāyattikas*, and so forth.
"One who wishes to confess must fulfill five requirements:
first, adjust one's robes;..."
Second, remove one’s leather sandals;
third, kneel with the right knee on the ground;
fourth, join the palms together.
The fifth is the declaration of the offense committed.
One should repent in this manner; if one does not do so, it is not called repentance.
There are five kinds of offenses that are easily removed:
First, an offense with guilt should be removed in the presence of one bhikṣu; if no bhikṣu is present, it may also be removed by making a vow in one's own mind.
Second, for the commission of a *duṣkṛta* (misdeed) or harsh speech, it is extinguished by confessing it before a single person.
Third, as with the *pāyattika* and the *svabhāva-sthūlātyaya*, one may eliminate them by repenting before a single person.

Fourth, the *sthūlātyaya* bordering on the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* and the *sthūlātyaya* bordering on the *pārājika* are removed through *karmavācanā* within an assembly of four or more; the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* is as explained above.

Fifth is the *karmavācanā* (formal act) from ground to ground; one should know that there is a general designation for this mentioned in the *Śīlaskandhaka* (Chapter on Receiving the Precepts). What is it?

From the *pārājika* offenses down to the seven methods for settling disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*), whatever constitutes a breach is termed an "offense"; therefore, this is called the "compilation of offenses."
Regarding the method of admonition: if a bhikṣu has committed an offense and other bhikṣus have seen, heard, or suspect it, they should first inform the senior monk (sthavira) and the Saṃgha.
If the senior monk and the Saṃgha grant permission, they should further ask the offender:
"We now wish to admonish you; will you listen?"
If the Elder and the Saṃgha who have committed an offense grant their consent (*chanda*), one may offer the admonition.
If neither of them consents, or if one consents while the other does not, in all such cases, the admonition must not be given.
One who offers admonition must first establish five virtues within themselves before offering that admonition:
first, to admonish at the appropriate time;
second, to have a sincere heart rather than a deceitful one.
Third, one offers admonition for the sake of benefit, not for the sake of harm;
fourth, one offers admonition with gentle speech, not with harsh or evil words;
fifth, one offers admonition out of a heart of loving-kindness, not because one seeks to find fault.
Regarding the one who offers admonition: once the assembly of monks has gathered and taken their seats in order, the person who has an issue sits separately.
The one who offers the admonition rises from his seat, approaches the person who committed the offense, and [addresses them] according to what was seen, heard, or suspected.
There are three categories of offenses:
first, those such as pārājika, saṃghāvaśeṣa, and sthūlātyaya, which are termed "precepts";
second, the destruction of right view and dwelling within wrong views; [and third, the destruction of right conduct and dwelling within wrong conduct].
Third, from the *pāyattika* down to harsh speech, these are termed "actions.
Seeing, hearing, or suspecting [an offense] arises in relation to these three bases.
The one who offers admonition may speak either in private or in the midst of the assembly, saying:
"You must recall the offense you originally committed.
You may not participate in the ritual acts of the Saṃgha; you should depart.
Once your offense has been removed according to the Dharma, you shall later return to join the Saṃgha."
This is called the admonition through recollection.
Regarding those for whom the method of admonition is not successful: once the Saṃgha has assembled, the one who has committed an offense sits in a separate place.
The admonisher asks:
"Does the one who has committed an offense listen to admonition? He replied, "I do."
If one who has business to attend to hears the matter and immediately departs, this does not constitute a formal admonition.
Likewise, if one who is to admonish another asks about the matter and then immediately departs—as was the case with the group of six bhikṣus—this also does not constitute a formal admonition.
Furthermore, if one asks a person regarding their offense and then immediately departs after asking, it does not constitute a formal admonition.
When is it called "the time for admonition"?

When the assembly of monks has gathered together and granted their consent (*chanda*), when the offender is present and grants his consent, and when the one who offers the admonition is present—these conditions together are called "the time for admonition."
At that time, the Venerable Sarvāstivādin spoke, saying:
"The one who offers admonition says to the offender:
'I am mindful of you; I speak to you; I admonish you.'"
The offender replied:
"It is well that you have remembered me, spoken to me, and admonished me."
Regarding those who receive admonition, one should not accept the admonitions of five kinds of persons:
first, those who lack a sense of shame and dread of blame;
second, those who have not studied extensively.
Third, constantly seeking out the faults of others;
fourth, delighting in quarrels and disputes;
fifth, desiring to discard the robes and return to lay life.
These five kinds of persons should not accept such admonition; this is called "not accepting admonition.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Once the one who admonishes has received the formal consent (chanda) from the person who has committed an offense, he must not depart and leave."
The one who departs incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*.

From this time forward, when one offers admonition, they should do so before the Saṃgha and then depart after having admonished the offender at a location within the monastery where the offender has agreed to meet—whether it be a gathering for drinking sweet gruel, eating congee, performing the *poṣadha*, the *pravāraṇā*, or any other formal monastic assembly.
"If there is no great assembly, one or two bhikṣus who possess knowledge and vision of the Tripiṭaka should admonish him before he departs.
The Venerable Mahīśāsaka said:
"Regarding the formal act of silencing (vācanīya-karman): if there is a bhikṣu who has first broken the precepts, second, broken his views, and third, broken his conduct..."
The community of monks should admonish this person because they ought to establish themselves in the five virtues.

If he is by nature unwilling to accept the words of others, and furthermore relies on his own cleverness and great wisdom, possesses a vast following, and additionally relies on the power of kings and ministers to refuse admonition, the community of monks should perform the *akṣānti-karman* (the rite of silence) against him.
This is called "stopping the recitation.
Regarding "stopping the recitation of the precepts," the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If there is anyone among the assembly who is not pure, you must stop and not recite the precepts."
Having heard the Buddha’s words, the group of six bhikṣus immediately went throughout the monasteries and proclaimed:
“The Buddha has forbidden it; the recitation of the precepts is not permitted.
The World-Honored One said:
"I do not suspend the recitation of the precepts for pure bhikṣus.
