If, among the seven classes of offenses, there is even one instance of harsh speech, those present in the assembled Saṃgha who have committed such an offense shall stop; those who have committed no offense may then recite."
This is called suspending the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*.
Regarding the suspension of the *Pravāraṇā*, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If there is anyone within the assembly who is not pure, the *Pravāraṇā* should be suspended and not performed."
One should perform the *prātimokṣa* ceremony for the *pravāraṇā*; those who are not pure should be investigated.
If they are serious offenders, they should be expelled; if their offenses are minor, they should be made to confess. Only then should the *pravāraṇā* be held.

If such an impure person, relying on their own cleverness and great wisdom, as well as the power of their followers, the king, or high ministers, cannot be expelled, they shall wait until the subsequent *pravāraṇā*.
"If the time for the *pravāraṇā* has arrived and you still do not come forth, the community of monks may perform the *pravāraṇā* separately and attain purity.
What is called the *Prātimokṣa*?
Prātimokṣa is called the supreme meaning.
For what reason is it called supreme?
Because the root of all virtues is precept, and through it all wholesome qualities arise; therefore, it is called the supreme meaning.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of ethical discipline:
first, the supramundane;
second, the mundane.
This mundane [virtue] can serve as the cause for the supramundane; therefore, it is called "most excellent.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of precepts:
first, those based on body and speech;
The second is the precept based on the mind.
Because one obtains the precept based on the mind by relying upon the precepts of body and speech, it is called the "foremost.
This *prātimokṣa* shall be explained in detail in the *Poṣadha-vastu*.
“Furthermore, there are five ways of reciting the *Poṣadha* in both expanded and abbreviated forms.
First, after reciting the *Pratimokṣa-sūtra* up to the four *Pārājika* rules, one says for all the remaining rules: ‘You have heard these repeatedly.
Second, after reciting the *Pratimokṣa-sūtra* up to the four *Pārājika* rules and the thirteen *Saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules, one says for all the remaining rules: ‘You have heard these repeatedly.’”

In the third [recitation], after the *Prātimokṣa* introduction, the four *pārājika* rules, the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules, and the two *aniyata* rules have been concluded, for all remaining precepts it is said: "You have heard these repeatedly.

In the fourth [recitation], from the *Prātimokṣa* introduction up until the conclusion of the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules, for all remaining precepts it is said: "You have heard these repeatedly."
The fifth point is as explained in detail above:

a bhikṣu must recite the Prātimokṣa according to the essential rules of the bhikṣus; if he does not recite it, he must reside at a place where the Vinaya is being recited during the three periods of the day.
Why is this? If one has committed an offense or harbors doubts, by repenting and resolving those doubts, one attains the removal of the transgression.
For this reason, the Buddha established that bhikṣus must recite the Prātimokṣa.
"Why is it called *poṣadha*? 'Cessation' (*puṣ*) is called *poṣadha*.
To be able to cease what has been transgressed, to be able to cease the afflictions (*kleśa*), and to cease all unwholesome phenomena (*akuśala-dharma*)—this is the meaning of *poṣadha*."
Purity is called *poṣadha*.
What is meant by the *poṣadha-karman*?

When the Saṃgha intends to perform the *poṣadha*, the junior-most member of the assembly should sweep the hall, spread out the sitting mats, take scented water to sprinkle upon the ground, and light lamps. All such matters as these are termed the *poṣadha-karman*.
"What is meant by *pravāraṇā* (self-indulgence)?
When a bhikṣu has completed the summer retreat (*varṣā*), he requests [the community] to point out any offenses regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected before a wise and pure bhikṣu.

The reason for making this request is that during the ninety days of the summer, he wishes to clarify that his observance of the precepts and other virtues remained entirely without transgression; therefore, it is only upon the conclusion of the *anvaya* (rainy-season retreat) that the term *pravāraṇā* is first applied."
For what reason does the Buddhist teaching perform the *pravāraṇā*?
First, so that each may exhort one another;
second, so that each may remind one another.
Third, they mutually instruct one another;
fourth, they each show mutual respect;
fifth, their speech is always in harmony with one another.
All six [types of *pravāraṇā*] have a basis and are not without a basis;
therefore, they are called *pravāraṇā*.

Regarding the *pravāraṇā-karman*, the lowest-ranking seat among the assembly should sweep the hall, spread out the bedding, light the lamps, and take up the incense and fire; such matters as these are all termed *karman*.
If food has been kept overnight in a place within a boundary that has not been formally consecrated as a pure kitchen,
no śramaṇas are permitted to eat it. At that time,
the Buddha was traveling through the country of Vṛji, journeying from place to place until he arrived at the country of Vaiśālī.
Hearing the loud voices of the bhikṣus, the Buddha asked Ānanda,
"What matter are these monks disputing over?
Ānanda immediately went to see and saw that the bhikṣus had accumulated a great deal of food.
He came and said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
The resident bhikṣus, śrāmaṇeras, and attendants wished to prepare food for the visiting bhikṣus; that is why they raised their voices."
The Buddha then addressed Ānanda, saying:
“Go and tell the bhikṣus:

‘From this day forward, except when the Saṃgha has assembled for a formal ritual (karmavācanā) at a purified kitchen, you must not eat food that has been stored overnight within the boundary (sīmā).’”

Again, at another time, the World-Honored One was in Vārāṇasī. At that time, there was a famine in the world, and the community of monks gathered grain and rice and stored it beyond the boundary; people all stole and carried it away.
The bhikṣus spoke to one another in succession and went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"In years of scarcity, I permit grain and rice to be kept within the boundary; this applies even to medicinal herbs in the same way."
"Furthermore, at another time, there was a period of scarcity when grain was expensive and people lacked propriety and righteousness.
While the bhikṣus were cooking their food outside the boundary, those who had the strength all seized and carried it away."
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who said:
"I allow you to cook food within the boundary and eat it within the boundary.
Later, when śrāmaṇeras and upāsakas divided and reduced the portions and took them away, they again informed the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"I permit the bhikṣus to cook their food with their own hands.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
There was a sick bhikṣu who habitually ate congee, and a donor used to send it to him every day.
One day, the city gates were closed, so he could not come; the bhikṣu thus missed his meal.
The Buddha then performed a formal act of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* within the boundary for this sick bhikṣu to designate a pure kitchen area, permitting him to cook and eat gruel in that pure place.
At that time, the bhikṣus became doubtful, saying: "This bhikṣu is eating food that has been kept overnight, rice cooked within the boundary, and food prepared by his own hand."
The Buddha said:
"It is not food stored overnight, nor food cooked within a boundary, nor food prepared by one's own hand.
This applies even to medicinal herbs in the same way."
At that time, the World-Honored One was in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.

During a period of famine, some bhikṣus were traveling along the road; they saw ripe fruits fallen on the ground, yet they did not take them for themselves, waiting instead for a kappiya-kāraka (a person authorized to handle such things).
Later, a layperson arrived and immediately took it away.
The bhikṣu informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to cover your head with grass while you wait for a *kappiya-kāraka*.
While he was covering his head with grass and waiting for the *kappiya-kāraka*, another layperson came, stripped away the grass, saw him, and immediately took him away.
He spoke again to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"I permit you to take it with your own hand, carry it to a pure place and set it on the ground, and then return to receive and eat it according to the Dharma."
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:

"Since the price of grain has been high, we pray that the World-Honored One will permit the bhikṣus to eat food kept overnight, to prepare their own food with their hands, and to gather fruit for themselves."
The Buddha said:
"This may be done during the period since the grain has become expensive.
If a bhikṣu receives food before the midday meal and, having gone elsewhere, receives enough food there, he may return and offer this food to the donor.
At that time, there was a famine in the world, and the donor ate [the food] himself.
A bhikṣu went to inform the Buddha:
"Yesterday there was leftover food which we gave to the donor, hoping to receive food again on a later day."
The donor then ate it himself.
The Buddha said,
"In years of famine, it is permitted for one to take up food for oneself even when no donor is present."
At that time, there was a community of monks of great virtue who were highly esteemed by the king and his ministers; various donors invited them into the village for a meal.
After they had eaten, they took the remains of the food back to the monastery and gave it to the other bhikṣus.

"Regarding those who wish to eat: during times of scarcity, one may eat without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (the ritual for leftover food); when times become abundant, one must perform the *kṛtapiṇḍa* ritual with the donor before one may eat."
If, at a later time, grain becomes expensive and the people suffer from famine,
and if monks obtain fruit after their meal and wish to eat it, they may eat it even without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (leftover-food) rite;
however, once the abundance returns, they may not do so.
In times of scarcity, if a bhikṣu obtains various edible roots of plants or medicinal herbs, he may take and eat them himself even without a donor;
however, this is not permitted during times of abundance.
"What is meant by receiving the *kaṭhina* robe according to the Dharma?
When the Saṃgha is assembled in its entirety and there are no obstacles present, and a donor offers a new robe in accordance with the Dharma, it should be accepted."
That which is in accordance with the Dharma is not brocade clothing nor clothing of superior colors; this is called clothing in accordance with the Dharma.

When the monks within the boundary who are ill or those engaged in affairs for the Three Jewels have granted their consent (*yadṛcchā*), and then a formal motion and one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) are performed, this is called being in accordance with the Dharma.
Why is it not called "acceptance"?
A group that is not in accordance with the Dharma and a community of monks outside the boundary—these are called "non-acceptance.
This is the "Method for Relinquishing the Kaṭhina Robe."

When the fifth month has concluded, and the community of monks has assembled together with no one present being hindered, and the monks within the boundary have granted their consent (*chanda*) according to the Dharma, performing a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* and not any other *karman*, this is called a formal relinquishment performed according to the Dharma.
There are eight ways of relinquishing the *kaṭhina* robe:
first, after having accepted the robe, one leaves the monastery enclosure; this is called "relinquishment by departure.

Second, if a bhikṣu, having accepted the *guṇa-vastra* (the meritorious robe), goes out from the monastery to wander and seek [alms] abroad, and hears that the Saṃgha has already completed the relinquishment of the robe, he forms this thought:
"I shall seek other robes.
This is called relinquishing at the time of exhaustion.
Having received the *guṇa-cīvara* (robe of merit) three times and finished traveling abroad, he hears that the robes have already been relinquished at the monastery, and he thinks thus:
"I shall no longer seek robes.
This is called "ultimate relinquishment" (atyanta-tyāga).

Fourth, if a bhikṣu, having received a robe, goes outside to seek further robes and, upon obtaining them, thieves immediately steal them, and he hears that [the original robe] has already been relinquished at the monastery, this is called "relinquishment by loss of time" (kāla-vipanna-tyāga).

Fifth, if a bhikṣu, having received a robe, goes outside to beg for the hope of obtaining another robe, but fails to obtain one, and hears that the *kaṭhina* has already been relinquished at the monastery, this is called relinquishment upon the cessation of hope.
6. If a bhikṣu, having received his robes, goes outside to seek them and hears that they have already been discarded at the monastery, he thinks:
"I shall seek the three robes again."
This is called "abandoning upon hearing. Seventh:

if a bhikṣu, having received a robe, goes outside the boundary with the expectation of returning immediately, but after many days have passed he returns while still outside the boundary and hears that the robe has already been abandoned at the monastery; this is called "abandoning while outside the boundary."

Eighth: If a bhikṣu, having received a robe, goes outside to seek further robes, whether he obtains them or not, he returns immediately to the monastery; when the Sangha then relinquishes the robe, this is called relinquishment in accordance with the Dharma.
Apart from these eight types, all other categories of non-dharmic items are neither termed "received" nor "renounced.
Regarding the distribution of the belongings of a deceased bhikṣu:

robes, alms bowls, sitting mats, needle-cases, woolen bags, *kuśa*-grass garments with hair three finger-widths deep, umbrellas, and razors—these are called the communal requisites that may be divided.
The Venerable Kāśyapamati said:
"Regarding the method for distributing the belongings of a deceased bhikṣu: first, having taken the deceased’s items away for safekeeping, the community of monks returns to the monastery."
The monks present should assemble; having assembled, they shall take the belongings of the deceased bhikṣu and place them before the community of monks, dispatching one person to distribute them.
Items that may be divided and those that may not be divided shall each be placed in separate locations.
The three robes should be given to the caregiver; the remaining items shall be distributed among the monks present.

If there are male or female slaves, they should be released and allowed to go; if they are not released, they should be made into *śaikṣaka* attendants for the Saṃgha. Elephants, camels, horses, oxen, and donkeys are to be used by the resident monks of the monastery for transporting goods.

If this deceased bhikṣu has any assets or property outside [the monastery], one should dispatch a *śaikṣa* or a *karmadāna* of the monastery’s communal property (*saṃghika*) to search for and recover them; once recovered, they shall be added to the permanent property of the monastic community of this monastery.
Objects made of clay or iron should be divided as property.

These include: iron ladles, iron bracelets, *śūrpa* winnowing baskets, axes, five-foot swords, door-hooks, needle-cases, knives, scissors, iron staffs, incense burners, braziers, bowls, umbrellas, umbrella handles, and incense containers; such items should be understood in detail.
Large copper bowls, small copper bowls, copper bracelets, copper staffs, and so forth—all such categories are counted in the same manner as those made of iron.
Why is it called "heavy clothing" (*guruka-cīvara*)?
There are two kinds of "heaviness": [the heaviness of weight and the heaviness of value].
First, it is of great value; second, it can ward off the cold; therefore, it is called "heavy.
Regarding robes, they must be pure and properly received; what is impure is not permitted.
There are two kinds of purity:
First, once it has been dyed and the color has adhered, it is called "pure";
second, once the color has adhered and the three dots have been applied, it is also called "pure.

If a robe has been made, washed, dyed, and marked with the three dots, when donors see it, they know it is the garment of a śramaṇa and not the clothing of a non-Buddhist; for this reason, it is called a "heavy robe" (saṃghāṭī).

At that time, the Venerable Pilindavatsa suffered from eye pain; as he traveled along the road, his two feet stumbled against one another, causing him to fall westward as he tried to walk eastward, so that he was unable to advance on the path.
The Buddha saw them from afar and asked the bhikṣus,
"For what reason?
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha:
"Because his eyes ache and he cannot see the path.
At that time, the Buddha said,
"I allow you to wear leather sandals."

The Venerable Pilindavatsa was held in high esteem by the people of the country; some offered him nets, while others gave him elephants, horses, camels, carriages, or even constructed a small monastery as a gift.
The Buddha permitted the acceptance of all such offerings.
Because the Venerable One suffered from eye pain, a donor had a lapis lazuli bowl made for him.
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will allow Pilindavatsa to keep this medicinal herb to treat eye pain.
The Buddha said, “This substance is expensive; however, for the sake of treating illness, I permit you to keep it.”
Furthermore, there were various donors who offered heavy items such as vessels made of copper, iron, or clay, as well as copper basins and copper helmets; the Buddha permitted their possession.
He also said: "If someone offers soft garments of the finest quality and price, one is permitted to accept them through the ritual of *śuddhaka-dāna* (pure giving) and keep them."
Furthermore, regarding any heavy property belonging to the teacher, the disciple must not take it for himself; he may take it only if the Saṃgha gives it to him.
The disciple shall not place this object before the Saṃgha; the Saṃgha must not take it for itself, but shall divide it through a formal act (karmavācanā).
Why is this? Because these items belong to the Saṃgha of the four directions.
Furthermore, why are they called "heavy items" (*gurudravya*)?
Previously, "heavy items" were designated by way of their clothing; now, "heavy items" are designated by way of the objects themselves.

Regarding those things that should not be divided: if there is a private monastery, as well as all its fields, orchards, fruit trees, elephants, horses, camels, oxen, donkeys, and even items such as beds, stools, jars, and vessels for sustaining life—all these likewise belong to the Sangha of the four directions.

If a large hall or small room is constructed outside the grounds of the four directions, whatever property is therein shall not be divided among the present community of monks; it likewise belongs to the Sangha of the four directions.
This matter should be understood in detail within the Cīvara-vastu (The Chapter on Robes).
"If a refuse rag is within the four walls [of a village], a bhikṣu should not take it.
If the robe is upon a fence or within a city moat, it likewise should not be taken."
If one makes a hole through a wall to remove a dead person’s clothing from outside the wall, it should not be taken.

The reason the Buddha established this rule was that during a great epidemic of the time, countless people died; being unable to place them far away in the cemetery, they would instead pierce a wall and lay them outside.
The royal family had a regulation that forbade placing corpses outside the walls.
The guards immediately announced:
"Who is taking this dead person's clothing away?"
"You should have him carry the corpse to the cemetery.
The people replied,
"A śramaṇa took it yesterday."
The Magistrate immediately ordered the śramaṇas:
"Carry the dead person to the cemetery and discard it there.
For this reason, the Buddha established a precept for the bhikṣus, forbidding them from taking [such things].
Regarding a corpse in a cemetery that has not yet decomposed, one should not take the clothing upon that corpse.
One should also not take the clothing suspended upon a stūpa erected over a corpse.
Pamsukūla robes such as these should not be accepted at all.
Suppose there is a bhikṣu living alone in a separate location who falls ill and passes away.
All the robes, alms bowls, and requisites belonging to this bhikṣu should belong to the *saṃgha* present before him (*pratyutpanna-saṃgha*).
There was a monk who tended to the sick and, not knowing the proper procedure, took these robes and went to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha immediately instructed him, saying:
"Take these robes and go to the Saṃgha to request them from the Saṃgha."
"Starting from the Elder, each person should be asked: 'How much portion have you received that you would give to me?
Once each has been asked, the community of monks shall perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation) to bestow it upon him."

Therefore, the Buddha permitted [the distribution of] alms for this person, as they have performed the service of tending to the sick; it is for this reason that the Buddha permitted the begging of alms.
Furthermore, there are certain items that should not be distributed.
Why is this? Whatever sūtras and vinaya texts exist at the time [of distribution] should be allocated to those capable of reciting them.
If it is not possible to allocate them in this manner, the *saṃgha* present there should give them to those capable of reciting them; these items must not be sold or divided up.

If a bhikṣu dies alone in a layperson’s house within a village, and later there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, or śrāmaṇerīs, whichever among them arrives first, the donor should apply these goods to them.
If no one arrives, one should offer [the items] to the community of monks at whichever monastery is nearest.
What are called "requisites for sustaining life"?
They are whatever things are necessary for a person.
What are things that are not requisites for nourishing life?
That which is not used by humans is called "not nourishing life.
Even down to what is required by animals is called "nourishing life."
That which is not required by animals is called "not for the nourishment of living beings.

If a bhikṣu takes another's property intended for the nourishment of living beings, he must inform the other; if the other gives it, he may take it, but if the other does not give it, he must not take it.
Regarding the articles for the sustenance of animals, with the exception of those that can speak, not one may be taken.
As for those that can speak, one must ask them; if they give it, it may be taken; if they do not give it, it may not be taken.
The items a bhikṣu should properly possess are:
the alms-bowl, the three robes, the sitting mat, the needle-case and thread-container, and the water-jar and pitcher.

Those things he should not possess are: women, gold and silver, all precious objects, all implements of war, and vessels for strong liquor or fermented wine; such items as these should not be accepted or kept.
The bhikṣu Nanda’s lust was so intense that when a woman paid him obeisance, he immediately discharged his impurity onto the woman’s head.
Both Nanda and the woman were filled with shame and went at once to inform the Buddha. The Buddha instructed them to make a bag to contain it.
The Buddha permitted the keeping of a knife for three purposes: first, for cutting skin;
second, for clipping nails;
third, for breaking open sores.
Fourth, for cutting cloth;
fifth, for trimming the hair and threads on cloth;
sixth, for purifying fruit and so forth, as various needs arise during mealtime; for these reasons, its possession is permitted.
"The method for shaving the hair:
one should remove only the hair on the head and the beard; the hair on all other parts of the body is not permitted to be removed at all.
The reason for shaving the hair is to eliminate the mind of arrogance and self-reliance."
If the hair is long, one must not use scissors; rather, it should be removed using a razor.
Regarding the scissors prohibited by the Buddha: the group of six bhikṣus used scissors to shave their hair, and the other bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
Because of the group of six monks, the Buddha prohibited the use of scissors.
If a bhikṣu has a sore on his head, he may use scissors to trim around the sore and apply ointment.
A bhikṣu is not permitted to make a sharp wooden blade to scrape away sweat or remove hair; for every single hair cut, there is one *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one removes the hair from the head and it is severed, each instance constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
This is called the method for cutting hair.
Furthermore, regarding those who shave their hair, such as the youth Rāhula.

At that time, the Buddha descended from the Nyagrodha tree and proceeded toward the city of Kapilavastu to beg for alms. Meanwhile, Gopī and Rāhula were on a high tower when they saw the Buddha entering the city.
Gopī pointed to the Buddha and said to Rāhula,
"This is your father.
Rāhula immediately descended from the tower, approached the Buddha, and prostrated himself before him.
After the Buddha’s hand had touched Rāhula’s head, he was already filled with supreme joy.
The Buddha asked Rāhula,
"Do you wish to leave the household life?"
Rāhula replied,
“I wish to leave the household life.
He then led Rāhula to the Nyagrodha Monastery and said to Śāriputra:
"He shall be the preceptor for Rāhula.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"How should he be instructed in leaving the household life?"
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"First have their hair shaved and give them the saṃghāṭī robe; instruct them to kneel with palms joined, and then bestow upon them the three refuges, the five precepts, and the ten precepts of a śrāmaṇera."
"This was the beginning of shaving the head, donning the kashaya, and receiving the three refuges, the five precepts, and the ten precepts.
At that time, King Śuddhodana, hearing that Rāhula had left the household life, immediately went to where the Buddha was."
He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, bowed his head, and with tears flowing, addressed the Buddha:
"World-Honored One, my brothers have already gone forth together; I hoped that Rāhula would succeed me so that the ancestral temple would not be discontinued."
"How was Rāhula ordained?
The Buddha then explained to the King, his father, the various merits and great benefits of renunciation. Consequently, he established a regulation for those who would renounce the world hereafter:
"If one wishes to go forth, one must first inform one's parents."
"If my parents do not grant permission, I shall not be allowed to leave the household life.
This is called the method for ordaining a śrāmaṇera.
It is the initial stage of seeking permission from one's parents in accordance with the Dharma upon leaving the household life.
When the Buddha was in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī, five sages named Siṃhamati desired to leave the household life.
Without informing their parents, they came directly to the monastery seeking ordination; the Saṃgha immediately shaved their heads and granted them the going forth.
Later, the parents did not know where their son was; they searched throughout the village but could find no trace of him.
They then went to the monastery and questioned the śramaṇas, but all said they had not seen him.
Entering the monastery, they searched room by room until they suddenly saw their son, who had already shaved his head and left the household life.
The parents were immediately filled with indignation and said,
"How can these śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas speak such falsehoods?"
"Indeed, the sons of those who deliver others all say they do not see [the Buddha].
The bhikṣus then addressed the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, if one wishes to leave the household life, they must inform their parents, and the parents must grant their permission.

If one wishes to ordain a śrāmaṇera, one must first inform the Saṃgha; then, having shaved the head, the candidate shall receive the Three Refuges, the five precepts, and even the śrāmaṇera precepts."
"If the Saṃgha does not grant permission, one must not ordain a śrāmaṇera.
The causes and conditions regarding the ordination of śrāmaṇeras are explained in detail in the Vinaya.
When the bhikṣus had first gone forth, their hair later grew long; they went and informed the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"I permit you to shave it repeatedly.
This is the first account of the circumstances regarding shaving the hair repeatedly.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in the city of Rājagṛha.
The Buddha’s hair had grown long, and because of their hearts of reverence, none among the bhikṣus would shave it.
There was a youth named Upāli who, together with his parents, came to where the Buddha was; having seen the Buddha, he immediately conceived this thought:
"I wish to shave the Tathāgata’s hair.
Having formed this thought, he knelt with palms joined and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I now wish to shave the Buddha’s hair."
"We pray that your great compassion will grant us this permission.
The Buddha then ordered him to shave his hair.
Standing by his side, his parents addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Is it well to shave the hair?
The Buddha said,
"Shaving the hair is very good, but you are drawing too close to my body."
The youth slightly withdrew his body and raised his head; his parents asked again, "Is shaving your hair good?
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, but you are holding your head too high.
He lowered his head slightly, and his parents asked the Buddha again,
"Is shaving the hair good?"
The Buddha said, "Excellent; however, your exhalation is too coarse.
Thereupon, the youth ceased breathing and entered the fourth dhyāna.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This boy has entered the fourth dhyāna; you may take the razor from his hand.
Ānanda immediately took it.
There are three causes and conditions for which this youth dared to shave the hair of the Tathāgata:
first, he shaved it out of ignorance;
second, he shaved it because the Tathāgata’s supernormal power intended to cause him to attain the fourth dhyāna.
Third, he shaved his hair so that sentient beings of future generations might know that there is great merit in shaving the head.
When the Buddha was about to shave his hair, he addressed the people, saying:
"This hair must not be placed in old clothing or old vessels; it must be contained in new items."

While his hair was being shaved, Prince Gopāla came to where the Buddha was and requested the World-Honored One’s hair so that he might take it back to his country to offer worship; the Buddha immediately granted his request.
The prince then again addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"With what kind of vessel should these hairs be placed for offering?
The Buddha said:
"One should use vessels made of the seven precious gems to hold it for offering.
Thereupon, as instructed by the Buddha, he fashioned a vessel of the seven precious gems and used it to hold the contents.
He then asked the World-Honored One again:
"If one travels on elephants, horses, carriages, or upon the shoulders of men, at which of these places may one ride?
The Buddha said,
"One may ride in all of them."
"However, when you depart, you should take him away accompanied by various kinds of music.

The prince departed according to the Buddha's instructions; on the way, hearing that bandits from another country were approaching, he immediately erected a great stūpa along the road to enshrine the Buddha’s hair. This stūpa is known as the Stūpa of the Buddha’s Hair.
The Venerable Kāśyapīya said:
"Regarding the method of shaving the hair, the elder (sthavira) should shave first.
There is another teaching which says that those with the longest hair should shave first.
Furthermore, there is another principle: one who has previously washed their head should shave first.
Again, there is another principle: one who intends to travel on account of some business or circumstance should shave first.
This is called shaving hair in accordance with the Dharma.
"Furthermore, it is the rule for a bhikṣu not to intentionally kill sentient beings for food.
There are three bases for such food:
seeing, hearing, and suspecting; one should not eat [meat] based on these three bases."
If there is a donor who, when intending to perform a sacrifice to the heavens,
forms the thought: "Whoever comes should all be given food," and kills living beings with a non-discriminatory mind while waiting for all who might arrive.
"If a bhikṣu obtains meat from such a place as this, he should not eat it.
Furthermore, at one time the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī; the grain was expensive and the world was in a state of famine, making alms-food difficult to obtain.
Among the bhikṣus was one possessed of supernormal powers who, by means of his psychic power, traveled to the country of the non-Buddhists to beg for food.
When the non-Buddhist practitioners saw the bhikṣu coming to beg, they found him impure; they placed the food on the ground, abandoned it, and departed.
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
"Because food is difficult to obtain, we have used our supernatural powers to go to the lands of the non-Buddhists to beg for alms.
When the non-Buddhists saw us, they treated us with contempt and disdain; they placed the food on the ground and abandoned it before departing."
"How should this be understood?
The Buddha said:
"Even though he does not receive it with his hand, once it has been brought and placed before him, the act of giving is already complete."
"You should simply accept it; this itself constitutes the acceptance of food.
This is called "deliberate enjoyment.

"That which does not accord with the Vinaya" refers to calling what is Dharma "non-Dharma," and calling what is non-Dharma "Dharma," and so on, up to calling what is taught "not taught," and calling what is not taught "taught. This is called "not acceding with the Vinaya."
Furthermore, regarding what is improper: a bhikṣu says to other bhikṣus, "I cannot train in this dharma;
what is the use of these minor matters, O Venerable Ones?"
"I also know that this dharma enters the Vinaya and enters the Sūtras.
One should understand this in detail: this is called "not conforming to the Vinaya.

As for "conforming to the Vinaya," it is as the Buddha has taught: "this should be done, this should not be done; this is an offense, this is not an offense. Thus, not contradicting what the Buddha has said is called the meaning of "conforming to the Vinaya."
"What are called the life-sustaining requisites for humans?
They are the monastery attendants (*śrāmaṇeraka*).

What are the life-sustaining requisites for non-humans? Elephants, camels, horses, donkeys, and oxen that can transport things from afar for the Saṃgha are called the life-sustaining requisites for non-humans."
"What is meant by 'eating fruit'?
At that time, there was a great householder in the city of Rājagṛha who possessed many fruit trees.
The householder sent a messenger to offer fruit to the community of monks, saying to the messenger:"
"When you arrive at the monastery, you should find the Śākya son Baddhālitta and show him the fruit, telling him to distribute it to the community of monks.
At that time, Baddhālitta had gone out to eat; by the time he returned, the sun had already passed the midday hour, and the bhikṣus were unable to obtain any of the fruit to eat.
At that time, the World-Honored One was wandering in the Madhuvana forest.
A certain bhikṣu fell ill and required harītakī to take as medicine. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha immediately permitted the consumption of the three fruits:
[harītakī, āmalaka, and vibhītaka].
Harītakī, vibhītaka, and āmalaka.
Depending on the cause of the illness, if it does not subside, one may take these for as long as one lives.

Furthermore, on another occasion, Viśākhā Mṛgāramātā obtained a great quantity of fruit from outside; fearing she might eat them herself, as they were so sweet and delicious, she immediately invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha for a meal, intending to offer the fruit as well to the Buddha and the Saṅgha.
After the Buddha and the community of monks had finished their meal and departed, Visākhā Migāramātā, being preoccupied with many urgent affairs, forgot to offer the fruit.
Only after they had left did she remember; reflecting within herself, she thought:
"The reason I originally invited the Buddha and the Sangha was because I had this fruit and wished to make an offering of it."
"How was it forgotten?
He then sent someone carrying the fruit to the Buddha and the Sangha.
The members of the Sangha felt doubt in their hearts and did not dare to accept it immediately, so they reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "If you eat it according to the ritual for leftover food (vighasa-vidhi), there will be no fault.
In the pure area of the Sangha's grounds, a fruit tree suddenly sprang up; as the tree grew large, one of its branches curved over toward the impure area.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Send a lay attendant (kappiyakāraka) to strike it with a rope and lead it toward a pure place.
Later, the bhikṣus had doubts in their minds:
"This fruit was originally in an impure place; now that it has been pulled to a pure place, may it be eaten?
The Buddha said, "If the fruit fell upon impure ground, it may not be eaten; if it did not fall there, it may be eaten."
Furthermore, there may be fruit growing in impure ground, yet its branches and vines all lean toward pure ground.
"If it falls onto pure ground, it may be eaten; if it does not fall, it may not be eaten."
On another occasion, the bhikṣus obtained a great variety of fruits; however, as there were few people and many fruits, they could not finish eating them all.
They did not know where to use the remainder.
He informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to press it and take the juice; you may drink it until the first watch of the night."
"If it has not reached the first watch of the night, and its flavor has changed such that it becomes bitter wine, one must not drink it.
Why? Because this wine has already undergone two stages of fermentation."
There was a bhikṣu who ate fruit that had not been purified.
A non-Buddhist criticized and reproached him, saying:
"The bhikṣus have no heart of compassion; this fruit possesses life—how can they eat what is living?"
Because the world was dissatisfied with this, the Buddha immediately established a rule: "O bhikṣus!
Fruits must be purified before being eaten; if they are not purified, they must not be eaten."
There are five kinds of purification:
first, purification by fire;
second, purification by the knife; [and so forth].
Third, purity through the removal of birds;
fourth, purity through natural decay on the fruit itself;
fifth, purity through the removal of seeds.
Furthermore, there are seven kinds of purification:
first, purification by removing the skin;
second, purification by breaking [the surface].
Third, purification by rotting;
fourth, purification by withering;
fifth, purification by scraping and paring.
Sixth is purification by being washed away by water;
seventh is purification by being covered with dust and soil.
These are the methods of purification.
“At that time, the World-Honored One entered nirvana between the twin śāla trees in Kuśinagara, in the kingdom of Pāvā.

Five hundred Licchavi Mallas came to where the Buddha was and bathed the Buddha’s body with various kinds of fragrant water. First, they wrapped the Tathāgata’s body in kārpāsa cloth; then they wrapped it again in five hundred layers of fine, soft white cotton cloth. They placed ghee and fragrant oil into an iron coffin, and only then did they place the Tathāgata’s body within it.”
Again, he took various kinds of fragrant wood and piled them into a pyre, and further ground various powdered incenses and scattered them upon the pyre.
A strong man then seized a torch and intended to ignite it, but the devas immediately extinguished it so that it would not burn.
Aniruddha said to the Mallas, "You need not exhaust yourselves; the devas do not wish for it to be so.
The Mallas then asked Aniruddha:
"Why do the devas not wish for this?
Aniruddha replied,
"The devas desire that Mahākāśyapa should behold the body of the Tathāgata."
At that time, the heavens rained down *māndārava* flowers as an offering to the Tathāgata.
At one point, a non-Buddhist ascetic named A-pa-ba obtained a single *māndārava* flower from the presence of the Tathāgata and carried this flower toward the kingdom of Pāvā.
While on the road toward the kingdom of Pāvā, he saw Mahākāśyapa traveling along the path with a retinue of five hundred followers.
Kāśyapa asked,
"From where have you come?"
He replied,
"I have come from the city of Kuśinagara.
He asked again:
“Do you see my Great Teacher, the Tathāgata?
He replied,
“Your teacher entered nirvana seven days ago.”
"The various devas have rained down flowers as an offering to the Tathāgata; these are those very flowers.
Mahākāśyapa was filled with grief and sorrow, and all the disciples rolled upon the ground like fish that had lost their water, their heads buried in dust, each saying:
"From this day forth, we shall forever lose our shelter."
In this manner, he spoke various words more than once.
Then, the Śākya son Upananda admonished the bhikṣus:
"There is no need for grief or distress!"
"When the World-Honored One was present, there were manifold prohibitions.
Now that he has entered nirvana, we are free; whether we do or do not act as we wish is a matter for each person's own nature.
Why must you trouble us?"
Upon hearing these words, Mahākāśyapa felt redoubled sorrow and distress, and spoke again:
"The Tathāgata is the lion among teachers of all doctrines; the Wheel of Dharma he has turned cannot be destroyed by any."
Furthermore, he was able to subdue all non-Buddhists and attained complete mastery over all dharmas, being a Dharma King and Lord of Dharma.

Although it has not been long since the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha entered parinirvāṇa, how can such an evil person, devoid of shame and remorse, utter such words in the midst of the great assembly?
After Mahākāśyapa had uttered this lamentation, he went with five hundred bhikṣus to where the Tathāgata was.
Upon arrival, he said to Ānanda,
"I now wish to see the body of the Tathāgata."
Ānanda replied:
"As for the body of the Tathāgata, the Mallas wrapped it in fine cotton cloth and white linen, placed it within a coffin, and piled up various kinds of fragrant wood to form a pyre."
"How can this be seen?
Having spoken these words, by the supernatural power of the Tathāgata, his two feet appeared.
Kāśyapa looked at the Tathāgata’s feet and saw that they were stained with grime; he asked Ānanda:
"Why has the Tathāgata’s foot become like this?

Ānanda replied, "There were women who, out of sorrowful longing as the Tathāgata was approaching parinirvāṇa, prostrated themselves with their heads at the Tathāgata’s feet; for this reason, it is stained."

After the Buddha manifested his feet for Kāśyapa to see and then withdrew them, Kāśyapa circumambulated the Tathāgata seven times and praised him with verses; immediately, the fire ignited of its own accord.
After the cremation and the completion of the offerings to the Tathāgata, Kāśyapa gathered five hundred great arhats at the Bamboo Grove Monastery on Vulture Peak near Rājagṛha and said to them:

"While I was on the road in the kingdom of Pāvā, I heard that the Tathāgata had already entered parinirvāṇa; I spoke of this to five hundred bhikṣus, and they were all overcome with grief and distress."
The Śākya son Upananda suddenly spoke these words:
"While the Tathāgata was in the world, the laws and regulations were strict and urgent; now that the Tathāgata has passed away, each may act according to his own nature.
Why need one be distressed?"
When the various non-Buddhists hear these words, they will say:
"The sons of the Śākyas followed the teachings and practiced while the World-Honored One was in the world, but after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, they have all abandoned them."
"We should gather together to compile the Sūtra Piṭaka so that the Dharma shall not perish.
The Arhats replied,
"To compile the Sūtra Piṭaka, we require Ānanda."
Kāśyapa replied, "Ānanda has not yet exhausted his outflows; how can he be among this assembly?
The arhats said:
"One should inquire about the place where [the teaching] was forgotten. Kāśyapa said:
"If that is so, one should perform the *jñapti-karman* (motion) for seeking permission to allow him to enter the Saṃgha."
After the five hundred monks had taken their seats, they compiled the five divisions of the sūtras into the Tripiṭaka.
From among those sūtras, the sections that expounded upon the bhikṣu precepts were compiled into the Bhikṣu-sūtra.
Those discourses among the various sūtras that speak of the Vinaya in connection with the bhikṣuṇī precepts are compiled as the Bhikṣuṇī Sūtra.

Those discourses among the various sūtras that relate even to the kaṭhina robe and so forth are compiled as the Kaṭhina Khandhaka, the Mātṛkā-khandhaka, the Ekottarika-bhikṣu-sūtra, and the Bhikṣuṇī-sūtra; these together constitute the Vinaya Piṭaka.
Those discourses spoken within the various sūtras that correspond to the *Dīrgha Āgama* are collectively designated as the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
Those discourses spoken within the various sūtras that correspond to the *Madhyama Āgama* are compiled as the *Madhyama Āgama*.
Those sūtras in which the numbers increase from one, two, three, four, up to eleven, are compiled as the *Ekottarika Āgama*.

Those sūtras associated with bhikṣus, associated with bhikṣuṇīs, associated with Śakra, associated with the devas, and associated with Brahmā—such scriptures as these are collectively termed the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.

Whether they be Dhammapadas, expositions of meaning, or Jātakas spoken by the Tathāgata—from the Sūtras down to the Upadeśas—all such sūtras that correspond to the Khuddakagantha are collectively termed the Khuddakagantha.
These five types are called the Sūtra Piṭaka.

The five types consisting of the *vibhaṅga* on questions, the *vibhaṅga* on non-questions, inclusion (*saṃgraha*), correlation (*saṃprayoga*), and location (*sthāna*) are called the Abhidharma Piṭaka.
These fifteen types of sūtras are compiled as the Tripiṭaka.
Ānanda, baring his right shoulder, kneeling with his right knee on the ground, and joining his palms, addressed Mahākāśyapa, saying:
"I have personally heard from the presence of the Tathāgata that he spoke thus:"
"After my parinirvāṇa, you should assemble the Saṃgha and discard the minor precepts.
Kāśyapa then asked Ānanda:
"Did you personally hear these words from the Tathāgata? And what, precisely, are these 'minor precepts'?"
Ānanda replied, "At that time,
being oppressed by grief and distress, I was bewildered and obstructed, and thus did not manage to ask.
Kāśyapa then rebuked Ānanda:
"What you have said is untimely.
Why did you not ask the World-Honored One previously, only now claiming that you did not ask?
At that time, Kāśyapa questioned the bhikṣus:
"We should together contemplate this matter:
what is the subtle precept?
One bhikṣu spoke, saying:
"Excluding the four matters, the remainder is called the 'subtle precepts' (sūkṣma-śīla).
He spoke thus for each case, even down to excluding the ninety matters; the remainder is called the subtle precepts.
Kāśyapa then said:
"What you have all said does not accord with the subtle precepts.
You should practice according to what the Buddha has taught; do not speak what the Buddha has not spoken."
If they were to abandon even the subtle precepts, the various non-Buddhists would give rise to slanderous speech, saying:
"After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, all the bhikṣus have already abandoned the subtle precepts."
The Dharma of the Śramaṇa Gautama is like the smoke and flames of a fire: having suddenly arisen, it is extinguished.
If one abandons even the subtle precepts, one merely maintains the four grave offenses while abandoning all the rest.
"If one upholds even the four grave offenses, how can they be called a śramaṇa?
For this reason, the Venerable Kāśyapa rebuked Ānanda on seven matters.
Furthermore, because Ānanda requested permission for women to leave the household life, he was censured for nine matters.

First, had women not gone forth from the household life, the various donors would have constantly each filled a vessel with food and knelt on one knee by the side of the road to present it to the śramaṇas.
Second, if women had not gone forth [into homelessness], donors and others would have constantly provided robes and bedding, seeking out śramaṇas on the road to offer them for their use.

Third, had women not gone forth from the household life, donors and others would constantly have mounted elephants, horses, and carriages by the side of the road, prostrating themselves with their five limbs touching the ground to request that śramaṇas step over them as they passed.
Fourth, if women had not gone forth into homelessness, donors would constantly have to spread their hair upon the roadways, seeking for śramaṇas to step over it as they passed.
Fifth, had women not gone forth [into homelessness], donors would have constantly invited śramaṇas to their homes with a respectful mind to provide them with offerings.

Sixth, had women not gone forth, donors, upon seeing śramaṇas, would have constantly swept the ground with a respectful mind, removed their upper garments, and spread them on the ground for the śramaṇas to sit upon.
Seventh, if women had not gone forth into homelessness, the various donors would have constantly removed their upper garments to brush the dust from the feet of the bhikṣus.
Eighth, if women had not gone forth into homelessness, the various donors would have constantly loosened their hair to sweep the dust from the feet of the bhikṣus.

Ninth, had women not gone forth [into homelessness], the majestic power of the śramaṇas would have surpassed that of the sun and moon; how much less could the various non-Buddhists have even looked directly at the śramaṇas?
Tenth: Had women not gone forth from the household life, the Buddha’s True Dharma would have remained for a thousand years.

Now it has been reduced by five hundred years. During one hundred years, there will be those who attain firm liberation; during one hundred years, those who attain firm concentration; during one hundred years, those who attain firm ethical discipline; during one hundred years, those who attain firm learning; during one hundred years, those who attain firm generosity; and during the first century, there will be the dharma of firm liberation.
"Abiding securely within this, one will be able to fully comprehend the meaning;
during the second century, there will again be firm stability;
during the third century, one shall not violate the precepts."
In the fourth century, there will be those capable of great learning;
in the fifth century, there will again be those capable of practicing generosity.
From this point on, the Dharma of the Tathāgata will gradually diminish moment by moment.
Just as when a wheel has been set in motion, it eventually comes to an end as it turns;
so too, the reason the True Dharma becomes obscured is due to the fault of Ānanda,
who entreated the Teacher of Men to allow women to go forth.
The True Dharma should remain in the world for a full thousand years;
five hundred years having already elapsed and diminished, the remainder shall all be as it was originally.
Therefore, during these five hundred years, the five dharmas shall arise in the world.
"Emancipation, meditative concentration, upholding the precepts, extensive learning, and generosity.
*Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra*, Scroll Three;
*Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra*, Scroll Four.
The translator’s name is lost; it is now appended to the records of the Qin dynasty.
When the bhikṣus wished to compile the Dharma-piṭaka, Mahākāśyapa struck the ground with his hand, and the sound that reverberated was like that of a bronze bell.
At that time, five hundred arhats who had long resided in the city of Rājagṛha, including Sīha Āraṇa, heard these words and said to one another:
"The time has come to assemble the Dharma-piṭaka."

The Venerable Pūraṇa, together with his retinue of five hundred arhats, immediately followed him toward Rājagṛha, to the Bamboo Grove Monastery on Vulture Peak Mountain, where they arrived at the place of Mahākāśyapa.
Having arrived, they spoke to Mahākāśyapa, saying:
"We have heard that five hundred arhats, including Mahākāśyapa, intend to assemble the Dharma-piṭaka at the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha; we also wish to hear it."
Mahākāśyapa then related to Pūraṇa and the others the circumstances regarding the compilation of the Dharma-piṭaka.
Pūraṇa said to the Venerable Mahākāśyapa:
"Venerable One!..."
Having now fully heard the account of how the Dharma-piṭaka was compiled, it is truly beyond words how excellent it is.
However, among the eight matters, there are those I do not understand.

Regarding these eight items—from eating food stored overnight within the monastery precincts to various roots by the side of a pond—I have personally heard from the Buddha that the Tathāgata permitted their possession.
"Furthermore, when you say that [the Buddha] did not permit it,
this point is not understood. Kāśyapa replied,
"It is truly as you have said."
When there was famine and grain was expensive such that alms were difficult to obtain, the Buddha, out of compassion for sentient beings, permitted the storage [of food].
When the world was prosperous and grain was cheap such that alms were easy to obtain, the Tathāgata therefore withdrew that permission.
Pūraṇa said: “Kāśyapa!

The Tathāgata is one who possesses all-knowing vision; when he intends to store something, he wishes for people to know that he is storing it, and when he intends to discard something, he wishes for people to know that he is discarding it.”
Kāśyapa replied:
"For this reason, the Buddha speaks knowing the proper time; at one time it is appropriate to store [possessions], and at another time it is not appropriate to store them."
Pūraṇa! For this reason, we should follow the Tathāgata: when he prohibits something, we shall prohibit it; when he permits something, we shall permit it.
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, has accomplished eight kinds of wholesome qualities:
First, they have excellently attained vajra-wisdom;
second, they have completely severed all afflictions and shattered the darkness of ignorance;
third, they are free from all obstructions regarding all phenomena.
Fourth, attaining mastery in all places;
fifth, being able to skillfully subdue the heterodox arguments of outsiders;
sixth, skillfully demonstrating to sentient beings what is beneficial and what is not.
Seventh, they are able to distinguish [teachings] for sentient beings in accordance with the Dharma;
eighth, they are skillfully able to establish the rules regarding what constitutes an offense and what does not, exercising sovereign and unimpeded mastery.
One who accomplishes these eight qualities is called a Dharma King and a Lord of the Dharma.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa asked Ānanda,
"What is the meaning of this?
Ānanda replied to Mahākāśyapa:
"As I have heard from the Buddha, it was as Kāśyapa answered Pūraṇa:
'If a person practices according to the Buddha's words, that person can cause the Buddha-dharma to blaze forth.'"
"Therefore, you should practice in accordance with the Dharma.
Having heard these words, the assembly of the Venerable Pūraṇa practiced in accordance with the Dharma; they were indeed those who caused the Buddha-dharma to blaze forth.
This is the Dharma-treasury compiled by five hundred bhikṣus in the Snowy Mountains.
Now, the compilation of the Dharma-treasury by seven hundred bhikṣus shall be explained.

One hundred years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, in Vaiśālī, the bhikṣus such as Vāriṣeṇa and others practiced ten matters as taught by the Buddha; those who followed these practices caused the Buddha-dharma to flourish.
1. One should use two fingers to pick up food when eating;

2. When obtaining food while entering a village, if one says they are full, they must not say they are not satisfied, nor may they eat further food at a later time without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (leftover-food) rite;
3. One may also perform ritual activities within the boundaries of the monastery.
Fourth, it is virtuous to perform ritual services while praising the assembly;
fifth, it is virtuous for a subsequent person to perform the same ritual service that a preceding person has performed;
sixth, one may eat ghee, oil, honey, and rock sugar when mixed with curd.
7. Having received salt on the seventh day, one may mix it with rice today;
8. One may drink *śalūka* wine;
9. A sitting mat whose fringes have not been trimmed may be spread out.
Gold, silver, and the seven treasures may be handled with one's own hands and may also be possessed.
For this reason, Yaśas, the son of Kalandaka, wishing to eliminate these faults and afflictions, convened seven hundred arhats at Vaiśālī.
When the assembly of monks had gathered, Yaśas, son of Kālaṇḍaka, asked the Venerable Revata:
"May a bhikṣu, when entering a village for alms, take food with two fingers?"
The Venerable Revata replied,
"One must not take up food with two fingers. Yasa asked:
"Where was this rule established that one must not eat by pinching up rice with two fingers?
Revata replied, "It was established at Śrāvastī,
in the place where the rules regarding leftover food were set forth."
Yaśas again asked the Venerable Revata:
"If a bhikṣu has finished eating his fill, may he eat further without performing the ritual for leftover food?
He replied:
"No," [the Venerable replied].
Yaśas asked the Venerable again,
"Is it permissible to perform formal monastic acts (*karmavācanā*) within the boundary?"
The Venerable One then asked:
"What kind of Dharma ceremony is being performed within the boundary?
He replied:
"A group may perform the ritual acts.
The Venerable One replied,
"It is not permitted."
Question: "Where was it enacted?
Answer: [He] replied:
"It was established in the *Poṣadha-khandhaka* within the *Rājagṛha-nagara*.
Yaśas asked again:
"Is it permissible to speak in such a manner when performing formal acts (*karmavācanā*) for various groups within a boundary (*sīmā*)?"
He replied: "I may not.
This was also established within the *Poṣadha-khandhaka* in the city of Rājagṛha."
Yaśas asked the Venerable once more:
"May that which was previously done be performed again?
The Venerable replied:
"What is meant by 'repeatedly performing'? Yasa replied,
"'This matter is being performed now and has been performed previously.'"
The Venerable replied:

"If this matter is inconsistent with the Abhidharma, the Vinaya, and the Sūtras, then what has been done should not have been done; what has not yet been done should not be done; and what is being done now should not be done."
"If this matter accords with the Tripiṭaka, then what has been done should have been done, what has not yet been done should be done, and what is being done now should be done.
Yaśas then asked the Venerable One:
"Did you obtain fine food?"
He replied,
"What constitutes fine food? Yasa said:
“Ghee, honey, rock sugar, and curd mixed together constitute fine food.
The Venerable One replied,
“It is not permitted to eat this.”
"Where was it prescribed?
"It was prescribed in the land of Śrāvastī, at the place where the rule on leftover food was established.
Yaśas asked the Venerable one again:
"Is the salt that has been received permissible to eat?
The Venerable replied,
"What kind of salt has been received?"
Yaśas said, "May the salt received yesterday be used today to season my rice?
The Venerable One replied:
"You must not eat it.
"Where was this prohibited?
"It was prohibited in the Bhesajjakkhandhaka of the Sāvatthī section."
He asked the Venerable once more:
"May one drink *śaluka* wine?
He replied:
"No. "Where was it established?
"In the kingdom of Kauśāmbī, it was established because of the bhikṣu Sāti."
Yaśas asked the Venerable one again:
"Is it permissible to possess a rug that has not had its fringes trimmed?
He replied:
"No. "Where was it prescribed?
"In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, it was prescribed on account of the group of six bhikṣus."
He asked the Venerable one again:
"Is it permissible to possess vessels made of gold, silver, or precious gems?
He replied:
"No. "Where was it established?
"In Rājagṛha, on account of the Śākya son Upananda."
For what purpose was the Dharma-piṭaka further compiled?
It was to cause the bhikṣus to abandon evil and cultivate goodness.

Whether in a dwelling of four persons or even in a dwelling of many people, it was intended that they would know the Dharma and practice according to the Dharma, so that the Buddha-dharma might flourish.
If one's preceptor (upādhyāya), ācārya, or those who know the Dharma are all able to act in accordance with the Dharma, then the Buddha-dharma will flourish.
There are two kinds of dharmas that must not be transgressed: first, the Dharma of the Buddha must not be transgressed; [the second is the Dharma of the Saṃgha].
"The dharma of the two types of Wheel-Turning Kings must not be contravened.
For this reason, the Sangha of seven hundred monks was again assembled to compile the Dharma-piṭaka.
As for what is called the *Vinaya-sūtra*, it refers collectively to those sūtras among all the scriptures that correspond to the *Vinaya*, namely the sūtras for bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs."
Those sections within the various sūtras that correspond to the kaṭhina robe are collectively termed the Kaṭhina-khandhaka.
The Bhikṣu-sūtra, the Bhikṣuṇī-sūtra, all the khandhakas, the Mātṛkā, and the Vinaya-ekottara—these five types constitute the Vinaya-piṭaka; therefore, they are called the Vinaya-sūtras.
"As for what is called 'the great and extensive exposition' (mahā-vistara-nirdeśa): it is called 'extensive exposition' because the matters explained are numerous;
it is called 'great' because I am now teaching the Great Dharma."
I now proclaim the Great Dharma and the Great Vinaya; therefore, it is called the "Great Extensive Exposition.
That which is taught by a Great Person (mahāpuruṣa) is termed "Great.
Who is the Great Person?
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are called "Great Beings" (*mahāpuruṣa*); because these Great Beings speak it, it is called the "Great Being's Teaching.

Furthermore, regarding what is called "extensive": there was a bhikṣu of great virtue who gave a brief exposition of a sutra before a multitude of bhikṣus, or before four, three, two, or even a single bhikṣu, expounding the sutra as he understood it, saying: "I have personally heard this teaching from the Buddha’s own presence."
An elder who possesses virtue and insight should take what has been said and contemplate this principle; if it accords with the Tripiṭaka, he should say:
"What the Venerable One has spoken is excellent; if there are later students, they should be taught by means of this Dharma."
If it does not correspond with the Tripitaka, one should say:
"Venerable sir!
Do not practice this dharma, nor teach others to practice this dharma."
Therefore, it is called the "Extensive Exposition.
Because it reveals the Great Discipline (Vinaya) before one's eyes, it is called the "Extensive Exposition.
Suppose there were a person of sharp intellect and superior talent, possessing these qualities himself, who took what he understood and contended with the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata.

It is like a person who holds counterfeit gold alongside genuine gold; if it is difficult to distinguish between the genuine and the counterfeit, one burns them with fire, and their authenticity will manifest of itself.
If false teachings are claimed to have been spoken by the Tathāgata, they should be compared with the Tripiṭaka sūtras, and their genuineness or falsity will be known thereby.
It is like having a true physician in the world, while another person who is not actually a physician falsely claims to be one.
Those who do not discern the difference may go to him for treatment and lose their lives in vain.
Just as worldly people who do not recognize the true Dharma and follow false and deceptive teachings can extinguish their wholesome minds and even their very lives,
those who do not extinguish the True Dharma— acting according to the Vinaya as taught by the Buddha— can cause the True Dharma to blaze brightly in the world.
Why is this? Because such a person knows what was spoken by the Buddha and knows what was not spoken by the Buddha; therefore, they are able to preside over the True Dharma.
This is called "extensive exposition."
The Venerable Sarvāstivādin said:
"There are four extensive expositions on the white and four extensive expositions on the black.
For what reason are they called 'extensive expositions'?"
By means of this sutra,
one knows that "this is the word of the Buddha" and "this is not the word of the Buddha.
If there is someone who possesses eloquence and clarity such that they can discern right from wrong and explain it to others, these words should be accepted.
The detailed explanation of the black should also be understood as being like the detailed explanation of the white.
Regarding the "four": whether they are many, or three, or two, or one—these are called the four.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu might speak as follows:
"In the city of Bhūmi, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

'Whether in a village or a hamlet, that which you have personally heard from the Buddha’s own lips and have received and upheld—this is the Dharma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction.'"
"What this bhikṣu has said is neither acceptable nor unacceptable.

If, when compared with the *Ekottarika Āgama*, the *Madhyama Āgama*, the *Dīrgha Āgama*, the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, the *Bhikṣu Sūtra*, the *Bhikṣuṇī Sūtra*, the various *Khandhas*, and the *Mātṛkā*, it accords with the principles of the Dharma, you should say to him:
'Venerable One!'"
"This dharma can be practiced diligently by oneself, and one may also teach others to practice it diligently.
If [the teaching] does not accord with the principles of the Dharma, one should say:
"Venerable Sir!..."
"This dharma should not be practiced by oneself, nor should one teach others to practice it.
This is the first detailed exposition;
the second, third, and even the fourth are likewise explained in this manner.
"First, before a great assembly; second, before four people; third, before two people; fourth, before one person—this is called 'extensive exposition.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"I have taught you a single word or a single verse, whether many or few. That which should be practiced, practice according to my words; that which should not be practiced, do not practice according to my words."
If what later bhikṣus say corresponds with the Tripiṭaka, it should also be practiced.
As for what I have said—whether more or less than that—if it is not to be practiced, do not practice it.
"Whatever later bhikṣus may say that should not be practiced, do not practice it either.
This Dharma is explained in detail in the *Ekottarika Āgama*.
Regarding those who provide an extensive explanation, when the Tathāgata was approaching his parinirvāṇa, he addressed Ānanda, saying:
"After my parinirvāṇa, you must not say,
'We are without a refuge.
Do not speak such words."
"The Prātimokṣa that I have established is your refuge and is your teacher.
Therefore, Ānanda, after my passing, you should practice the Dharma in reliance upon the Prātimokṣa; each of you should practice it with humility."
"You all should eliminate arrogance and settle your minds in the pure Dharma. Ānanda!
From this day forward, those of lower rank should address those of higher rank as 'Venerable Elder,' and those of higher rank should address those of lower rank as 'Wise Life' (Āyuṣmat)."
"Ānanda! If a person sees the twelve links of dependent origination, this is called seeing the Dharma and also seeing the Tathāgata.
When the Tathāgata was about to enter parinirvāṇa, wishing to benefit sentient beings, he spoke these four extensive teachings.
For this reason, it is called the "Extensive Explanation.
The Buddha further declared:
"There are things that, because they are combined, should be kept; there are things that, because they are not combined, should not be kept."
What is meant by "conjoined" (*saṃsṛṣṭa*)?
For example, when Śāriputra obtained an outer piece of fine cloth and sewed it onto his patched robe, the Buddha permitted him to keep it; therefore, it is called "conjoined."
"Improperly combined" means that although high-quality brocade and high-quality white cloth may be combined, they should not be kept; therefore, it is called "improperly combined.
It is just as wine may be drunk if mixed with medicine, but cannot be drunk if unmixed.
If superior-quality cloth is combined with inferior-quality cloth, it may be kept; if they are not combined, it may not be kept.
There are two kinds of combination:
first, combination by color; second, combination by garment.
Regarding the combination of colors: first use a strong dye, then use a weak dye;
or again, first use a superior color, then use an inferior color.
These two are called "combination of colors" and should be kept.
What is called "superior color"?
The five primary colors are called superior colors.
The Sarvāstivādins say:
"Regarding 'superior colors,' these are pure blue, pure red, pure yellow, pure black, and pure white; these are called the five kinds of superior colors.
Regarding 'the blending of great colors,' one first uses blue dye and subsequently uses other colors to dye it;
or one first uses other colors to dye it and subsequently uses blue dye."
The five kinds are likewise; these are robes that may be kept.
Regarding the combination of robes: if one robe has been formally purified (*pariśuddha*) while the patch has not yet been purified, one may sew the patch onto the robe.
If a robe has not yet been purified, but the patch has already been purified, one may sew the patch onto the robe;
both of these are called "purified robes.

If a robe has not reached ten days and has not yet undergone the ritual of purification (*pariṣkāra*), but the patch has already undergone purification, one may sew the patch onto the robe and keep it.
If a patch has been applied for less than ten days and has not yet been formally dedicated as a gift (pariṣkāra), one may keep it by sewing it onto a robe;
this is therefore called the "integration of the robe. This is the method for the formal dedication of a gift.

If one obtains an item on a certain day, one must perform the ritual of *pariśuddhi* (purification) that very day; if ten days pass without performing *pariśuddhi*, one commits an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

Furthermore, if one fails to declare the purification due to negligence, because of the corruption of the mind, one commits an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) even before the ten days have elapsed.
"What are those things that should not be kept when one is not in communion, yet should be kept when one is in communion?

Those that should be kept when not in communion are: mountain-grown *śāliparṇī*, *vijñātaka* grass, *jambuka*, *vibhītaka*, *uḍumbara* honey, fermented vinegar, *yavattika*, and ginger; such medicines as these should not be kept [when not in communion]."
Why is this? If each of these medicinal ingredients is mixed with food individually, it is not suitable for consumption;
however, once they have been boiled together until they are thoroughly cooked and then poured into a single vessel, after a short period of time, the milk and water separate.
This milk, when mixed with salt, is unfit for consumption; it is not fit to be consumed while mixed with salt.
As for the medicinal herbs listed above, they must be combined and blended together; it is not permissible to consume them by adding them one by one.
It is also like milk mixed with salt, which is unfit for consumption; it is excellent when taken separately.
This is called "use through non-mixture.
At that time, for the sake of sick bhikṣus, the Buddha permitted the drinking of *suvīra* gruel; it may be drunk with salt added, or it may be drunk without it.
This is called "combined use.

Regarding medicines to be taken for as long as one lives: ginger, pepper, *pippalī*, *harītakī*, salt, and *achyranthes*—these and others like them are all called medicines to be taken for as long as one lives.
This is explained in detail in the Bhaiṣajyavastu (The Chapter on Medicines).

Regarding what should be done within the monastery—from formal legal acts (*karmavācanā*) and all other monastic affairs, down to eating, drinking, lying down, and rising, as well as wearing the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* and *kaṣāya* in the open air—all these are included therein.
Furthermore, regarding those of middling capacity: if one sees gold or silver on the ground within a monastery, whether the owner is known or unknown, one should pick it up and set it aside.
If the owner is later identified, it should be returned to them.
If one does not know the owner, one should announce it among the assembly of monks:
"Yesterday, I found gold and silver on the property of the Sangha.
To whom does this belong?"
If someone comes and says, "This is my property," one should ask:
"How many items are there in this object, and what is its weight?
What materials were used for the wrapping, carrying, and binding?"
"If it is said that each [item] may be exchanged for one that is appropriate, but not for one that is inappropriate, then there are further things within the monastery that may be used.
If monks or nuns make a canopy from wood leaves, make a canopy from tree bark, or weave grass to make a canopy—such items as these may all be used within the monastery."

Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who obtains an article for use within the monastery: a heavy leather boot with a thick lining that is worn down at the heel. He may wear it when going out to a village during rain or snow, but he must not wear it when there is no rain or snow.
Regarding the leather sandals one wears—whether they be four-layered, three-layered, or even single-layered—they may all be worn within the monastery.
When entering a village, they may be worn during rain or snow; there is no time when they are not permitted.
"One may also wear them when ill.
This is explained in detail in the *Kavadi-khandaka* (The Chapter on Sandals).
"In the monastery, one should keep iron keys, wooden keys, ladles, staffs, and benches for the bathhouse."
These are the items that should be kept within the monastery.
When a monk is dispatched by the Saṃgha to enter the forest, he should be granted a period of seven days.
If he cannot return within seven days, he should be granted a period of fifteen days.
If one cannot arrive on the fifteenth day, one should be granted a month;
this is called "one who should enter the forest.
If a bhikṣu develops an ulcer on his body, the bhikṣu may use coarse and rough powder to wash the ulcer.
The Buddha said:
"I permit the bhikṣus to use fine, soft powder to wash sores.
This is the method for applying the powder.
They were placed in a jar with its mouth sealed, or even hung upon a stake;
these matters should be understood in detail from the Bhaiṣajyavastu (The Chapter on Medicinal Herbs).
"If a bhikṣu suffers from the disease of white leprosy, his own skin cracks open and pus and blood flow out."
The bhikṣus used coarse and rough powders for application and washing.
The Buddha said:
"One should use fine, soft powders for application and washing."
This should be understood in detail from the *Kṣudraka-vastu*.
"If a bhikṣu develops a new sore whose pain and inflammation do not subside, he should apply a medicinal ointment that causes it to suppurate."
"In the future, you should keep various medicines for healing wounds to treat them until they are cured.
If a bhikṣu has hemorrhoids in his lower parts, he should make a wound-wrapping garment so that pus and blood do not flow out and soil his robes."
"Following the physician's prescription, it is permitted to make and keep such garments.

If a bhikṣu develops sores on his head, or sores on his face, or sores on his lips, or sores on his shoulders, or sores under his armpits, or sores on his sides, or sores on his navel, or sores on his seat, or sores on his knees, or sores on his calves—if he has sores on his head, it is permitted for him to wrap his head and cover his head when entering the dwellings of laypeople."
If there is a sore on the face, one is permitted to look at it by reflecting in the water of one's bowl.
Or, if one sees the sore by reflecting on a wall, one may apply medicine to it oneself.
If there is a sore on the lips, one is permitted to chew food while keeping the two lips from touching each other.
If there is an ulcer on the tongue, it is permitted to place it in the mouth and swallow it without chewing.
If there is an ulcer on the shoulder, it is permitted to hold the ulcer with the hand and enter a layperson's house while covering it with a cloth.
Furthermore, it is permitted for one with sores on the shoulders to enter the house of a layperson provided that the upper garment does not cover them.
If there are sores under the armpits, it is permitted to enter the house of a layperson with the hands placed behind the waist.
If there is a sore on one's side, it is permitted to fold the robe over the shoulder when entering the house of a layperson.
If there is a sore on one's navel, it is permitted to tie down the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (inner robe).
If there is a sore on one's seat, it is permitted to enter the house of a layperson while squatting.
If there is a sore on the knees, it is permitted to lift the robes above the knees to enter the house of a layperson.
If there is an ulcer on the abdomen, it is permitted to wear the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (inner robe) high up when entering the house of a layperson;
therefore, this is called "permission for those with ulcers.

If within a monastery of the Saṃgha there are three or four people who have built a separate large hall, the dwelling place should have a deep trench dug around its four sides to block water, and within the trench, latrines of appropriate size should be constructed.
This matter is explained in detail in the *Śayanāsana-vastu*.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Take the key and go from room to room to tell the bhikṣus: [as follows]."
"I wish to travel south to visit various kingdoms.
Who among you can follow me? You may prepare your robes and bowls accordingly.
Ānanda immediately accepted this instruction and went from room to room to inform them.
