In small rooms where many people are present, one sits with the knees drawn close together; this is also called "sitting.

When the Venerable Revata arrived at the side of Sarvakāma, Sarvakāma saw that Revata had come from a great distance and his body was weary; he therefore sat in a cramped manner himself so as to allow Revata to sit more comfortably.
Revata thought to himself:
"The Venerable Sarvakāmin is the foremost elder in Jambudvīpa;
how can I be lax and negligent in his presence?"
He then drew his body together, sat upright, and focused his mindfulness in contemplation.
Sitting in this manner, as these two persons do, is called "sitting.
What is meant by "not lying down"?
One must not share a room or lie down with a woman;
nor may one share a room or lie down with a śrāmaṇera who has been expelled.
Regarding "requisites for bedding": beds, rope beds, mats of grass, mats of leaves, and whatever bedding belongs to a practitioner—all these are termed "bedding requisites."
There was a bhikṣuṇī who, while wandering for alms, entered a village.
As the master of the house was not at home, the nun entered the dwelling and sat down.
When the master returned from outside and saw the nun sitting there, he asked the members of his household:
"Who among you settled this nun so that she dwells here?
The palace attendants replied, "The nun came of her own accord; no one settled her."
The householder spoke with displeasure:
"How can a bhikṣuṇī sit down directly without first announcing her arrival?
Having heard this, the Buddha established a rule:
"A bhikṣuṇī must not sit down in the house of a donor without first asking permission.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs asked the Buddha:
"When renunciants enter a village, if the number of monks is large and the dwellings are cramped, how much space should each person be allotted?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣuṇīs:
"Divide [the space] among the rooms according to their width and narrowness.
"If a person lies on the ground out of pride while being free from illness, one should not preach the Dharma to them."
"If a sick person is lying down and wishes to hear the Dharma, one should preach it for them.

At that time, the bhikṣu Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa had gone forth under Kātyāyanīputra in the country of Avanti; he maintained the precepts, practiced the Path with diligent and tireless effort, and attained arhatship.
Having attained the fruit [of Arhatship], he traveled from the country of Āvantī toward the country of Campā and arrived at the place where the Tathāgata was.
Seeing that he had come from afar and had simultaneously attained the fruit of Arhatship, the Buddha, for these reasons, addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Spread out a mat for me; likewise, spread out a mat within my room for this bhikṣu."
"This is the method for a bhikṣu to lie down within the Buddha’s chamber: he must face the Buddha and must not lie with his back to the Buddha.
At that time, there were also other bhikṣus who, because they were attached to the pleasure of sleep, neglected the three types of action.
The Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva silently thought to himself:
"The Tathāgata attained Buddhahood only after undergoing various ascetic practices for three asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
Now these bhikṣus, because they are greedily attached to the pleasure of sleep and reclining, no longer practice the Path; how can this be?"
Having thought this in their minds and spoken it aloud, the bhikṣus heard them and reported all these matters in detail to the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Those who consume the faithful offerings of others should not be indolent."

"During the three periods of the night, one should spend two periods sitting in meditation, reciting the sūtras, and walking in meditation; during the remaining one period, one may rest at one's own leisure.
This is called bedding and seating.
"There were some bhikṣus who sat on the open ground; the elders and those of long standing all suffered from back pain."
Thus it was passed on in succession until it reached the World-Honored One.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"For those who sit in the open air and suffer from back pain, with the exception of highly colored white leather, all other materials may be used to make a meditation belt for sitting; at that time, one should use the belt to bind oneself."

"The method for making the meditation belt (*dhyāna-kaṭi-sūtra*) is as follows: it shall be one span (*vitasti*) in width, and its length shall be made according to the measurement of the individual's body.
This is called the meditation belt.

"At that time, when a bhikṣu first went forth, the Buddha had not yet permitted the use of a cord to fasten the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (undergarment); [the bhikṣu] used two ends joined together at the waist."
Later, when he arrived at the house of a donor, his bowl suddenly slipped from his hand and fell to the ground amidst the assembly; everyone laughed.
The bhikṣu felt ashamed and, for this reason, went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit the weaving together of long and short pieces so that they may wrap twice around the waist, with two chi remaining.
If one makes a cord, it shall wrap three times directly around the waist, with each end having a length of one chi remaining."
This is called "carrying along with the causes and conditions.

When the preceptor (upādhyāya) or the instructor (ācārya) intends to go on a journey, the co-practitioner disciple or the co-resident disciple should inspect this cord to see whether there are any places where it has been gnawed by insects or rats.
Having examined it thoroughly, one should then pass it on.
If there is no disciple for a bhikṣu dwelling in an araṇya, a junior monk should examine it thoroughly in this manner before presenting it to the senior monk.
If a bhikṣu suffers from a headache, he should fasten his waistband tightly.
If a bhikṣu possesses a waistband with tassels at the ends, he should not keep it.
When the group of six bhikṣus kept such a band, the Buddha immediately prohibited it.
"There was a bhikṣu who, for the sake of a joke, hid another's rope and did not return it when the time had passed, causing its owner distress.
The Buddha did not permit this.
At that time, Śāriputra entered the house of a layperson; encountering a violent gust of wind that blew against his body, his kāṣāya fell to the ground and he stood there with his body exposed."
The Buddha thereupon established this rule:
"From this day forward, monks must all attach buttons to their *kāṣāya* robes; a hook should be fixed on one side to catch within the button so that the garment does not fall."
This is called the method for securing the fastening hook of the robe.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus tucked their saṃghāṭī robes over their backs; carrying heavy loads, they walked with their heads bowed, causing their bodies to be exposed and drawing the resentment of the laypeople.
Upon hearing this, the Buddha established a regulation:
"From this day forward, it is not permitted for bhikṣus to carry heavy loads or wear their robes folded over the shoulder.
If there is a necessary cause related to the Three Jewels that requires wearing the robe folded over the shoulder, one must properly arrange it so that the body is not revealed."
This is called the method of folding and tucking.
"A bhikṣu should keep a small crossbow. Why is this?
If there is a threat of bandits, one should aim into the air and discharge a crossbow to frighten them away.
There are phenomena that share the same name but differ in their function; for example, both the *tūṇa* (crossbow) and the sugarcane are called *ikṣvāku*.
When a thief asked for *soca*, it was known that he sought a small bow;
at mealtime, when one asked for *soca*, it was known that he sought sugarcane.
Thus, the names are the same, but their uses differ.
"In the walking-meditation area of a bhikṣu, one should spread out woolen or cotton mats; one must not spread leather, though it is permissible in cold places.
In the walking-meditation area of one's upādhyāya or ācārya, a disciple must not walk there; he may walk at the side."

In the place where an elderly practitioner of the Way—whose number of years since ordination is similar to that of one's own Upādhyāya or Ācārya—walks in meditation, a junior bhikṣu must not walk there.
When the Upādhyāya or Ācārya is walking in meditation, if the disciple has something to inquire about, he should ask with palms joined, body bent, and head bowed.
"There is a multi-storied pavilion; the upper roof is about to collapse toward the impure ground."
The bhikṣus were doubtful in their minds and went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"Provided that it is not damaged and has not fallen into a state of impurity, it is called a 'pure room'."

If the monastic community has no pure kitchen (*śuci-kutī*) at their residence, and if they were to designate the very best room through a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) as the pure kitchen, the Buddha does not permit this; rather, they should use the second-best room as the pure kitchen.
If a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) has already been performed [for that room], it should be rescinded, and the second room should be designated as a clean kitchen (*kalpiya-śālā*).

"The reason why brocade is not permitted to be spread upon the walking path (*caṅkrama*) is that there was a donor who brought a piece of brocade highly valued in his own country to offer to the Saṃgha; once the Saṃgha had received it, they used it to spread over the walking path."
Later, when the donor saw this, he spoke with reproach:
"How can a bhikṣu lack a sense of care? How can such a precious object be spread upon a walking path and then trampled underfoot?"
When the World-Honored One heard of these successive reports, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, you must not spread out fine, precious, or heavy items given by donors upon the walking path."
“There are two kinds of bhikṣus who may not stay overnight with the Saṃgha:
first, a bhikṣu performing *parivāsa* (probation);
second, a bhikṣu who acts contrary to the Dharma, and when wise ones admonish him, he refuses to heed their words and abruptly leaves the monastery.”
These two persons must not stay overnight together.
If a donor offers land to the Sangha, the Buddha permits its use;
this is what is called "land."
"There are five kinds of trees that a bhikṣu must not cut down:
first, the Bodhi tree;
second, the tree of a spirit."
Third, the Jambū tree;
fourth, the Aśvattha tree;
fifth, the Nyagrodha tree.
"There are several sons of the Śākyas who have gone forth; Upāli was the barber for their household, so they summoned him and said:
'You have served us for a long time.'"

Now, as I wish to depart, I have nothing else to offer you; I can only give you the fine jeweled robes, necklaces, bracelets, and armlets I am wearing upon my body, along with the sword adorned with the seven precious gems—all these I relinquish to you.
Having received it, Upāli thought to himself:
"This man is of noble character and high status, yet he was still able to renounce his possessions to seek the Way.
How much more so should I, who am lowly and base, continue to suffer while guarding these treasures?"
He then wrapped it in three layers of cloth and hung it upon a tree, saying:
"Whoever needs it, let them take it as they please.
He then followed the son of the Śākyas to the Buddha and went forth into homelessness.
"If a bhikṣu plants three kinds of trees for the sake of the Three Jewels—first, fruit trees;
second, flower trees; and third, leaf trees—this brings only merit and no fault."

There was a bhikṣu who delighted in dwelling in empty, quiet places beneath trees during the rains retreat; he went to inform the World-Honored One, saying, "May I dwell beneath a tree for the rains retreat?
The Buddha said:
"May I observe the rains retreat?
A doubt arose in his mind, and he asked the Buddha again:
"May I also observe the rains retreat under large or small trees?"
The Buddha said:

"The larger ones are the better; if none are available, those at least as tall as a person will suffice, provided their branches and leaves spread out in all directions, being so dense and thick that they do not leak from rain or snow, nor allow sunlight to penetrate."
"In this way, one may observe the rains retreat beneath a tree.
A certain bhikṣu observed the rains retreat in a tree; having bound wood together to make a bed, he did not descend from the tree to relieve himself beneath it.
"There is a great ghost in this tree who, out of anger and resentment, struck and killed this bhikṣu.
The Buddha said:
"From now on, it is not permitted for a bhikṣu to dwell in a tree for the rainy season retreat, nor to relieve himself beneath a tree."
"Before the Buddha had yet established the precepts, the bhikṣuṇīs all practiced dhyāna and walked in meditation in cemeteries, under trees, and in secluded places.
The bhikṣuṇī Puṣpā had attained the fruit of non-attachment; her conduct and posture were excellent and possessed proper form."
As the leader of the bandits was traveling along, he encountered him and immediately conceived faith.
After going elsewhere to eat, he had some leftover meat; wrapping it in a cloth, he hung it upon a tree and made this vow:
"If there be any Arhat who has attained the Way and comes here before midday, they may obtain this midday meal."
The nun Puṣpavarṇā, who was endowed with the six supernormal powers, heard these words from afar. On the following day, she sent a śrāmaṇerikā to fetch [the food].
At that time, the World-Honored One proceeded along the road, reached a tree, spread out his seat, and sat down.
He encountered the son of Vairaṭa, Sañjaya, who provided sixty wagons laden with black rock honey as an offering for the Buddha and the Saṅgha;
the causal conditions regarding the tree are to be known in detail in this manner.
"A certain bhikṣu was sitting alone under a tree with a woman. When a layperson saw this, he spoke with disdain:
'How can a śramaṇa sit alone under a tree with a woman?'"
Having heard this, the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I do not permit a bhikṣu to sit alone with a woman under a tree."
"If there are trees that have withered on the land belonging to the Saṃgha, one must not take them alone to burn as fire. Why is this?
Because this belongs to the Saṃgha of the four directions."
If there is a fine tree on monastic land, the community may, if in harmony, use it to construct a stūpa or a monastery; if they are not in harmony, they may not.

If three or four individuals within the great assembly separately build a large dwelling for communal residence, and there was already a tree on the site where the dwelling is built, the community of monks shall divide the site and allow them to use that tree.
If the Sangha has not formally assigned the site, it may not be used.
If one builds a dwelling, one may use trees that have grown spontaneously on that land.
If the original dwelling was built long ago and no later monks have resided there, one may use those trees without needing to inform the Sangha.
If there is vacant space within the dwelling where one resides, and the owner of the house has planted trees for the sake of that building, they may be used to repair the dwelling.
If the person who planted the trees is absent and other monks are residing there, these trees may be used even without having to inform the Sangha.
Regarding flowering trees and fruit trees: except for when the Saṃgha acts in harmony to repair a stūpa or construct a dwelling, one must not cut them privately.
There are five kinds of trees that must not be cut:
first, the Bodhi tree; second, sacred trees; third, large trees on main roads; fourth, trees in the Śītavana cemetery; and fifth, the Nyagrodha tree—except in cases of necessity.
Regarding the causes and conditions: if a Buddha-stūpa is damaged, or if a monastery is destroyed by water, fire, or burning, one may cut four kinds of trees, with the exception of the Bodhi tree.
There are five kinds of trees that may be utilized for use:
First, burned by fire; second, burned by dragon-fire; third, dried up naturally; fourth, blown over by the wind; fifth, washed away by water—trees such as these may be utilized.
"What is meant by 'strife, dispute, contention, and litigation'?

When two people compete together, it is called strife (*raṇa*). When factions assist one another, it is called dispute (*vivāda*). When one goes to inform the Saṃgha, it is called contention (*abhyākhyāna*). When each asserts their own reasoning, it is called litigation (*adhikaraṇa*)."
"Furthermore, there are four kinds of disputes:

first, disputes regarding speech; second, disputes regarding not accepting admonition; third, disputes regarding transgressions; and fourth, disputes regarding formal acts. These are called disputes."
"What is meant by 'schism'?
There are two kinds of schism:
first, the schism of the Wheel of Dharma; second, the schism of the Saṃgha."

As for the Wheel of Dharma, it is called the "corruption of the Dharma" when the Eightfold Noble Path is not practiced and false teachings circulate; when wisdom is regarded as false and folly is taken as correct, such that wisdom is obstructed and falsehood is manifested. This is what is meant by the corruption of the Dharma.

Regarding "schism in the Saṃgha": within a single monastery, if one person performs the *poṣadha* ceremony while others perform it separately, or if one person performs a *karmavācanā* for two people while others perform it for the great assembly, or if the great assembly performs a *karmavācanā* for themselves [in defiance of the unity], this is called schism in the Saṃgha.

"Those who accompany Devadatta shall all incur a *sthūlātyaya* offense; those who return to the Saṃgha and perform repentance shall be cleared of it, while those who do not return assist in the schism of the Saṃgha, yet they do not incur the full offense of causing a schism."
Only Devadatta alone incurs the offense of causing a schism in the Saṃgha.
Furthermore, there is another teaching which states that there is no such thing as a schism in the Saṃgha; rather, the non-functioning of the Wheel of Dharma constitutes a schism in the Saṃgha.
"Furthermore, there are two kinds of schisms:
first, schism through factionalism; second, schism through views.
For example, when the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī dispute in factions, they do not rely on the Abhidharma, Sūtra, or Vinaya, taking what is wrong to be right; this is due solely to their ignorance."
This is explained in detail within the Kauśāmbī-khandhaka.
Regarding "breaking through views," it is like Devadatta’s schism of the Saṃgha; this is called the breaking of views.
This is explained in detail within the Saṃghabheda-khandhaka.
Regarding the eighteen kinds of schisms as explained above:
"At that time, there was a bhikṣu dwelling alone in retreat who heard that another bhikṣu intended to carry out the method of causing a schism in the Saṃgha."
This bhikṣu felt doubt in his mind: "If I go to admonish him, I fear it will break the *anvāya* (rainy-season retreat); yet if I do not go, I fear that evil teachings will spread.
When the Buddha heard this, he addressed the bhikṣu, saying:
"If it is for the sake of the Dharma, it does not break the *anvāya*."
The same applies to bhikṣuṇīs; for the sake of the Dharma, they do not break the summer retreat.
The reason for the admonition is that, out of compassion, one fears they might fall into hell and undergo retribution, and thus offers the admonition.

Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who heard that the schism in the Saṃgha within that place had already been finalized; wishing to go and reconcile them, he feared he would lose his *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) and felt doubt in his mind.
The Buddha, knowing this, told him:
"If one acts for the sake of reconciling those who have caused a schism in the Saṃgha, one does not lose the *varṣā*."
The same applies to bhikṣuṇīs.
They cause a schism in the Saṃgha by means of the fourfold method:
declaring what is Dharma to be non-Dharma, and declaring what is non-Dharma to be Dharma;
To call what is not *vinaya* "vinaya," and what is *vinaya* "not vinaya";
to call what is not an offense "an offense," and an offense "not an offense";
to call what is light "heavy," and what is heavy "light."

By these four phrases, or by a bhikṣu’s mind, if within a single monastery there is a separate group of followers, such that they perform the eighteen types of legal procedures—including the *poṣadha* and *karmas*—entirely on their own and not in common with the Saṃgha.
This should be understood in detail from the *Bhikṣu-sūtra* and the *Bhikṣuṇī-sūtra*.
This is called "schism.
What is "reconciliation"?
For one who causes a schism in the Saṃgha, he speaks of what is Dharma as being Dharma and what is non-Dharma as being non-Dharma;
he speaks of what is an offense as being an offense and what is not an offense as being not an offense;
he speaks of what is Vinaya as being Vinaya and what is non-Vinaya as being non-Vinaya.

What is grave is declared as grave, and what is light is declared as light; even down to the *poṣadha* and *karmans*, all are performed together with the Saṃgha and no longer separately. This is called "harmony" (*saṃghasāmagrī*).
Furthermore, there are five kinds of conjunction:
first, the conjunction of seeing phenomena;
second, the conjunction of seeing the beginning.
Third, harmony through desire;
fourth, harmony through faith;
fifth, harmony through silence.
"By means of these five dharmas, one can bring about harmony within the Saṃgha.
Thus it should be known in detail.
Upāli then questioned the World-Honored One:
"What benefit does one who reconciles a schismatic in the Sangha obtain?
The Buddha said:
"One who reconciles a schismatic in the Sangha will be reborn in heaven and receive retribution for one kalpa."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If a dispute has arisen within the Saṃgha and has not yet been confessed, can it be called 'in harmony'?
The Buddha said:
"Failure to confess is not called harmony; only after one has repented according to the Dharma is it called harmony.
*Vinayamātṛkā Sūtra*, Scroll Five;
*Vinayamātṛkā Sūtra*, Scroll Six.
The translator’s name is lost; it is now appended to the Qin Records:
"If there is a bhikṣu who wishes to vacate his dwelling for another purpose, he should first sweep the interior of the room and plaster it to make it clean.
He should fold and stack his bedding materials, move the bed away from the wall, and place the bedding upon the bed, putting the better quality items underneath and the inferior ones on top."
The two types of bedding should be understood in detail as described above.
When departing, one should inform the Upādhyāya and Ācārya; if they permit it, one may depart, but if they do not permit it, one should remain.

If one has more than ten years of ordination (*daśavarṣa*) and there is a superior Dharma matter that will certainly be beneficial, one may go of one's own accord even if the Upādhyāya or Ācārya does not permit it; there is no fault in this.

When departing, one should go outside the monastery and observe the destination and location of the journey. Furthermore, one should deliberate upon whether the traveling companions are suitable to accompany one or not.

If one wishes to pass through a country where one might be plundered and have one's goods seized by tax-collectors, one should not travel with such companions; if they are robbers, one should not associate with them as companions; and if they are those who lack faith or hold wrong views, one should likewise not associate with them as companions.
Although there are many such [cases], I shall now speak of two or three in general.
Furthermore, one should reflect: when traveling together on the road with companions from the same monastery, are they able to attend to one another in the event of illness?
If you already know that his mind is certainly good, you may go together; if you do not yet know him, you should wait for a better companion.
Reflect further: will this traveling companion act in common with me regarding whatever I intend to do?
Furthermore, one should reflect: "Does this person's deportment always remain restrained?
Is this person not indolent?
To me, will this person bring benefit or decline?"
Is he trustworthy or untrustworthy?
When traveling together with him, is it suffering or pleasure?
Furthermore, one should reflect: from the very beginning, has there ever been illness, or has there been no illness?
Is one capable or incapable?
Will one not abandon [the path] while on the way?
Thus deliberating as one proceeds along the road is called "one who goes."
"When the senior elder (sthavira) of the monastery departs, he should first attend to his own quarters and then instruct the junior bhikṣus:
'In the future, you must attend to this room just as I have done while I was here.'"
Furthermore, the method for entrustment by the Elder consists of everything from the *poṣadha* and the recitation of the precepts up to the assignment of all duties.
Having thus entrusted [the community], he then departs from the monastery and goes outside.
He further asked the bhikṣus traveling with him:
"Have you not forgotten anything, from your robes and bowls down to all your personal belongings?
He then added this admonition:

“O bhikṣus, you should now proceed together; at all times speak little, guard your speech, and restrain your sense faculties. Should anyone see you at various points along the way, cause them all to rejoice and give rise to wholesome thoughts.”

Upon hearing the admonitions and instructions spoken by the senior elder, all the junior practitioners of the same community joined their palms, knelt with their right knees on the ground, and replied:
"We shall joyfully practice in accordance with your instructions."
"When these bhikṣus travel along the road, those of lower rank should always respectfully praise and honor those of higher rank, surrounding them as they walk before and behind.
Whenever they stop to rest or set out from a place, the elder (upādhyāya) should inspect everywhere to ensure that nothing has been left behind."
If there is anyone present, one should tell them to take it.
Furthermore, regarding the practice for walking on the road, the junior monks go in front and the senior monk follows behind.
He then says to the junior monks:
"Each of you should collect your minds and not allow them to become distracted.

If a junior monk falls ill while on the road, the senior monk should preach the Dharma for him so that his wholesome mind may continue uninterrupted; even in the face of urgent or difficult circumstances, he must not abandon him.
While traveling on the road, if a junior member of the assembly encounters difficulties, the senior member should assist in managing them:

first, difficulties involving parents; second, difficulties involving brothers and sisters; third, difficulties involving close relatives; fourth, difficulties involving kings and ministers; fifth, difficulties involving bandits; sixth, difficulties involving wild beasts. The senior member should exert all his strength to ensure they are delivered from these hardships.

If one is unable to do so through one's own strength, one should go to a village, district, county, city, or town where there is a monastery, and speak to a virtuous bhikṣu esteemed by the people, or even to a devout brāhmaṇa, a great donor, or a high minister, requesting them to take care of the matter.
If he can be liberated, that is well;
if he cannot be liberated, you should go in person to the gate of the king’s palace to manage the matter, so that he may be set free and not made to suffer.
"If a bhikṣu enters a village at an improper time, he should inform his upādhyāya and ācārya, and speak to those sitting nearby before entering; this is called the rule for entering a village."

"An untimely assembly refers to all occasions for performing formal acts (karmas) other than the times for eating, the times for eating gruel, and the times for drinking sweet beverages; when these are conducted according to the Dharma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the Buddha’s teaching, it is called an untimely assembly."
If the monks assemble at an improper time, there is a senior elder among them, and that senior elder should ask:
"Venerable sirs,
for what reason has the Saṃgha assembled at an improper time?"
The bhikṣus replied:
"Because there are such matters of the Dharma that ought to be performed, we have gathered.
The elder should then perform the *karmavācanā*, whether it be a single motion (*jñapti*), two motions, or four motions.
This is called the untimely assembly of the elders for the recitation of the Dharma.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of gatherings:
first, the assembly that spends the entire night discussing sūtras and engaging in debate; second, the assembly that sits silently and upright, practicing meditation and contemplation.
"Furthermore, there is a method of assembly once every five days.

At the time of assembly, the three grades of the community—superior, middle, and inferior—all gather together. Having assembled, they all restrain their deportment, adjust their robes, sit upright and still, and moreover, each show mutual respect."
Their dignified deportment and ritual rules were such that onlookers never grew weary of them, and they were able to give rise to wholesome thoughts in others.
This was the method for the five-day assembly.
Those who listened focused their minds on the Dharma without any other distractions; if the speaker should happen to forget or err, the audience should each recall it for themselves.

If one is free from forgetfulness or error, and does not incur reproach for being verbose or obstructed in meaning, one should revere both the Dharma and the teacher of the Dharma as if serving Śakra, and should neither disparage oneself nor disparage the Dharma teacher.

One should not be distracted amidst the Dharma taught by those possessed of wisdom, but listen with a concentrated mind, maintaining a continuous succession of moments of thought without interruption.
When listening to the Dharma, one should establish five virtues within the inner mind:
first, that this Dharma never heard before is now being heard for the first time;
Second, to cause me to once again master the Dharma I have already heard;
third, to sever my doubts;
fourth, to rectify my views.
The five ways of increasing the pure mind constitute the five internal virtues.
These matters should be understood in detail from the *Ekottarika Āgama*.
There are nine benefits of hearing the Dharma:
First, generating faith for a lifetime;
second, rejoicing because of that faith;
third, delighting in that joy.
Fourth, abandoning the craving for gain and offerings while listening to the Dharma without doubt;
fifth, the accomplishment of right view;
sixth, severing ignorance so that the mind of wisdom arises.
Seventh, they sever the fetters of the mind;
eighth, they attain the purity of the Dharma-eye regarding the Four Noble Truths;

ninth, they attain the contemplation of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self within the five aggregates; having attained this contemplation, their hearts leap with joy, their faith deepens beyond measure and cannot be destroyed, and they attain liberation from afflictions, realize the path to Nirvana, and experience the bliss of deliverance.
For this reason, one should listen to the Dharma with a sincere mind.

If there is an elder present among those seated in the assembly, he should first sit in stillness for a brief moment; having finished sitting in stillness, he should briefly explain a small portion of the Dharma for the sake of the great assembly.

Having spoken thus, he should observe whether there are seven capable individuals within this assembly; the Elder should then personally request one of them to preach the Dharma for the great assembly.
Furthermore, the Elder should observe the sequence of the Dharma teacher’s discourse, its meaning and flavor, as well as his eloquence: are these words and phrases not inverted or contradictory?
Is it consistent with the meaning?
Are the words and their meanings continuous and uninterrupted in sequence?
And are they all clearly understood?
Does what has been taught accord with the Three Baskets?
Furthermore, observe whether the Dharma Master’s preaching of the Dharma accords with the sentiments of the assembly.
If the phrasing and meaning of what is taught do not accord with the Three Baskets, or even if the speech is unclear, one must not criticize or disparage it.
The Elder should say to the Dharma-preacher:
"Please speak briefly.
There are many Dharma-teachers in this assembly, and all wish for you to speak."

If the Dharma master’s spoken words and phrases are well-ordered and their principles are excellent, and even his eloquence is clear and distinct, such that it accords with the Tripitaka and satisfies the hearts of the great assembly.

The Elder should first express his thanks to the Dharma Master for his tireless efforts and praise the subtlety and profundity of the teaching; the assembly should likewise join in praising and rejoicing together.

Within this assembly are donors of sincere faith; the Elder should extensively explain to them the benefits gained from the causes and conditions of hearing the Dharma, so that their wholesome resolve may increase and become firm, never regressing.
If there is a bhikṣu in this assembly who wishes to preach the Dharma for the fourfold assembly, he must not speak directly;
he must first inform the bhikṣu sitting beside him, and that bhikṣu, in turn, must inform the elder (sthavira).
An elder shall not hastily permit someone to preach the Dharma; he must first examine that person’s knowledge and virtuous conduct.
If they are indeed capable, the elder should request them to preach before the great assembly;
if he knows their talent is insufficient, he should remain silent and let the matter rest.

If any non-Buddhists should come to the assembly with the intent to subvert the True Dharma, the Elder shall engage them in debate and discourse to subdue them, instructing them in the meaning and purpose of the teachings in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s instructions.
One who possesses such virtues is called the Elder (Sthavira) among the assembly.

If a Dharma-preacher upholds the Prātimokṣa, personally restraining the three karmas of body, speech, and mind through virtuous conduct, and reveres the Upādhyāya, the Ācārya, and the Elders as described in the preceding text, this person shall accomplish the Dharma of the Four Foundations of Mindfulness (Catur-smṛtyupasthāna) and conceive a sense of great dread toward even the slightest transgression.
One should skillfully train in such practices that accord with the Dharma.
Regarding the precepts and conduct I have taught, one must cause others to believe and accept them.
As for receiving the Dharma through hearing it with the ears, if the mind remains focused without distraction and one acts according to what was heard, this is called "receiving."
Whether I speak of wisdom, or concentration, or nirvana, you should listen and receive it.
Pay close attention with your faculty of hearing and do not cling to other sounds; whatever I say, I intend for you to understand.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who preaches the Dharma first practices the forest-dwelling life himself and then praises the forest-dwelling life; if I speak of the forest-dwelling life, you should attend with your faculty of hearing and listen well to grasp it."

Whatever I dare to say, I desire that it be understood. Regarding the practice of begging for alms up to the wearing of the three robes and the teaching of the Dharma, the speaker should personally practice what they preach.

Furthermore, one should praise the practice of begging for alms up to the wearing of the three robes; one should teach others to practice them and also teach others to praise them. If I have spoken concerning the practice of begging for alms up to the wearing of the three robes, you should listen attentively and receive these teachings with care, for what I have now said is intended to be understood.
Furthermore, a monk who preaches the Dharma should deliberate upon the assembly: what teaching should he preach so that they may receive and understand it?

If the assembly should hear the profound Dharma, he should preach the profound Dharma; if they should hear the shallow, he should preach the shallow Dharma. To fail to benefit those present is called "evil preaching."
Why does it not benefit those people?
Upon hearing this shallow teaching, they have no desire to listen and do not seek to understand it.
What, then, is called the profound teaching?

Discourse on ethical discipline, discourse on meditative concentration, discourse on wisdom, discourse on liberation, discourse on the knowledge and vision of liberation, discourse on the twelve links of dependent origination, and even discourse on nirvana—these are called the profound teachings.
One should hear such teachings as are profound from those who speak them; to delight in hearing them, to reflect upon them, and to seek their understanding is called "benefit.
If one delights in the shallow, one should be taught the shallow.
What are the shallow teachings?
They are discourses on ethical discipline, discourses on generosity, and discourses on rebirth in the heavens.

If one teaches the profound to a multitude that delights in the shallow, they will have no desire to hear it, will not seek to understand it, and it will not benefit them; this is called "evil teaching."
To explain shallow teachings to those who are shallow is called "skillful exposition" because it brings benefit.

Furthermore, a monk who preaches the Dharma should understand the meaning, the phrasing, and the vocal tones of both men and women; moreover, he should be able to skillfully employ expedient means in preaching the Dharma so that he causes his listeners to understand according to what he knows.
Furthermore, one should skillfully understand the meaning and flavor of the words and phrases, ensuring that the preceding and succeeding parts do not become confused or intermingled.
If one is adept at teaching, even the most subtle of dharmas can cause the listener to incline toward them, leading them all the way to the final practitioner.
Regarding the reason for speaking of "the final practitioner," there are two kinds of "final":
first, being the last in the sequence of preaching the Dharma, which is called "final";
second, the Dharma taught being the most superficial, which is called "final."
Furthermore, regarding the meaning of the term "person," there are two kinds of "last":
first, as in the case of Subhadra, who attained the Way at his final moment, and is thus called "the last."
Second, as with bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs who attain arhatship in this very body of retribution, this body is also called "the final.
Furthermore, when a Dharma-preacher wishes to preach the Dharma, they should first observe the fourfold assembly: the assembly of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
If they are bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs, one should explain for them the observance of morality, concentration, wisdom, and nirvāṇa;
if they are upāsakas or upāsikās, one should explain for them the observance of morality, giving, rebirth in heaven, and even the dharma of complete purity.

"Furthermore, if one is to preach the Dharma, one should eliminate greed; with a mind free from attachment, free from malice, free from delusion, free from self-deprecation, and free from disparaging the assembly; with a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of sympathetic joy, a mind of benefit, a mind of patience, an unshakable mind, and a mind free from doubt—one should preach the Dharma while establishing such states of mind."
"Furthermore, the teacher of the Dharma should not preach the Dharma for other incidental reasons.

He should preach the Dharma for its own sake, because the Dharma is profound and difficult to hear; this Dharma is a treasure and a medicine that can benefit people, and it is for this reason that he preaches it."

The speaker should preach the Dharma to others with a mind of loving-kindness and compassion; even if they can cause another person to understand a single four-line verse according to reality, it will bring benefit and peace for a long night.
He further reflects:
"By means of this sequence, I shall fulfill the meaning of the phrases so that the audience may attain equal understanding.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu preaching the Dharma should not preach for others with a mind of greed arising from seeing material gain, nor should he preach for others with a mind of fear.

Why is this? If one preaches the Dharma to others with a mind of fear, it will cause the body to become exhausted and weary; furthermore, what is spoken will lack coherence and the voice will be indistinct.
If one preaches the Dharma without skill, the meaning will also be difficult to understand.
If one preaches the Dharma for others with a composed and settled mind, even the nuances of the meaning will be clearly elucidated.

Furthermore, the bhikṣu who preaches the Dharma should preach in accordance with the proper sequence; he should further preach for the assembly the Dharma of revulsion and the Dharma of detachment, so as to cause the minds of those before him to give rise to joy, seeking liberation and swiftly attaining nirvāṇa.

If a bhikṣu who preaches the Dharma should further constantly practice mindfulness and contemplation of the body as suffering, empty, impermanent, non-self, and impure, he must not allow this to cease. Why is this?
This is because one shall attain the twelve recollections that constitute the noble Dharma.
What are these twelve recollections?
First, the recollection of accomplishing one's own person;
Second, the thought of accomplishing the welfare of others;
third, the thought of aspiring to obtain a human body;
fourth, the thought of being born into a noble family.
Fifth, to attain faith in the Buddha-dharma;
sixth, to awaken to the Dharma without exerting effort in whatever place one is born;
seventh, to have all faculties complete in whatever place one is born.
Eighth, the recollection that one encounters a Buddha, a World-Honored One, appearing in the world;
ninth, the recollection that in whatever place one is born, one always hears the True Dharma being preached;
tenth, the recollection that the Dharma thus preached may always endure for a long time.
Eleventh, by recollecting the aspiration that the Dharma may long endure, one attains practice in accordance with it;
twelfth, by recollecting the constant mind of compassion for all sentient beings.
By being fully endowed with these twelve recollections, one will certainly attain the Noble Dharma; this is called preaching the Dharma for a specific purpose.
From the Dharma that is difficult to obtain up to the uninterrupted contemplation of the body—this is the Dharma taught by the teacher of the Dharma.
"If, among the assembly listening to the Dharma, there is a senior elder who observes the teacher of the Dharma and finds him not even to the point of conforming to the sentiments of the assembly..."
The Elder should say to the speaker of the Dharma:
"Venerable sir, you should not speak in such a manner. Why is that?"
There are five causes and conditions that create obstacles for the True Dharma, such that it cannot abide for long, but becomes obscured and fails to appear. What are these five?

First, the sūtras one recites are incomplete; the teachings one studies cannot be fully mastered; the disciples one instructs do not receive complete texts; and both teacher and disciple fail to explain the teachings with full clarity or thoroughness.

Second, if those who study and learn come to fully know the Tripitaka, possessing both its words and meanings and clearly understanding what is taught, yet do not instruct the fourfold assembly of disciples, then once their bodies perish, the Dharma will likewise perish with them.

Third, if the senior monk (*sthavira*) who serves as the leader of the Saṃgha does not cultivate the three types of action, but instead delights in performing worldly activities pertaining to birth and death, and if the disciples and followers he trains under him likewise do not cultivate the three types of action but delight in worldly affairs, such a group of followers will cause the True Dharma to perish.

Fourth, if there are bhikṣus who are by nature perverse and prone to anger, who do not follow the words of others, and who give rise to resentment whether they hear good or evil, and who abandon and avoid any bhikṣus renowned for their wisdom and insight in a given land, never returning to them again—this is the root of the destruction of the Dharma.
Fifth, if there are bhikṣus who constantly delight in quarreling and litigation, forming factions to assist one another in disputing over status and material gain—
these five matters can swiftly cause the True Dharma to perish.

If the speaker of the Dharma is eloquent and clear in speech, possesses correct pronunciation, is fully endowed with the mastery of both the phrasing and the meaning of the texts they have studied, and moreover accords with the inclinations of the assembly.
Regarding such an exposition, the entire assembly should offer praise and sympathetic joy.
Furthermore, there are five causes and conditions that can prevent the True Dharma from quickly disappearing:

first, the textual passages of the sūtras one recites and studies are complete, with their preceding and succeeding sequences and all their meanings thoroughly mastered, and one further teaches the assembly of disciples so that they come to know what one knows.
Such a person is able to cause the Buddha-dharma to abide long in the world.
Second, they possess a broad knowledge of the texts and meanings of the Tripiṭaka in their entirety, and are further able to teach the fourfold assembly according to what they have understood.
Although his physical body has perished, he causes the True Dharma to continue in succession without interruption for future generations.
Such a person is able to prevent the True Dharma from falling to the ground.

Third, if within the Saṃgha there is a virtuous Elder (sthavira) esteemed by the fourfold assembly, who is able to diligently cultivate the three types of action and renounce worldly affairs, and if his followers and disciples likewise continue this succession one after another, this too will cause the True Dharma to abide for a long time.

Fourth, if there are bhikṣus whose nature is gentle and whose speech is free from contradiction—who follow what they hear that is good and avoid what they hear that is evil—and who, when instructed by those of high talent, wisdom, and virtue, respectfully accept and practice their words, these too can cause the Buddha-dharma to endure for a long time.
Fifth, if monks live in mutual harmony and concord, and do not form cliques based on power or material gain to assist one another in disputing right from wrong—
these five matters can ensure that the True Dharma continues to flow without interruption.
"This is what is called the Elder among those who preach the Dharma.
At that time, King Bimbisāra was on the upper terrace and saw all the laypeople departing together.
The king asked those nearby:
"Where do these various crowds intend to go?
The ministers replied, "There is a place where the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) preach the Dharma; they are going there to listen to the Dharma."
The king thought to himself:
"Since both sides are listening, why not go to the Buddha to hear the Dharma?
At that time, the Buddha was in the city of Rājagṛha.
The king immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side. He addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The non-Buddhists preach the Dharma every day, and the laypeople provide them with great offerings every day.”

"In my heart, O World-Honored One, I pray that on the six days of the fast, you will assemble the śramaṇas to discourse and debate; I, your disciple, shall provide various offerings to feed the Buddha and the Saṃgha, while simultaneously hearing the Dharma."

"The non-Buddhists claim that their own teachings are the true and correct ones; if the Buddha does not preach the Dharma, people will not recognize the True Dharma and will all enter onto the wrong path.
For these reasons, the Tathāgata immediately assembled the bhikṣus; once the bhikṣus had assembled, they sat in silence.
When all the donors had assembled with the intention of listening to the Dharma, they spoke to the bhikṣus.
Having heard this, the bhikṣus immediately informed the World-Honored One.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"I permit you to chant.
"Chanting" refers to the words of speech.
Although the Buddha permitted speech, it was not yet known what kind of Dharma should be spoken.
The bhikṣus again questioned the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"From the sūtras up to the upadeśas, you may speak as you please."
"O bhikṣus, although the Buddha has already permitted the recitation of the twelve divisions of the sūtras, he wished to manifest this specific meaning; yet, others still harbored doubts:
'If one were to explain the text sequentially, the assembly is so large and the text so voluminous that they might become weary and disheartened.'"
"If we were to briefly compile elegant phrases to directly reveal their meaning, what do you think?
For this reason, he reported the matter in full to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha immediately granted permission for the bhikṣus to cite essential passages and sublime phrases from the sūtras to directly manifest their meanings.
At that time, the Buddha permitted the preaching of the Dharma; however, there were two bhikṣus who, sitting together on the same seat, simultaneously expounded the same teaching.
When the Tathāgata heard this, he immediately established a prohibition against it.
At that time, there was another bhikṣu in the assembly who stood not far from the Buddha and recited a sutra in a loud, melodic song-like voice.
Upon hearing this, the Buddha immediately established a prohibition against using such a tone for sutra recitation, as there are five faults associated with it, as explained above.
There are five further faults in preaching the Dharma using the melodic chants of non-Buddhists:
first, it is not called "self-retention";
second, it does not accord with the audience.
Third, the devas are displeased;
fourth, the speech is incorrect and difficult to understand;
fifth, because the speech is unskillful, the meaning is likewise difficult to understand.
These are called the five kinds of faults.
"At that time, King Bimbisāra had deep faith in the Triple Gem; whatever the Buddha and the Saṃgha required, he gave them according to their wishes, even including bathing pools, all in this manner."

In the early morning, King Bimbisāra, leading a great multitude of people, went to the pond intending to bathe. From afar, he heard voices within the pond reciting scriptures with an exceedingly loud sound.
He immediately asked those nearby, "Who are these people?"
The attendants informed the king,
"These are the group of six bhikṣus.
The king immediately halted his retinue and forbade them from proceeding further, fearing he might disturb the śramaṇas.
The king remained for a very long time, yet the bhikṣus had still not finished bathing.
Unable to bathe, the king immediately turned his carriage back toward the palace.
When this occurred repeatedly, the World-Honored One heard of it and immediately established a rule for the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, it is permitted to bathe once every fifteen days.
When bathing, loud voices and clamor are not permitted.
This is called the rule regarding speech.
"At that time, the bhikṣus gathered in one place, intending to focus their minds in contemplation and taking no pleasure in speech.
The Buddha, knowing the intentions of the bhikṣus, immediately addressed them:
'I permit you to remain silent; whether you focus your minds in contemplation or walk in silence, I also permit you to fix your thoughts and contemplate the meaning.'"
This is called the Dharma of Non-Speech.
Regarding the method for nurturing a community of disciples, one should provide instruction; through two causes and conditions, one should gather the assembly:
first, gathering them through the Dharma; second, gathering them through robes and food. One should gather as many disciples as one is able to support according to one's capacity.
When a bhikṣu nurtures a circle of disciples, he should always employ skillful means to instruct his followers so that they do not become overly acquisitive.
He should guide them to practice sitting meditation, recite the sūtras, and cultivate merit; within these three activities, he should teach them various skillful methods:
first, teaching them to seek the Dharma extensively; second, teaching them not to abandon their practice; and third, teaching them to diligently apply skillful means in their cultivation and study.
Furthermore, one should observe their followers: do they not delight in much talk?
Are they not greedily attached to much talk?
Do they not diligently apply skillful means toward such talk?
Furthermore, do you not delight in excessive sleep?
Are you not attached to sleep?
Within your sleep, do you not diligently seek out the conditions for sleep?
Furthermore, he observes the assembly: do they not take much delight in the household life?
Are they not greedily attached to the household life?
Do they not diligently seek out means to create many conditions for the household life?
Furthermore, one should observe the assembly: do they not delight in gathering in large numbers for frivolous play and amusement?
Are they not attached to such frivolity?
And do they not diligently employ skillful means to create conditions for frivolous play?
Furthermore, one should observe their followers: among the assembly, who acts in accordance with the Dharma and who acts contrary to it?
If they act in accordance with the Dharma, one should provide them with clothing, food, and even the flavor of the Dharma, instructing them repeatedly.

If they do not act in accordance with the Dharma, one should tell them to leave; however, if at a later time they develop a mind of repentance and reform, they may be permitted to return to the assembly, where they shall be provided with food and clothing and taught the flavor of the Dharma.
This is called the method for nurturing a community of disciples.

When the leader of the bhikṣu-saṃgha enters a great assembly, he should restrain his demeanor, adjust his robes, keep his body upright, gaze straight ahead, speak with humility, and humble himself to show respect to those before him. His deportment should be orderly and dignified, his faculties serene, so that those who observe him never grow weary.
The method for entering the Saṃgha requires that one cultivate such virtuous conduct.
As for the "assembly," it refers to the fourfold assembly.
Within these four assemblies, there are those that are in accordance with the Dharma, those that are not in accordance with the Dharma, and one's own personal assembly.
Just as one enters the assembly according to one's own practice, all teachers of the community should likewise enter the assembly.
This is called the method of entering the assembly.

Regarding the method for a bhikṣu acting as the leader of the assembly: while in the midst of the assembly, he should observe this group—whether they are engaged in seated meditation, walking meditation, silent reflection, contemplation, or in verbal exchange and discussion regarding the meaning of the sūtras—and consider which dharma they delight in.
If there are those who delight in verbal discourse and debate, whatever sūtra they may have studied, one should join them in discussing what they have studied and not oppose them.
This is called the Dharma of the Community Leader.
The senior elder among the assembly should observe what kind of dharma the people of that time would find pleasing:
would they delight in discourse on generosity, discourse on ethical discipline, or discourse on rebirth in heaven?
Is it a discourse on the delight in nirvāṇa?
Whatever discourse the assembly delights in, that one should preach to them.
Furthermore, one should observe the great assembly: among the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, which dharma will they take pleasure in?
He teaches according to what is appropriate for those in the assembly;
this is called the method for a senior elder (*sthavira*) preaching the Dharma in the midst of the assembly.
At that time, the World-Honored One was reflecting in his quiet chamber:
"I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
The causal circumstances are as explained in the preceding text.
The five ways of reciting the precepts are also as in the preceding text.
When a bhikṣu reaches five years of ordination, he must recite the Prātimokṣa until it is mastered.
The causes and conditions for a bhikṣu’s recitation of the precepts are explained in detail as above.
The procedures for the upoṣadha ceremony for one person, or for two or three persons, are as explained above.
All matters performed during the *poṣadha* are termed *karmas*, as explained above.
The procedure for undertaking the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) is also as described above in the section on the *varṣā* rules.

A visiting bhikṣu should first inform the resident bhikṣus; if there are difficult circumstances that do not permit the observance of the rains retreat, he should seek another place, and must not remain by force.
If the place for the rains retreat is favorable but there is no donor with whom one may speak, one should personally resolve the mind and perform the formal rite of entering the rains retreat.

Regarding a bhikṣu’s place for the summer retreat—whether it be within a monastery, in a separate pavilion, or at the foot of a tree—he should first go there to inspect whether bedding and requisites are available.
"Is this dwelling free from the disturbance of noise?
Is it free from dangers such as lions, tigers, wolves, thieves, mosquitoes, insects, water, and the like?
Can one dwell here in peace and security until the end of the retreat?"
Is there a stone cave or a stone fence?
If there is, one should clear away all the grass and wood within it; furthermore, this stone cave should be plastered and repaired.
Thus it should be understood in detail.
When a bhikṣu is observing the summer retreat (varṣā), he should reflect to himself:
"Is the food and drink provided for this retreat sufficient?"
If one is ill, can medicine appropriate to the ailment be obtained?
Furthermore, one should observe whether those living together are compatible and whether one can engage in harmonious affairs as desired;
are the co-residents trustworthy?
Do you dwell in peace and security while practicing the Path?
When we are walking, standing, sitting, or lying down together, do you not create obstacles for me?
And when I am ill, do you not abandon me and depart?
Having thus deliberated on these various matters and reached a consensus, they then enter the rains retreat (*varṣā*).
Furthermore, they observe the assembly during the summer retreat: "Is there anyone in this assembly who is prone to vigorous quarreling?"
"Have I not given rise to evil thoughts or harsh speech?
Am I not able to create obstacles for him?
He reflected further: "As the World-Honored One has said, one must rely upon the Prātimokṣa during the summer retreat."
Is there anyone among this assembly who knows the Dharma, understands the Vinaya, and understands the Mātṛkā-piṭaka?
Let me not, during this summer retreat, commit any offense that I would wish to eradicate but find no one to turn to for guidance.
Furthermore, as the World-Honored One has said, those who are ignorant and lack understanding must not be separated from their reliance [on the Sangha] for as long as they live.
He further reflects: "Is there anyone in this assembly who is like a monk who instructs his children as parents do?"

If there are those of renowned virtue and far-reaching reputation who are revered by both the monastic and lay communities, should I commit an offense, I shall go before them and, with great shame and remorse, seek their confession; out of compassion, those elders shall from time to time instruct me so that I do not fall into negligence.
As the Blessed One has said, the schism of the Saṃgha is a great evil, like something hard, astringent, bitter, and pungent, devoid of any pleasure.
Within this community of this residence, is there no one who is prone to fierce quarreling? During the summer retreat, have no matters arisen that would cause a schism in the Saṃgha?
"Will there not be any obstacles for me?
Having thus deliberated and found no obstacles, one then enters the rains retreat (*varṣā*).
This is called the method of deliberation when wishing to enter the rains retreat.
“Monks, regarding the procedure for entering the rains retreat (*varṣā*), once the formal acceptance of the retreat has been completed, one should then accept the dwelling and bedding.
Within the room, one should repair and plaster it, and every single seat and bed must be properly attended to.”
During the summer retreat (*varṣā*), one must not go elsewhere unless there is a valid reason.

If there is a reason—such as for the sake of the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha, or for the sake of the sick—one should receive the seven-day authorization (*saptāha-kāraṇīya*) and go outside the boundary, returning to this place to continue the retreat.

One must not go outside the boundary for the sake of food, drink, or material gain; however, for the sake of a bowl, robes, medicine, a needle, or a woolen mat, one may go outside the boundary by receiving the seven-day authorization (*saptāha-kalpa*).
At that time, Prince Pāṭaliputra had gone forth into the Buddha’s Dharma. His father, the king, having made extensive offerings for the sake of the stūpa, sent a messenger to summon his son, saying:
"Come, let us together make offerings to the stūpa."
"During the summer retreat, one must not go on journeys. For this reason, [the monks] reported the matter in full to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"For the sake of the stūpa, I permit the bhikṣus to receive the seven-day leave; when the seven days are complete, they shall return to the retreat here."
Regarding the method for the summer retreat (varṣā) of the bhikṣus: they may receive a seven-day leave, but once the seven days are complete, they must not exceed them.
If they do not return to their place of retreat within the seven days and the night, the bhikṣu’s summer retreat is forfeited according to the law.

Regarding the causes and conditions concerning the previous robes, alms bowl, and even the needle and woolen mat, one should apply oneself with diligent skillful means so that those who have not understood may understand, those who have not attained may attain, and those who have not realized may realize.
This is called the procedure for entering the rains retreat (*varṣā*).

Within the assembly observing the retreat, the senior monk (*sthavira*) should inquire about the location of the boundary markers for the great precinct (*mahā-sīmā*); he should further inquire about the locations where robes may be lost or not lost; he should also inquire about the pure site (*śuci-sthāna*), the site for the *poṣadha*, the person appointed to recite the precepts, the person appointed to preach the Dharma, the person appointed to offer blessings (*svastyayana*), the person appointed to manage affairs, the person appointed to console the manager of affairs, the person appointed to distribute voting tallies (*śalākā*), and the monastic attendant (*vaiyāvṛtyakara*).
If the bhikṣus go outside the boundary for seven days, fifteen days, or even up to one month, they must perform the formal act of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.
They should instruct junior bhikṣus themselves and encourage others to provide instruction.
All such matters as these should be attended to by the *upādhyāya* (senior elder) during the summer retreat (*varṣā*).
Furthermore, he should inspect the cells to see who is using the bedding and requisites in accordance with the Dharma and who is not.
Regarding those who use things in accordance with the Dharma, one should instruct, benefit, gladden, and praise their conduct.
Regarding those who do not act in accordance with the Dharma, one should admonish them to bring it to mind, saying:
"Venerable sir!..."
"You should use [the requisites] in accordance with the Dharma; there are five faults in using them contrary to the Dharma.
You should keep this matter in mind as the Tathāgata has prescribed the precepts.
This is the procedure for the *upādhyāya* (senior monk) during the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*).
When it is time for the midday meal, when eating congee, or when drinking sweet gruel, the senior monk (sthavira) among the assembly should announce:
"So much time has already passed; so much time remains."
If the senior monk (*sthavira*) within the assembly conducts himself in such a manner, he is called the father and mother of the Saṃgha, and is also called the teacher of the Saṃgha.
This is known as the Dharma for the senior monk during the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*).
"A bhikṣu in retreat may perform one specific act at the time of the *pravāraṇā*:
namely, declaring at the time of the *pravāraṇā* any offenses seen, heard, or suspected.
After the *pravāraṇā*, he may perform four acts:"
First, the dissolution of the great boundary (mahā-sīmā);
second, the re-establishment of the great boundary.
There are two causes and conditions for dissolving the boundary:
First, it may be swept away by a great flood, its boundary markers destroyed and its location unknown;
second, due to the threat of bandits, all the bhikṣus may have gone outside the boundary.
Because of these two causes and conditions, it is necessary to dissolve and then re-establish the boundary.
Third, receiving the *kaṭhina* robe;
fourth, receiving bedding and utensils at the conclusion of the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*).
These matters pertain to the causes and conditions following the *pravāraṇā*.
“There are four assemblies:
the assembly of bhikṣus, the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs, the assembly of upāsakas, and the assembly of upāsikās.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of saṃghas:”

There are four types of monastic communities: first, the community of ordinary persons; second, the community of noble ones; third, the community of those with a sense of shame; and fourth, the community of those without a sense of shame.
Regarding the community of bhikṣus: one, two, or three individuals do not constitute a saṃgha; it is with four individuals that a saṃgha is formed, up to twenty individuals forming a saṃgha.

A community of four monks may perform the *jñapti-ekakarmavācanā* (one motion and one proclamation) and the *jñapti-dvikarmavācanā* (one motion and two proclamations); however, they may not perform the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism), may not confer full ordination (*upasampadā*), and may not perform the *āpattivyutthāna* (expiation of offenses). Apart from these three, they may perform all other legal acts (*dharmakarma*).
A community of five monks may perform the *pravāraṇā* and the *poṣadha*.
In border regions, one may receive full ordination if there is a *vinayadhara*; this is not permitted in the central lands.
In the central lands or border regions, the *ābṛhaṇa* (act of reconciliation) may not be performed.
A community of twenty monks may perform all ritual acts of the Dharma.
A community of ten monks may perform all ritual acts of the Dharma, with the exception of the *ābhāṣaṇa* (rehabilitation rite).

If four persons perform a formal legal act (*dharmakarma*) and one person is missing, the legal act is not accomplished; this is called performing a legal act that is contrary to the Dharma (*adharmakarma*).
If five persons perform a formal legal act and one person is missing, the legal act is not accomplished; this is called performing a legal act that is contrary to the Dharma.
If ten people perform a formal ritual (karmavācanā) and one person is missing, the ritual is not accomplished; this is called performing a ritual in an illegal manner.
If twenty people perform a formal ritual and one person is missing, the ritual is not accomplished; this is called performing a ritual in an illegal manner.
This is called the business of the Saṃgha.
Regarding the method for entering the Saṃgha—from maintaining a composed demeanor up to generating wholesome thoughts in others—it is as explained in the preceding text.

As for the method of mental application when entering the Saṃgha: it is like sweeping the ground with a broom; one does not perceive right or wrong, but gives rise universally to a mind of loving-kindness. One should enter the Saṃgha with such a mind.
This is called entering the Dharma of the Sangha.
Regarding the method for sitting within the Sangha:
when entering the assembly, one should show reverence to the elders and take cognizance of one's own seat; furthermore, one must not be lax or take up excessive space for a seat.

If one sees an unlawful act being performed within the Saṃgha and wishes to offer admonition, yet fears that the Saṃgha will not accept their words, they may remain seated in silence while keeping this in mind.
When a bhikṣu enters the midst of the Saṃgha, they should deliberate upon the legal procedures being performed by the Saṃgha: whether they are in accordance with the Dharma or not.
Is it in accordance with the Vinaya or not?
If it is in accordance, that is well.
If it is not in accordance, those who are like-minded and practice the Vinaya according to the Dharma may join in admonishing him; if there are none, one should remain silent and sit.
This is called the matter of entering the Saṃgha.
"When the Saṃgha assembles, the elder among the assembly should observe whether the middle-ranking and junior monks maintain proper deportment in sitting and rising according to the Dharma."
Is he not baring his body?
If one sits improperly and is furthermore baring their body, the senior monk (upādhyāya) should snap his fingers so that the junior monks know.
If they still do not take notice, he should send a messenger to inform them.
Regarding matters within the Saṃgha, the senior monks (sthavira) should all attend to them.
When a monk of middle rank sits among the assembly, he should observe whether the senior and junior monks are sitting in accordance with the Dharma.
Does the robe cover the body?
If it is not in accordance with the Dharma, one should snap one's fingers to make it known.
If they still do not perceive it, one should speak to a person who knows the Dharma and have them go and inform them.
When the senior monk knows it is time, he says to the junior monk, "Venerable sir, you yourself know the time.
He should then offer service, respect, honor, and praise to the senior monk.
This is called the procedure for those of middle rank.
Regarding the procedure for those of lower rank sitting among the assembly:
once the assembly has settled into their seats, one should observe whether the seating and the robes of the elders and those of middle rank conform to the Dharma.
If they do not act according to the Dharma, one should snap one's fingers to make them aware.
If they still do not understand, one should also dispatch a person who knows the Dharma to go and say:
"Venerable sirs, you yourselves should know the proper time."
Furthermore, one should offer worship, respect, reverence, and praise to those seated in the upper and middle positions.
Among the monks seated in the lower positions, one should take water and sprinkle it upon the ground, as well as sweep and smear it clean; and within the monks' bathhouse, one should kindle a fire.
The Buddha ordained that all rites to be performed among the junior monks must be carried out;
this is termed the "Dharma of the Junior Monks.
From those with no years of seniority up to those with nine years of seniority, these are termed "junior monks."
From ten years of ordination up to nineteen years of ordination, these are called middle-ranking elders (madhyama-sthavira).
From twenty years of ordination up to forty-nine years of ordination, these are called senior elders (sthavira).
Those who have exceeded fifty years of ordination and above, who are honored by kings, householders, and renunciants, are called venerable elders (vṛddha-sthavira).
One should study all the dharmas practiced by the Saṃgha and study the pure upholding of the precepts.

Regarding the pure upholding of the precepts: one is able to receive and maintain all the precepts established by all Buddhas without the slightest transgression; therefore, it is called "upholding the precepts" and attaining the purity of the pure precepts.

The precept of the mind refers to the precept of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-śīla*); by maintaining the mind so that it does not scatter and attaining union with samādhi, it is called the attainment of the precept of the mind.
The precept of pure wisdom refers to upholding this wisdom without allowing it to become distracted so as to perceive the Four Noble Truths; this is called the precept of pure wisdom.
If any person possesses faith and maintains the precepts, they should give rise to this thought:
"If I feel fear at the transgression of even a minor precept, it is no different from the transgression of a grave one."

One who maintains the precepts in this manner has a pure holy life (*brahmacarya*), and the *prātimokṣa* vows they uphold are likewise pure. They should cultivate all bodily, verbal, and mental actions so as to accomplish virtuous conduct, even to the point of being able to restrain body, speech, and mind from committing the ten unwholesome deeds.
This is called the Dharma practiced by all people.
At that time, the World-Honored One was in Vaiśālī.
The Licchavis and others prepared a meal and invited the Saṃgha, providing various kinds of fine foods.
The monks, having eaten too much, all suffered from a lack of well-being.

Jīvaka, the King of Physicians, examined their condition and prescribed a remedy, concluding that if a bathhouse were obtained, this illness could be cured; he further desired to establish a bathhouse within the Jetavana Monastery.
For this reason, the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
The Buddha permitted the bhikṣus to construct bathhouses.
Regarding the method for a bathhouse: it should be built by piling mud; however, in places where earth is unavailable, one may build it of wood and must coat it with mud.
In this bathhouse, fire is lit beneath one wall to provide heat, while beds are spread beneath the remaining walls for bathing.
Regarding the method of entering the bathhouse to wash:

one must follow the senior monk (*upādhyāya*); if it is too hot, the door should be closed, and if it is too cold, it should be opened; the junior monks (*navaka*) must not contravene the wishes of the senior monk.
When entering the bathhouse to wash, the senior monk (*upādhyāya*) should enter first and take a good seat to bathe.
This method for entering the bathhouse to wash was established by the Buddha because of the group of six monks (*ṣaḍvargika*).

On another occasion, bhikṣus entered a bathhouse with laypeople to wash. When the Buddha heard of this, he did not permit it; bhikṣus must not wash together with white-robed laypeople at the same time in a bathhouse. However, if there is a donor of sincere faith, he is permitted to do so.
Later, on one occasion, all the bhikṣus entered the bathhouse naked to bathe together; as they looked at one another, they were all filled with shame and embarrassment.
This matter was passed from one to another until it reached the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I do not permit you to enter the bathhouse together while naked, nor may you wash one another.

If one person has a robe and another is without a robe, the one with a robe may pour water for the one without a robe and may also wash them; however, the one without a robe must not pour water to wash another."
"If the bathhouse is far from a water source, it is permitted to install a pool within the bathhouse, or even to dig a well.
The method for entering the bathhouse to wash should be understood in detail in this manner.
When entering the bathhouse to wash for the senior monk (*sthavira*) among the Sangha, if one sees that it is very hot inside, one should open the door slightly to allow it to cool briefly.

Furthermore, one should explain the causes and conditions of bathing to the monks who have entered the bathhouse. One should explain that those who bathe do not do so for the sake of adorning the body or for personal cleanliness; rather, one should speak to them of the method of cultivating revulsion toward the body, and further speak of the method of subduing the mind. One should give rise to a heart of compassion and preach the Dharma so that they may attain few desires and contentment.

Furthermore, it was explained to him again: "This bathing is not for any other purpose; it is solely intended to remove the diseases of wind and cold within the body, so that one may practice the Path in peace and security."
This is called the ritual procedure for the Elder in the bathhouse.

"The manner in which the co-practicing disciples and co-resident disciples serve their Upādhyāya and Ācārya, and the manner in which the Upādhyāya and Ācārya maintain their disciples—all of these are as explained in the preceding text."
"The Dharma for Śrāmaṇeras:

A śrāmaṇera may clear the ground by removing weeds, take willow branches, and gather flowers and fruits; having brought these back, he should inform his upādhyāya, and the upādhyāya or ācārya should accept and make use of them."

A śrāmaṇera should know how to feel shame and remorse; he should dwell well within the dharma of serving his teacher and must not be indolent or self-indulgent. He should exercise self-restraint in body and speech, humble himself, and respect others. He should always delight in upholding the precepts and take no pleasure in frivolous play or jesting, nor should he rely on his own talent or strength.
Furthermore, do not be frivolous or impulsive; you should know shame and modesty.
Moreover, you must not utter words that are indeterminate or confused; whatever you say should be orderly and reasonable.

You should always know for yourself the dharmas that are pure and those that are impure. You should constantly follow your upādhyāya and ācārya to recite and study the sūtras and dharmas. Among the entire Saṃgha, in all matters you undertake, you must never act in opposition.
Thus it is known in detail.
Regarding the rules for a bhikṣu walking ahead when traveling with companions: while in front, he should look back to see whether the robes worn by those behind are properly arranged.
Is it not uneven? Is it not shrunken?
Is the mind not concentrated?
Do you act with improper decorum?
