When entering the homes of others, do you not give rise to defiled thoughts regarding exquisite forms?
Upon seeing rare and precious jewels, do you not give rise to the intent to steal?

There was a bhikṣu whom the Saṃgha sent to the house of a donor to perform repentance. Upon arriving at the donor’s residence, the messenger bhikṣu should enter first and speak these words to the donor:
"This bhikṣu has already been fully disciplined by the Saṃgha; you may now accept his repentance."
This is called the dharma for a bhikṣu who goes ahead.
As for why he is said to "go ahead": when he receives a commission from the Saṃgha and enters the house of a donor (dānapati) first to speak, he is called one who goes ahead.
Furthermore, when traveling together on the same path, the Sangha may dispatch this bhikṣu to lead the way ahead to the donor's residence; this is also called "going in front.
A bhikṣu walking behind should accomplish five dharmas:
first, he should not go ahead while traveling.
Second, one must not stay far behind; one must follow immediately in succession.

Third, if the preceding bhikṣu is one’s preceptor (upādhyāya), teacher (ācārya), or elder (sthavira), one must not oppose or contradict what they say. If they ask about one’s practice of the path, recitation of sūtras, or the cultivation of spiritual disciplines, one should answer truthfully and must not conceal anything—except for matters concerning the attainment of dhyāna or the realization of the fruits of sainthood.
If there are previously stated wholesome dharmas that are superior, one should rejoice in them and praise them.
Fourth, if there are points of failure or errors, one should state that what was said in those places does not accord with the Buddha’s intention.
Now, regarding those who wish to speak of what is improper, one must avoid vulgar speech.
Fifth, if one obtains wealth in accordance with the Dharma or whatever is placed within the alms-bowl, one should take charge of managing it all.
These are called the five virtues of a later bhikṣu.
"If a bhikṣu acts as a teacher for laypeople, instructing and transforming them as a field of merit, there are five things he must not do:
first, he should not reside in the house of this donor."
Second, one should not fixate the mind on coveting gain and offerings.
Third, one should not preach the Dharma to a donor as a whole to instruct, encourage, benefit, and gladden them; rather, one should specifically instruct them to further cultivate other dharmas.
As for the other dharmas: [one should] practice giving, maintain the precepts, and receive the eightfold fast (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa); each of these is to be explained in this manner.
Fourth, one must not engage in playful amusement or mutual entertainment with householders.
Fifth, one must not fixate the mind with the constant desire to see [the donor].
Furthermore, there are five things that must not be done:
first, if the donor is not a close acquaintance, one must not go to them by forcing a pretense of intimacy.
Second, one must not seek to influence the lay patron’s household affairs;
third, one must not engage in private, secret conversation with the lay patron;
fourth, one must not speak to the lay patron regarding auspicious times or dates for performing sacrifices to spirits and deities.
Fifth, one must not overstep what is requested from relatives or donors.
A bhikṣu should accomplish five qualities so that he shall be respected and honored by his donors.
What are the five?
First, one should not visit places where one has no long-standing kinship or friendship;
second, one should not seek personal influence to manage the household affairs of a donor.
Third, one must not engage in private conversation with a donor that causes suspicion to arise within the donor's household;
fourth, one must not instruct a donor on auspicious times or dates for performing sacrifices to spirits;
fifth, one must not exceed the scope of what is requested.
"When a bhikṣu enters the home of a donor, he should accomplish five dharmas:
first, speaking softly upon entering;
second, restraining the actions of body, speech, and mind."
Third, they walk with a humble and reverent mind;
fourth, they restrain all their sense faculties;
fifth, their dignified deportment inspires goodness in others.
These are called the five methods for entering the house of a donor.
There are nine matters regarding a bhikṣu:
first, knowing the donor’s mind, one should not sit and preach the Dharma.
When a bhikṣu enters another’s house, even if a donor performs a prostration, he should not sit if he knows that no sincere heart of respect has arisen.
Second, even if the donor goes out to meet him, he should still not sit if the mind is not earnest and respectful.
Third, although one is invited to sit, if one knows that the mind [of the host] is not sincere, one should likewise not sit.
Fourth, although one is requested to sit, if the place provided is not respectful, one should again not sit.
Fifth, if there is something being said, whether it be words of the Dharma or words contrary to the Dharma, if one does not take them to heart, one should not sit.
Sixth, although one hears of virtuous qualities, if one does not believe and accept them, one should not sit.
Seventh, if one seeks something and knows that there is much available yet the person gives little, one should not sit.
Eighth, when arriving at a house, if fine food is present but not served while coarse food is prepared, one should not sit.
Ninth, although one may provide for their necessities, if they are given according to the manner of a market transaction, one should likewise not sit.
Furthermore, there are nine circumstances in which one should know the donor’s intention and sit to preach the Dharma.
First, knowing that there is a mind of reverence, one performs the prostration;
second, knowing that there is a mind of reverence, one goes out to meet and welcome them;
third, because of the knowledge that there is a mind of reverence, one invites them to enter.
Fourth, because he knows the gravity of the matter, he prepares a high seat;
fifth, because he knows that the mind is receptive to instruction, he accepts and utilizes both words of the Dharma and words contrary to the Dharma;
sixth, knowing that hearing of his virtues will give rise to faith.
Seventh, knowing that what was previously scarce and difficult to obtain has now been obtained in abundance;
eighth, knowing that there was formerly coarse food, yet one prepares fine and delicious food instead;
ninth, knowing that when there is something desired, one gives it with a generous heart.
If one knows the mind of a donor through these nine causal conditions, one should sit and preach the Dharma for them.
"When a bhikṣu enters the house of a layperson, he should collect his mind like the metaphor of moonlight."
When entering a village on almsround, one should proceed with humility, reverence, and a sense of shame; one should not walk with an arrogant mind, heedlessness, a lack of shame, or distraction.

The method for gathering the mind is like a person whose feet tread upon a high mountain, a precipitous cliff, or a perilous ledge of but a single square foot; in every thought-moment fear arises, and no other thought remains.
It is also like a person standing at the edge of a deep abyss on a precipitous height; they give rise only to a sense of fear and have no other thoughts.
When entering a village, one should likewise collect the mind so that it does not scatter.
"O Bhikṣus! When you enter a village with your minds collected, do so as Kāśyapa enters a village.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus:
"When you enter a village, do you proceed slowly like the moon?
Do you possess a sense of shame and dread of blame?
Do you reflect within your own minds upon the conduct you have practiced?"
Does this analogy of the high cliff and deep abyss cause a sense of fear to arise?
Does it lead one to restrain body, speech, and mind?
Does it cause one to abandon negligence?
Are you not like a long-haired sheep that enters a thicket of brambles and remains stuck therein?
Are you not being pulled and held fast by the six sense-objects and the pursuit of gain?
When entering a village, do you not regard it as if entering a prison or facing shackles and fetters?
"When you enter a village, do you not give rise to a mind of attachment? Are you like a deer caught in a snare that has escaped?
Do you keep in mind your original destination?
For this reason, when a bhikṣu enters a village, he should conduct himself according to the various analogies mentioned above.
When entering a village, one should be like a bee gathering from flowers: without damaging their color or fragrance, it takes their nectar.
When entering a village, one should not be attached to forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects; one enters the village solely for the sake of practicing virtue.
As the Blessed One said:
"If a bhikṣu wishes to enter a village, he should give rise to this thought:
'May all that belongs to the donor be given to me alone; let nothing be given to others.'"
"I pray that you give me much, not little;
I pray that you give me what is excellent, not what is inferior.
May you give with a respectful heart, not without respect."
Having formed this thought, he entered the village; however, whatever he sought did not accord with his wishes.
In all places where he sought, he conceived a mind of retreat, becoming sorrowful, anxious, ashamed, and distressed, finding no joy.
If there is a bhikṣu who, wishing to enter a village to beg for alms, does not form such a thought as this:
"May all that the donor possesses be given to me alone; let nothing be given to others."
"I pray that you give me much, not little;
I pray that you give me what is good, not what is bad—
even to the point of giving without respect."

When entering a village without forming such thoughts, one does not give rise to feelings of sorrow, remorse, or distress regarding whether what is obtained is much or little, good or bad, and so forth.
"O monks! When Kāśyapa enters a village, he never gives rise to such thoughts.
Because he does not give rise to these thoughts, he does not develop a mind of retreat regarding any matter—whether good or bad, much or little."
"Furthermore, do not give rise to thoughts of suffering or discontent.
'As you travel constantly, like a bee gathering from flowers and trees,
among what is obtained— whether good or bad— you shall receive it whether slowly or quickly.'"
Just as a bee takes the nectar from a flower without destroying its color or fragrance,
so too does the seer move through the world while practicing virtue.
Without conflicting with others, he correctly contemplates their faults and afflictions.
You should examine yourself: whether what is good or bad has been done or not.
Do you have the requisites spread out?
Are you released from the bonds of the household?
"It is like sitting while wrapping oneself up, as a silkworm dwells within its cocoon.
"Therefore, one should enter a village and move about like a bee, not taking the flavor of the six sense objects."
Just as a hand in the air meets with no obstruction, so too should the mind be without obstruction when entering a village.
As the World-Honored One said, addressing the bhikṣus:
"What do you think, bhikṣus? By practicing what kind of conduct is a bhikṣu fit to serve as a teacher and model for the families of donors?"
The bhikṣu then replied to the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, you are the root of all dharmas; you also know the sequence of all dharmas, and you are the Great Physician.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this for us, so that upon hearing it, the bhikṣus may attain understanding.”
The World-Honored One immediately moved his hand through the air and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"This hand now turns within the air without obstruction or bondage."
When monks go about in the world, their minds should likewise be without obstruction or bondage.
If a person seeks wealth, they must discipline their mind and body before it can be attained.
If one seeks to attain merit, one must fix the mind on the suffering of the body and only then will the retribution be obtained.

If there is a bhikṣu who maintains equanimity toward both the pleasant and the unpleasant, and upon seeing others obtain gain, feels as if it were his own and gives rise to sympathetic joy; [he shall attain merit].
Such a bhikṣu is worthy to serve as a teacher for the people of the world. Bhikṣus!
When Kāśyapa enters a village, he is unobstructed, unbound, and without grasping.
Those who wish to obtain profit seek profit; those who wish to obtain merit seek merit.
Just as one rejoices when oneself obtains profit, so too does one rejoice when seeing others obtain profit.
Just as a hand moves through the air without obstruction or bondage:
"If one enters a village well, With a mind of equanimity toward loss or gain,
Entering the village together with fellow practitioners of the holy life, One does not give rise to a jealous mind."
"In the house of those you know intimately, there is no place for other relatives or old friends; this is called the practice of the Teacher’s conduct.

Regarding the practice of a bhikṣu when entering the home of a donor: one should not engage in frivolous play; one should not act with self-reliance or arrogance; one should not be flighty or impulsive; one should not speak without restraint or difficulty; one should not engage in confused or incoherent speech; one should not lean forward from a distance to join others in conversation because one's seat is far away; nor should one sit so as to crowd others while talking; one should not squat to one side or sit in a precarious manner; and one should not sit laughing loudly.

Although one maintains dignified deportment, one should not sit displaying the appearance of possessing virtuous qualities; one should not sit with the thighs crossed, nor with the knees crossed, nor with the feet crossed; one should not sit fumbling about to the left and right with the hands, nor sit with the feet moving restlessly; one should not sit upon a large jar or vessel; one should not sit alone in a quiet room with a bhikṣuṇī, nor sit alone in a room with a woman; and one must not sit in a lower position while preaching the Dharma to someone seated on a higher seat.
"A bhikṣu should always practice patience amidst all forms of decline and gain; this is called the rule for a bhikṣu sitting in a layperson's home.
This is the rule for the senior bhikṣu entering a layperson's home."

The Elder should know the proper time, know the appropriate measure, know himself, know the assembly, and know the high or low level of others' virtue. He should instruct the bhikṣus in dignified deportment, preach the Dharma according to the law for laypeople, and teach them to listen to the Dharma and to recite it; in this manner, he should extensively teach various wholesome dharmas.
"When the time for the recitation of blessings arrives, one should again recite the blessings;
this is called the rule for the senior elder (sthavira) within the household.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Śrāvastī.
In the country of Kośala there was a dwelling where a great number of bhikṣus wished to enter the summer retreat.
The bhikṣus deliberated among themselves, saying:
"During our summer retreat, how may we practice the Path in peace, security, and happiness?"
They further deliberated together, saying:
"Those who wish to practice the Way in peace and security should establish a regulation: no one shall be permitted to speak.
If anything is required, one must seek it by making gestures with the hands."
When the summer retreat had concluded, the bhikṣus went together to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves, and paid their respects.
Seeing them, the Buddha, though already aware of the matter, asked intentionally:
"Did you dwell in peace and joy during the summer retreat, and were you able to practice the Path?"
The bhikṣus replied to the World-Honored One, saying:
"We have attained peace and security in our practice of the Path.
The Buddha asked again:
"Have you all made a mutual agreement?
They replied,
"We have made an agreement on the practice of silence."
The Buddha said:
"This is the practice of creating enmity by imposing restrictions on communal living; since this leads even to suffering, how can it be called happiness?
From this day forward, I do not permit the bhikṣus to establish a rule of silence."
"When this assembly of senior elders was performing the *poṣadha*, if a donor (*dānapati*) were to arrive, they should have preached the Dharma to him and comforted him.
Among those in the assembly was a bhikṣu named Upasena, who was by nature dull-witted and had not studied the Tripiṭaka; furthermore, his speech was stammering and inelegant."
When the Sangha was assembled, a donor arrived; yet they were unable to preach the Dharma for him, nor could they offer words of comfort or gratitude.
The donor’s mind became suspicious, wondering for what reason the monks appeared displeased and remained silent, saying nothing at all.
When the World-Honored One heard of these successive events, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, when the assembly gathers, if laypeople come, the senior monk (upādhyāya) should preach the Dharma to them and offer words of consolation."
If the Elder is unable [to perform the task], he should inform the second Elder; if the Elder does not inform him, he incurs an offense.
If he informs the second Elder and the latter does not follow his advice, the second Elder also incurs an offense.
"When a bhikṣu is traveling on a road, if he sees fellow renunciants or laypeople, he should ask them about their place of origin and say:
'Have you come in safety and peace?'"
This is called the method of verbal expression.
Once, there were many bhikṣus traveling along a road; their bodies were utterly exhausted and they desired to rest, yet out of doubt they did not dare to do so.
At a later time, they went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"I allow the bhikṣus to rest by the roadside when traveling on a journey."

"If the preceptor or ācārya commits an offense and the community of monks performs the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of expelling him, once that formal act is completed, the disciple immediately loses his dependence."
If a disciple commits an offense and the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) of the Sangha has been completed, they also lose their dependence.
Furthermore, if the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) or teacher (*ācārya*) says to the disciple:
"From this day forward, you need not stay by my side."
If one has made a firm resolution, at that moment one loses the basis of reliance.
Furthermore, if the first light of dawn has not yet appeared, one also loses the basis of reliance by parting from one’s preceptor (upādhyāya) or teacher (ācārya).
"If a bhikṣu has committed an offense within the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha imposes a penalty upon him,

should that bhikṣu request a one-day leave of absence to go elsewhere on the following day, the Elder (sthavira) should grant him the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure), the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment), the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation), the *yathādharma-prakāśanīya-karman* (act of making manifest according to the truth), the *pātra-nikubjana-karman* (act of overturning the bowl), or the *apravāraṇīya-karman* (act of not inviting)."
After performing the confession through this *karmavācanā*, the community of monks shall subsequently perform the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation) for him.
This is called the method of release.
"One should practice walking meditation only at the designated place for walking meditation; one must not practice it elsewhere."
One should practice seated meditation only in a designated place for meditation, not elsewhere.
When walking, one should walk without giving rise to weariness or aversion, and without giving rise to a distracted mind.
If the ground at the place for walking is uneven, one should level it so that there are no elevations or depressions.
At that time, the World-Honored One was in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī and addressed his attendant Nāgabodhi:
"Bring me my bathing robe.
Having received it, he put on the robe and walked up and down in meditation.
As the Buddha was walking for exercise, Śakra transformed himself into a golden pavilion and, approaching to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet, addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I pray that you will accept this golden pavilion for walking meditation."
At that time, the Buddha was walking up and down in meditation at Vaiśālī, and the group of six bhikṣus followed him while wearing leather sandals.
The Buddha said:

"According to the rules for disciples, one must not wear leather sandals while walking up and down in meditation before one’s *upādhyāya* or *ācārya*, nor even within the area designated for walking meditation."
"How much more so when I am wearing leather sandals and walking upon the place where I am to practice walking meditation!
Thus it should be understood in detail.
There was a bhikṣu practicing *mānatva* who walked upon the place where the Saṃgha practiced walking meditation.
When the Buddha saw this, he immediately established a rule:
"It is not permitted for a monk who has committed an offense to practice walking meditation in the same place as a pure monk.
There was a monk who practiced walking meditation in the open air; encountering heavy rain, his robes became completely soaked and wet, and he was distressed and unhappy.
Having heard this, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"I allow bhikṣus to construct a walking-hall.
While the bhikṣus were practicing walking meditation on the open ground of Vulture Peak Mountain, they were beset by a sudden storm of wind and rain, as well as the oppressive heat of the sun.
When the Buddha heard of these circumstances, he permitted the bhikṣus to construct walking halls (*caṅkrama-śālā*).
On another occasion, at a residence for bhikṣuṇīs, a junior bhikṣuṇī was walking in meditation before a senior bhikṣuṇī; she was arrogant and conceited, lacking any sense of reverence.
The group of six bhikṣuṇīs saw that the junior bhikṣuṇīs were emulating them by troubling the seniors, so they came before the seniors to practice walking meditation (caṅkrama).

Because the World-Honored One heard of this matter, he did not permit junior bhikṣuṇīs to practice walking meditation before the seniors; a junior bhikṣuṇī must not practice walking meditation within the area where a senior bhikṣuṇī practices walking meditation.

There was a bhikṣu who developed an ulcer on his body; the physician prescribed a method of treatment, instructing him to apply saliva to the ulcer and apply a heated tile as a compress, so that the ulcer would slough off and he might recover.
The Buddha approved of the physician’s arrangement.
On one occasion, while the bhikṣus were newly plastering and painting a monastery cell, they lit a fire for warmth; the smoke熏 (xūn) [smothered] the pigments, causing them all to spoil.
The Buddha heard this and did not permit it. To those who were cold, he instructed them to light a fire in the open air to warm themselves.
Later, the bhikṣus informed the World-Honored One:
"When we light a fire in the open air to warm ourselves, warming the front leaves the back cold, and warming the back leaves the front cold; it cannot make us truly warm."
When the Buddha heard this, he permitted them to light fires within their rooms to warm themselves, provided there was no smoke.
"In the courtyards and alleys before the rooms where the bhikṣus reside, urine has defiled the ground everywhere; the foul odor makes it impossible to walk about."
When the Buddha heard of this, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"From this day forward, I do not permit the bhikṣus to relieve themselves here and there throughout the saṃghārāma. You must gather together in a secluded and private place, such as a clay jar or a wooden tube buried in the ground, and relieve yourselves therein."
"Once they have finished their minor duties, cover the feet with an object so that no odor arises.
At that time, there were bhikṣus who washed their feet in the open air during the cold season; the biting cold was extremely painful.
When the Buddha heard of this, he permitted the use of vessels made of copper, clay, or wood to be kept inside the dwellings for washing one's feet therein.
"The bowls used by the bhikṣus have become worn and cracked; because food and drink remain in the broken places, they become foul-smelling and unfit for use."
The Buddha permitted the making of an incense burner for bowls; one may use crushed sesame seeds or linseeds to coat the bowl and place it inside the burner to fumigate it.
Once the fumigation of the bowl is complete, it should be carefully handled so as not to let it be seen by the rain.
"If a bhikṣu abides in the air by means of supernormal powers and wishes to receive the precepts, while the preceptor and the Saṃgha remain on the ground, he cannot receive the precepts."
If the preceptor is in the air while the candidate for ordination and the assembly of monks are on the ground, the ordination cannot be conferred.
If the assembly of monks is in the air while the preceptor and the candidate for ordination are on the ground, the ordination cannot be conferred.
If the preceptor, the disciple, and the assembly of monks are all in mid-air, they likewise cannot receive the precepts.
Why is this? Because in mid-air there are no boundaries that can be demarcated for the establishment of a *sīmā*.
If a bhikṣu, during the night, places his three robes over his shoulders and travels to another place by means of supernatural power (ṛddhi), he does not lose possession of the robes.

If the robes are on the ground and the bhikṣu is traveling through the air by supernatural power, provided that the dawn has not yet appeared and he descends and steps upon the edge of the robes with his feet, he does not lose possession of the robes.
If the light of dawn appears and one's feet do not step upon the ground bordering the robe, the robe is lost.
Why is this? Because empty space constitutes the area outside the boundary.
There were some bhikṣus traveling through the air by means of supernatural powers who desired to drink water. The Buddha permitted them to drink it.
Although he permitted them to drink water, they did not know in which direction they could find it.
If one carries one's robes while entering the water, there is fear they will fall into it; if one places them on the bank, there is again fear of losing the robes.
The Buddha taught that when taking water, one may take it provided one foot is in the water and one foot remains on the bank.
This is called the dharma of empty space.
"There are two kinds of wind: first, upward-moving wind;

second, downward-moving wind. When expelling them, do not face another person and open your mouth to let them out; rather, you must turn your face toward a place where no one is and open your mouth to let them out."

If gas wishes to escape, do not allow it to be released within the assembly; rather, employ a skillful means to go outside to a place where no one is present so that it may be released. Only then should you return to enter the assembly, ensuring that you do not cause the community to feel reproach, disdain, or contempt.
When entering a stūpa, one must not release flatulence.
Within a stūpa chamber, near a stūpa tree, or in the midst of the great assembly, one must never allow gas to escape.
In the presence of the teacher or before a virtuous elder (*sthavira*), one must not let wind escape with sound.
If there is an urgent illness within the abdomen, one should go outside so as not to cause others to feel contempt or disdain.
Regarding the method for sweeping the floor: one should not sweep while standing above those who are below, nor should one sweep against the wind.
Regarding the method for eating congee: one must not make a "ha" sound by opening the mouth wide; once the congee has cooled, one should sip it slowly and quietly.
This is called the method for consuming congee.
At that time, the World-Honored One was in Rājagṛha.

There was a bhikṣu of Brahmin lineage who was naturally pure but had become defiled; while using the latrine, he scraped his anus with a wooden stick, and scraping it repeatedly, he wounded and tore it. Having been injured, his countenance became displeased.
The bhikṣus asked him, "Why is your complexion so haggard? What affliction or suffering do you have?
He immediately replied:
"When I am using the latrine, I loathe this impurity; when I use a wooden stick to scrape myself thoroughly, it injures my body, and for this reason I do not enjoy it.
The bhikṣus reported these circumstances in full to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha called this bhikṣu and asked:
"Is it true that you did so?
The bhikṣu replied to the Buddha:
"It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"You have defiled your own body, let alone others.
After the Buddha had rebuked this bhikṣu in various ways, he said to him:
"You ought to protect yourself."
When one wishes to relieve oneself, one must not release the excrement with force at will so as to produce a sound; rather, one should cause it to come out slowly and gradually.

When departing for the latrine, one should first take a cleaning stick (*śalākā*) and, upon reaching the door, snap the fingers three times to make a sound, so that humans and non-humans may be alerted.
Place your clothes on the designated clothing rack in front of the door before entering; if you encounter rain and there is no place to store your clothes, wrap yourself well with them.
Open the door and look inside the latrine to ensure there are no poisonous insects.
Having finished looking, when you wish to relieve yourself, you should slowly and gradually pull up your robe; you must not suddenly lift it so as to expose your body.
Regarding the method of sitting and rising: one should not lean or sit to one side, but should sit in the center, ensuring that the excrement does not soil both sides of the latrine.
When wishing to rise from the seat, one should lower the robe gradually and step by step; it must not be dropped all at once.
The rules for using the latrine are explained in detail, one by one, within the *Samathakhandhaka*.
When the bhikṣus were using the latrines, they found it precarious and exhausting to sit down and stand up.
Having heard of this, the Buddha permitted them to install well-secured wooden planks at the places for walking and coming and going, ensuring they were not uneven or sloping.
When the evacuation is finished, one should use a cleaning stick (*śalākā*) to scrape it clean.

If there is no cleaning stick, one must not wipe it clean on a wall; one must not wipe it clean on the boards, beams, or rafters of the latrine; one must not use stones; and one must not use fresh grass.
I do not permit the bhikṣus to use lumps of earth, soft wood bark, soft leaves, or exotic woods; none of these may be used.
What should be used are tally-sticks made of wood, bamboo, or reeds.
Regarding the method of measurement: the longest is one span (*vitasti*), and the shortest is four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
Once used, it must not be shaken so as to soil what is clean; nor shall it be placed among clean counting-sticks (*śalākā*).
This is called the method for using a toilet scoop when using the latrine.
The Venerable Kāśyapīya said:
"One may use stone or pottery [for the scoop]."
T'an-wu-te did not permit it.
"There are two areas for the latrine:
first, the place for defecation and urination; second, the place for using water."
When sitting or rising at the place for washing with water, one should lift up one's robes; all other matters are no different from those at the place for defecation.
Before the door of the latrine, one should place a vessel of pure water, and furthermore, a small bottle should also be placed there.
If you have your own jar, you should use it yourself; if you do not have a jar, use the small jar by the latrine. You must not directly use water from the large communal jar, lest you defile it.
This is called the method for using water when attending to the toilet.
Regarding the method for chewing *dantakāṣṭha* (tooth-sticks):
at that time, the bhikṣus did not chew tooth-sticks, and their breath was foul and offensive.
There are five faults and afflictions in not chewing *dantakāṣṭha* (tooth-sticks):
first, the breath becomes foul;
second, the throat becomes impure.
Third, phlegm, undigested food, wind, and cold are not eliminated;
fourth, one has no desire for food or drink;
fifth, it increases eye diseases in people.
Chewing the *dantakāṣṭha* (tooth-stick) has five kinds of merit:
first, the breath becomes fragrant and pure;
second, the throat becomes clear and clean.
Third, the removal of phlegm and undigested food;
fourth, reflection on food;
fifth, freedom from eye disease.

There were some bhikṣus who, while chewing tooth-sticks, did so either within the monastery, on the communal pure grounds of the Saṃgha, in the walking-meditation areas, before their teachers, or before venerable senior monks.
When the Buddha heard of this, he prohibited it all.
Furthermore, there were some bhikṣus who used tree bark as tooth-sticks.
There were also some bhikṣus who chewed short tooth-sticks, which entered their throats and caused them distress.
The Buddha also prohibited this.
Regarding the proper measure for a tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*), the longest is one span (*vitasti*) and the shortest is four finger-widths (*aṅgula*).
According to the rules for disciples, they should fetch tooth-sticks in the early morning and present them to their *upādhyāya* and *ācārya*.
Kāśyapīya said: "Regarding the method for chewing the tooth-stick:
it should be four finger-widths long, and one should chew two finger-widths.
In front of a stūpa, before the community of monks, or before one’s preceptor (upādhyāya) or teacher (ācārya), one must not open the mouth wide to spit or drool upon the ground."
"If you wish to blow your nose or spit, you should do so in a secluded place so as not to cause others to feel revulsion or contempt.
This is called the rule for blowing the nose and spitting.

"Monks, when it is necessary to clean the teeth after a meal, one should use a tooth-stick made of copper, iron, bone, bamboo, wood, or reed; the tip must not be too pointed, lest it cause injury or breakage."
Once the teeth have been cleaned, they should be thoroughly rinsed so as not to leave behind stale food remnants that might cause others to view them with contempt.
This is called the method for cleaning the teeth.
At a time when the ears of the bhikṣus were filled with dust and grime, the Buddha permitted the use of copper, iron, bone, horn, bamboo, wood, or reed to remove the impurities from within the ears.

"Once one has finished chewing the *yāshí* (tooth-stick) upon rising in the morning, if it is necessary to scrape the tongue, the Buddha permitted the use of scrapers made of copper, iron, wood, bamboo, or reed.
This is called the method for scraping the tongue."
"The method for urination:
when one wishes to perceive the need, one should immediately rise and depart; one must not remain for a long time.
This is called the method for urination."
One should place wooden sandals at the place for urination; when wishing to relieve oneself, one should wear the sandals upon them so as not to soil them with snot, spittle, or urine.

If there are monks residing there who are elderly or infirm and unable to travel far to the latrine, they are permitted to use a private, secluded spot—such as a large jar or a wooden tube buried in the ground—as a place for defecation and urination; these must be well-covered so that others do not see them.
On the path by which one comes, one should place a clean board above it so that it is not defiled by impurities.
What is meant by "not practicing"?
One who has received full ordination (*upasampadā*) is said to be "practicing," while one who has not received full ordination is said to be "not practicing."
"What is meant by one who practices the Dharma?
One who has received full ordination is called a practitioner of the Dharma; one who has not received full ordination is called a non-practitioner of the Dharma.
This is what is meant by 'practicing the Dharma'."
Furthermore, "practice" refers to practicing that which the Buddha has authorized; this is called practice.
That which the Buddha has not authorized, even if one practices it, is called non-practice.
Why, then, is it also called practice?

To say that which is Dharma is Dharma, to say that which is non-Dharma is non-Dharma, to say that which is light is light, and to say that which is heavy is heavy—this is called right conduct (*caryā*).

That which is not right conduct is to say that which is Dharma is non-Dharma, to say that which is non-Dharma is Dharma, to say that which is light is heavy, and to say that which is heavy is light; this is called the practice of non-conduct (*acaryā-dharma*).
"Furthermore, 'practice' refers to the three types of bodily karma up to the ten wholesome karmas;
'non-practice' refers to the three types of bodily karma up to the ten unwholesome karmas."
Furthermore, for the practitioner, the Eightfold Noble Path is practice, while the eightfold wrong path is not practice.
Moreover, practicing in accordance with the precepts established by the Buddha is what is called practice.
That which does not accord with practice is called non-practice;
this is the dharma of practice and non-practice.
The third matter is concluded.
This is a brief designation for all chapters and phrases; thus they should be understood in detail.

The translator’s name is lost; it is now appended to the Qin Records:
"There are generally three kinds of offenses: first, the causal conditions for the initial commission of an offense; second, the establishment of a precept because of that commission."
Third is the "repeated formulation" (*punaḥ-prajñapti*).
What is meant by "condition" (*nidāna*)?
At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling through the country of Śūrasena.
Kalandakaputra Sudinna, in order to continue the lineage and ensure its succession, conceived a lustful mind and engaged in sexual intercourse with his former wife.
Because of this initial transgression, the Buddha assembled the bhikṣus; this is known as the causal condition (*nidāna*).
What is meant by "prohibition"?
If a bhikṣu engages in unchaste conduct, even with an animal, he commits a pārājika offense and is no longer in communion; this is called a prohibition.
What is meant by a "re-enactment" (or "heavy regulation")?
At that time, the World-Honored One was in the kingdom of Vṛji.

There was a son of the Vṛjis who had gone forth as a monk; later, he took no pleasure in the Path and constantly dwelt upon thoughts of sensual desire. He returned home and immediately engaged in sexual intercourse with his former wife.
Having finished engaging in sexual desire, he immediately felt remorse and went to his original monastery, where he confessed the offense to the bhikṣus.
Upon hearing this, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"At the very first instance of transgression, one commits a pārājika offense.
This is like the case of the bhikṣu who was begging for alms in the forest near Vaiśālī."
"This is a formal re-enactment of the precept.
At that time, the Venerable Upāli rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"If someone engages in sexual misconduct with an animal, does this constitute an offense?
The Buddha told Upāli:
"The very first entry [into the act] also constitutes an offense."
Upāli asked again:
"If one engages in sexual intercourse by means other than the [proper] path, does this constitute an offense?
The Buddha said:
"Entering for the first time also constitutes an offense.
The causes and conditions for an offense upon initial entry are explained in detail in the Vinaya.
"The re-enactment of the rule is based on two kinds of causes and conditions:"
First is urgent, and second is lax.
As for the urgent: even when animals and humans commit the same offense together, this is called urgent.
What is meant by lax?
If there is a bhikṣu who wishes to abandon the path, return to lay life, and engage in sexual misconduct, he is permitted to relinquish the precepts and return home.
If at a later time he again takes pleasure in remaining on the path, he is permitted to go forth and receive full ordination.
This is called laxity.
For example, when the bhikṣu Nandika committed a grave offense, he was permitted to perform repentance in a position below the fully ordained monks but above the śrāmaṇeras; this, too, is laxity.
For example, when a king has offenders, there are two approaches: one is urgent and the other is lenient.
Within the establishment of heavy precepts, it is likewise: one is lenient and the other is urgent.
Therefore, there are three points for determining whether an offense has been committed.
Furthermore, there are three points for determining that no offense has been committed:
first, the circumstance; second, the formal rule; and third, the subsequent reiteration of the rule.
Regarding the "condition" (*nidāna*): when the Buddha had not yet established the precepts, the first occurrence of an offense constitutes this condition.
Regarding the "establishment" (*prajñapti*): the establishment of the rule that one must not commit an offense for the first time is what is called the establishment.

Regarding the "re-enactment" (heavy regulation): if a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī lacks autonomy and is coerced by force, and they engage in sexual intercourse against their will without experiencing pleasure, there is no offense; this is called the re-enactment.
These are called the three points for determining that there has been no offense.
Furthermore, there are three points for determining an offense: first, the basis;
second, the formal enactment; and third, the subsequent re-enactment.
Regarding the "circumstance" (*nidāna*): at that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Rājagṛha.
The bhikṣu Dhanika took timber belonging to King Bimbisāra without it being given to him.
Desiring to prevent other bhikṣus from committing such transgressions in the future, the Tathāgata assembled the bhikṣus for this reason; this is called the "circumstance."
If a bhikṣu, whether in an open space or within a village, takes what is not given, he commits a pārājika offense.
This is called the formal rule.
Whether he takes it himself, or instructs another outsider to take it, or sends someone else to take it—in these three cases, taking what is not given constitutes a pārājika offense.
This is called a "heavy regulation.
If one takes what belongs to another while not perceiving it as belonging to another, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This, too, is a heavy regulation.
All transgressions are definitively resolved through these three points; this should be understood in detail.
Furthermore, there are two types of re-enactment of the precepts:
first, the urgent; second, the gradual.
The "urgent" refers to even grass, trees, small leaves, or other objects; one must not take them if they have not been given—this is called urgent.
The "relaxed" refers to taking another's property while not perceiving it as belonging to another—this is called relaxed.
This is called the determination of offenses through three points.
Furthermore, there are three points for determining non-offenses:
first, the circumstance; second, the rule; and third, the reiteration of the rule.

As explained above regarding the causes and conditions, "the initial prohibition" (制) refers to the fact that there was no offense prior to the formal enactment of the precept; this is called the initial prohibition.

"The re-prohibition" (重制) refers to the case where one regards another's property as belonging to another, does not take it, and does not even give rise to the thought of theft; this is called the re-prohibition.
"At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at Vaiśālī.

There was a bhikṣu dwelling by the side of the Vaggumudā River who, having conceived a perception of impurity and developed a sense of revulsion toward this body, hired another bhikṣu with his robes and bowl to kill him."
Because the Tathāgata wished to sever such evil causes and conditions, he assembled the bhikṣus; this is called the "condition" (nidāna).
As for the "prohibition" (prajñapti): if a bhikṣu takes the life of a human being, he commits a pārājika offense and should not live in community with the others.
This is called the original rule (*prātimokṣa*).
As for the re-statement of the rule: from the time one enters the mother’s womb until the time of old age, anyone who takes the life of a human being incurs a *pārājika* offense.
This is called the re-statement of the rule.

"Furthermore, there is the 'heavy regulation': if a person is ill and seeks to commit suicide, and a bhikṣu either personally provides a knife or instructs another to provide a knife, or personally provides medicine or instructs another to provide medicine—many such expedients as these are all termed 'heavy regulations.'"
There are two reasons for re-enacting a precept:
first, urgency; second, laxity.
Urgency refers to the rule that one must not kill any living being, down to an ant; this is called urgency.
"Relaxed" means that if one kills another while perceiving them as a non-human, no offense is committed; this is what is called "relaxed.
These are the three points for determining what constitutes an offense.
Furthermore, there are three points for determining what does not constitute an offense:
First, the occasion; second, the enactment; third, the re-enactment.
Regarding the occasion, it is as explained above.
Regarding the enactment: when the precept had not yet been enacted, acting [in such a way] was not an offense; this is termed the "enactment."
Regarding the "repeated precept" (*guruka-śikṣāpada*): not giving rise to the intent to kill toward any sentient being is called the repeated precept.
For this reason, it is termed "decisively determined as non-offense in three instances."
Furthermore, there are three points of definitive adjudication:
first, the occasion (nidāna); second, the enactment (prajñapti); and third, the re-enactment (anuprajñapti).

As for the occasion: at that time, the World-Honored One was staying at the Mahāvana Monastery on the Markaṭahradatīra River in Vaiśālī; there, some bhikṣus uttered intentional falsehoods for the sake of alms-seeking.
The Tathāgata, having severed these causes and conditions, assembled the bhikṣus; this is called the "condition" (nidāna).

As for the "prohibition" (prajñapti): if a bhikṣu claims for himself a superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma), that bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense and should not live in communal residence with the others.
This is called the primary rule (*prātimokṣa*).

As for the secondary rule (*anu-prātimokṣa*), it refers to those who claim to have attained mindfulness of the body, up to and including claiming to have attained the fruits [of the path]; this is called the secondary rule.
Furthermore, the secondary rule is of two kinds:
There are two types: the urgent and the relaxed.
Regarding the urgent: one must not speak falsely at all, even in jest; this is called the urgent.
Regarding the relaxed: if one intentionally intends to speak falsely, but the speech is not completed and does not cause others to understand, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
This is called laxity.
This is called the determination of offenses in three respects.
There are three respects in which there is no offense:
First, the occasion; second, the initial formulation; third, the subsequent formulation.
Regarding the occasion, it is as explained above.
Regarding the initial formulation: when the precept had not yet been formulated, that which was performed did not constitute an offense; this is termed the "initial formulation."

Regarding the "re-enactment" of the rule: it is like a bhikṣu of overweening pride who, though he had not actually attained the Path, heard a person from the outskirts say that he had attained it and believed in his heart that he truly had.
Later, through unremitting diligence, he attained the fruit of Arhatship and realized that his previous claim of attainment was not real.
The mind harbored a doubt and questioned the Buddha; the Buddha said there was no offense.
This is called a "repeated regulation.
This is the definitive judgment that in these three instances there is no offense.
In this manner, even down to the *śaikṣa-dharmas*, all may be understood by inferring through these three factors.
Furthermore, one should further infer based on the following:
first, the alms bowl; second, the robes; third, the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*); fourth, the needle case; fifth, those traveling on the road; sixth, people; and seventh, the dwelling.
Regarding the occasion for the bowl: At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Rājagṛha.

In Rājagṛha there was an elder whose house possessed a large sandalwood tree from which a bowl had been fashioned; eventually, he gathered the bhikṣus together—this is what is known as the "occasion."
Regarding the "prescription" (vidhi): one should not keep a sandalwood bowl; this is called a prescription.
Regarding the "repeated prescription" (punar-vidhi): one should not manifest supernatural powers before laypeople; this is called a repeated prescription.

Furthermore, there is a further regulation: a bhikṣu should not possess wooden bowls, stone bowls, gold bowls, silver bowls, jeweled bowls, or pearl bowls; he should not place bowls on a shelf, nor should he place bowls on a lump of mud, and so forth, up to: he should not place a wet bowl inside a bowl-bag.
This is explained in detail within the *Saṃkīrṇaka-vastu* (Miscellaneous Khandas).
This is called the determination of offenses based on three points:

one should not sit upon a bowl, one should not lie upon a bowl, and one should not use water contained in a bowl to wash hands or feet; in all circumstances, it should not be used except for the purpose of treating illness.
One should not use the alms bowl to remove filth, nor should one fail to protect it; one should revere it as one's own eyes, except in cases of illness.
This is called the definitive ruling on offenses in three instances.
“Furthermore, there are three points regarding which one should resolve that no offense has been committed:
first, the occasion (nidāna); second, the formal enactment (prajñapti); and third, the re-enactment (punar-prajñapti).
As for the occasion: at that time, the Blessed One was staying in Vārāṇasī.”
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What kind of alms bowl should we keep?
This is called the introductory narrative (nidāna).
Regarding the "prescription" (vidhi): it is permitted for the bhikṣus to keep mouth-covers for their bowls and upright bowls;

this is called the prescription. Regarding the "repeated prescription" (punar-vidhi): it is permitted for the bhikṣus to keep iron bowls, *sumana* bowls, and even red bowls—all these should be kept; this is called the repeated prescription.
Furthermore, there is a further regulation: if a bowl hanging from the shoulder or under the arm becomes broken, it is permitted to place it in a basket.
If a *soma* bowl is broken, one may mend it by sewing with threads of *karpāsa* or hemp, even using lacquer to glue it together.
If an iron bowl develops holes or cracks, one should hammer the iron thin and patch it with lacquer for use.
An extra bowl should not be kept for more than ten days.
If a bowl is broken but has not yet reached five repairs, one should not discard it to seek another bowl.
When a bhikṣuṇī obtains a bowl, she must perform the ritual of *viśuddhi-dāna* on that very day; it should not be kept overnight.
This is also a double regulation.
Regarding the "circumstances concerning robes," there are three: first, the circumstances; second, the regulation; third, the double regulation.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Śrāvastī.
The group of six bhikṣus kept robes of superior color; the Buddha assembled the bhikṣus—this is called the "circumstance.
The regulation was: they were not permitted to keep robes of superior color—this is called the "regulation."

Regarding the "re-enactment" (saṃvara): one must not possess brocade garments or white robes; it is not permitted to possess garments with fringes or net-like patterns—this is called the re-enactment.
Furthermore, it is not permitted to walk with the head wrapped, nor is it permitted to possess leather leggings, except in cases of special necessity.

One must not wrap the *saṃghāṭī* with wood, fresh flour, cow dung, grass, or soil; one must not tread upon the *saṃghāṭī* with one's feet; one must not fold the *saṃghāṭī* and use it as a seat; one must not wear the *saṃghāṭī* directly against the body; and one must not fail to cherish and protect the *saṃghāṭī* as one protects one’s own skin.
This is called the "Re-enactment" (Pratikarṣaṇīya).
These are the three points for determining an offense.
Furthermore, there are three points for determining non-offense:
First, the occasion; second, the enactment; third, the re-enactment.
Regarding the occasion: at that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Vārāṇasī.
There were certain bhikṣus who addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What kind of robes should we wear?"—this is called the occasion (*nidāna*). The regulation (*prajñapti*) is:
"I permit the bhikṣus to wear robes made of discarded rags (*pāṃsukūla*). This is called the regulation.
Regarding the re-enactment of the rule: it is permitted to keep ten kinds of robes, even those made of discarded rags (*pāṃsukūla*).
Furthermore, a bhikṣu may keep an extra robe for no more than ten days.
If one has lost a robe due to fire, water, or thieves, and a donor arrives with many robes to offer as alms, one may accept up to three robes but must not take more than that.
When a bhikṣu obtains a new robe, he should perform the purification by making three dots.
If a bhikṣu’s robe is torn, he is permitted to wear it as a patched garment.
This is called the definitive resolution in three points regarding non-offenses.
Regarding the *niṣīdana*, there are three points for determining an offense: first, the occasion (*nidāna*);
second, the formal rule (*prajñapti*); and third, the reiteration of the rule (*anuprajñapti*).
As for the occasion: at that time, the Blessed One was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus possessed kaṭhina-cloths (niṣīdana) that were excessively long and wide. Consequently, the Buddha assembled the bhikṣus; this is called the introductory narrative (nidāna).
As for the regulation: if any bhikṣus possess a kaṭhina-cloth that exceeds the prescribed measure, it is called an offense.
Regarding the measurements: the length shall be two and a half Sugata-spans, and the width one and a half Sugata-spans.
Regarding the secondary regulations: one should not possess a superior-quality *niṣīdana* (sitting mat), nor one made of brocade, silk, or leather.
One must not use a *niṣīdana* to wrap wood, persimmons, pears, or even soil.
One should protect the *niṣīdana* as one protects one's own skin.
This is called the "Re-enactment" (*punaḥ-prakāśana*).
These three points resolve what constitutes an offense.
Furthermore, there are three points that resolve what does not constitute an offense:
first, the basis; second, the initial promulgation; and third, the subsequent re-promulgation.
Regarding the "condition" (*nidāna*), it is as explained above.
Regarding the "prescription" (*prajñapti*), it refers to making [the robes] according to the measurements prescribed by the Buddha; this is called the prescription.

Regarding the "re-presentation of the prescription" (*anuprajñapti*), it refers to making the ten types of *kāṣāya* according to the Buddha’s proportions, and also dyeing the cloth material to the color of the *kāṣāya*; this is called the re-presentation of the prescription.
In these three instances, it is determined that there is no offense.
Regarding the needle case, there are three points of determination:
first, the basis; second, the formal enactment; and third, the subsequent re-enactment.
Regarding the causal circumstances: at that time, the World-Honored One was staying in the city of Rājagṛha.
There was a master craftsman who made needle-cases; having faith in the Triple Gem, he invited the community of monks to receive a constant offering of needle-cases.
He constantly gave alms without ceasing until he was so impoverished that he could no longer sustain himself.
When the Buddha heard this, he assembled the bhikṣus; this is called the "circumstance" (nidāna).
As for the "prohibition" (prajñapti), he did not permit bhikṣus to possess needle-cases made of bone, ivory, or horn; this is called the "prohibition."
Regarding the "re-enactment" (or "additional regulation"): there were certain bhikṣus who made needle-cases from dyed fabrics, brocades, silks, and leathers.
The Buddha did not permit the making of needle-cases from dyed fabrics up to and including leather; this is called the re-enactment.
This needle-cushion roll should be kept well concealed; it is not permitted to be carried by a layperson. Why is this?
Once, a bhikṣu was traveling along the same road as some merchants, at which time the bhikṣu said to the merchants:
"I have a matter that requires me to travel by a different road; you may take this needle-case for me.
We shall meet again in a moment.
After the practitioner had departed, [the merchant] placed a pearl worth a hundred thousand taels of gold inside the needle-case.
When the practitioner returned, he gave the needle case to him without saying a word to let him know.
Upon passing through the customs station, the practitioner was called back for inspection.
The tax collector found this precious jewel inside the needle case and rebuked the practitioner in various ways, causing him extreme suffering and distress.
Upon hearing this, the Buddha established a regulation, saying:
"From this day forward, it is not permitted to carry a needle case while traveling with a layperson.
This is called a "re-enacted regulation" (chóngzhì).
These are the three points for determining an offense.
Furthermore, there are three points for determining non-offense:
first, the basis; second, the formal enactment; and third, the subsequent re-enactment.
What is meant by "condition" (*nidāna*)?
"Condition" is as explained above.
"Prohibition" (*prajñapti*) refers to the state where one does not commit an offense because the precept has not yet been established; this is called "prohibition."

Regarding the "re-enactment" (punar-vidhi): it is permitted to store needle cases made of copper, iron, lead, tin, bamboo, reed, wood, clay, or stone; furthermore, it is permitted for bhikṣus to cut the ten kinds of cloth to make needle-cases for use. This is called the re-enactment.
This constitutes a definitive determination regarding the three instances where there is no offense.
Furthermore, there are three instances for definitively determining what constitutes an offense:
first, the objective condition (*nidāna*); second, the formal rule (*prajñapti*); and third, the supplementary regulation (*anuprajñapti*).

Regarding the circumstances: at that time, the group of six bhikṣus were constantly traveling through various countries. During the summer months, they sometimes encountered torrential rains and rising floods that swept away their robes and alms bowls; at other times, they harmed living beings or even trampled upon growing grass.
The various donors complained, saying:
"Even those non-Buddhists who observe the precepts do not travel during the summer retreat for fear of harming or killing living beings.
How much more so for the disciples of the Buddha who possess a compassionate heart; they never grow weary of seeking alms throughout both winter and summer."
"Even birds rely on forest trees and wild beasts rely on mountains; all have their times of dwelling.
How is it that a bhikṣu has not even a moment’s rest?
For this reason, when the World-Honored One heard this, he assembled the bhikṣus; this is called the "circumstance."
A "rule" (*sikkhāpada*) refers to the prohibition against a bhikṣu traveling during the summer retreat; this is called a rule.
A "repeated rule" (*anu-sikkhāpada*) refers to the case of a certain bhikṣu who, while observing the summer retreat, departed without cause after having already entered the retreat boundaries.

Now, regarding the practice of the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat): once the *varṣā* has been formally entered, one must not go out without a valid reason. For instance, it is not permitted—as in the case of the Śākya-son Pānanda—who went about with a tuft of wool hanging from the end of his staff. All such actions are forbidden.

"Furthermore, as with the group of six bhikṣus who traveled along the same road with bhikṣuṇīs, they likewise must not travel along the same road with bandits; nor may they act as the Śākyaputra Pūraṇa did by carrying a precious parasol while walking on the road; nor may they hang their bowl-covers from the top of a banner while traveling. All such improper actions during travel should be understood in detail in this manner."
This is called a "heavy regulation.
These are the three points for determining what constitutes an offense.
Furthermore, there are three points for determining what does not constitute an offense:
First, the causal condition; second, the initial regulation; third, the subsequent regulation.
Regarding the causal condition, it is as explained above.
Regarding the regulation: if one does not participate in either the earlier retreat (*pūrvavārṣika*) or the later retreat (*paścimavārṣika*), there is likewise no offense.
Furthermore, it is not an offense if one goes out without a specific reason; this also does not constitute a transgression.
Again, there was a bhikṣu who, having received the seven-day leave, went to his home. Knowing that the days were about to end and wishing to return, his mother would not permit it.
After seven days had passed, he conceived the thought that his *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) was lost and went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"If his mind was firmly resolved that he wished to come, but his mother did not permit it, he has not lost his *varṣā*."
"When a bhikṣu has completed the summer retreat (varṣā), he should move to another place to reside.
If there is a valid reason and he is unable to go, he does not commit an offense.
If there is no such reason, even if he stays outside for one night after the retreat is finished and then returns, he likewise does not commit an offense."
This is called the "heavy regulation.
These are the three cases that definitively determine non-offense.
Furthermore, there are three cases that definitively determine an offense:
First, the occasion; second, the enactment; third, the re-enactment.
Regarding the occasion: at that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Rājagṛha.
There were seventeen groups of youths there, the eldest of whom was seventeen years old and the youngest twelve.
Among them, the wealthiest had eight billion coins, while the poorest had eight hundred thousand coins.
Within this group of youths, there was one who was beloved by his parents and named Upāli.
The parents conceived this thought:
"I have only this one son.
After my death, how can I ensure that this son lives long and reaches old age without suffering, always attaining peace and happiness?"
I wish to have him study writing and recite the sutras, yet I fear his eyes will become fatigued and he will suffer.
If I wish to teach him painting, I fear his feet will ache from standing for long periods.
If I teach him astronomy and calculation, I fear it will exhaust both his body and mind.
Furthermore, he thought to himself:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, always dwell in seclusion and quietude, seeking the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta); this is indeed a great bliss, and they may be settled among the śramaṇas."
Furthermore, there were seventeen groups of youths who were his companions; they came repeatedly to summon him to go forth together with them.
Thereupon, his parents permitted him to go forth, and the teacher immediately conferred the full precepts (*upasampadā*) upon him.
However, because he was young, he ate twice during the day; when night had not yet dawned, he would cry out again, begging for food.
The Buddha, hearing his cries with his divine ear, immediately assembled the bhikṣus; this is called the causal occasion.
The "Regulation" (vidhi) refers to the allowance for one who has reached the age of twenty to receive full ordination; this is called the regulation.

The "Re-regulation" (punar-vidhi) refers to the prohibition against receiving the precepts if one has not yet reached the age of twenty, as well as the prohibition against thirteen types of persons receiving the precepts.

Among these thirteen types, if one receives the precepts from a single person, and knowing that they should not have been granted the precepts, nevertheless grants them, the preceptor also commits an offense.
This is called the "repeated regulation.
These three points constitute the determination of what constitutes an offense.
Furthermore, there are three points for determining what does not constitute an offense:
First, the occasion; second, the enactment; third, the re-enactment.
Regarding the occasion, it is as explained above.
Regarding the enactment: prior to the promulgation of the precept, there was no offense; this is termed the "enactment."
Regarding the re-enactment of the rule: if one is twenty years of age and confers the precepts upon them, there is no offense.
If it is unknown that the person is under twenty, and the recipient of the precepts also does not know it, then conferring the precepts upon them constitutes no offense.

There was a śrāmaṇera who, being less than twenty years of age, received full ordination; doubt arose in his mind as to whether he had obtained the precepts or not, so he went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:

"I allow you to count the years spent in the womb; if that is still insufficient, I allow you to count the intercalary months; if that is still insufficient, I allow you to count the fourteen-day *poṣadha* observances."
After fourteen days had passed, the *poṣadha* ceremony was still not completed.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus, "Has this person attained the fruit of arhatship yet?
The bhikṣus replied to the Buddha:
"Truly, he has attained the fruit of Arhatship.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"This is the supreme formal acceptance of the precepts (upasaṃpadā)."
"If it is as stated here, then even if one has not yet reached twenty years of age, one may obtain full ordination without committing an offense.
This is like the case of the noble son Yaśoda and others, who received the precepts and attained them without transgression."
Up to and including Sañjaya, Gavāmpati, Kolita, and others—these two hundred and fifty people and the rest received the precepts and attained ordination.
This is called the "repeated regulation."
These are the three points for determining non-offenses.
Furthermore, there are three points for determining offenses:
first, the basis; second, the enactment; and third, the re-enactment.
Regarding the circumstances: At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Rājagṛha and permitted the bhikṣu Ārāḍa to construct a private dwelling.
This bhikṣu Ārāḍa made his dwelling very large in both width and length; the materials required were exceedingly many, and his requests were manifold.
The people living in the village where this bhikṣu resided saw him from afar and all fled into their houses, unwilling to meet him.
When the Buddha heard of these circumstances, he assembled the bhikṣus; this is known as the "circumstantial introduction" (nidāna).

The "Regulation" (prajñapti) refers to when a bhikṣu, having no patron, privately begs for materials to build a hut; it must be built according to the prescribed measurement, otherwise one commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
This is called a regulation.
The "Reiteration of the Regulation" (punar-prajñapti) refers to such cases as when the Venerable Chanda privately built a hut and requested timber from the king.
The king said,
"Take as you please.
He then cut down every tree in the road that was held in high esteem by the people.
The people of the world complained, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu, lacking a heart of compassion, cut down a tree and take its life?
Because of this, the Buddha established a precept: one may not privately construct a dwelling by felling large trees standing along the road.
This is called a "heavy regulation.
Furthermore, at one time the Blessed One was staying in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
The bhikṣu Chanda privately constructed a dwelling, using water containing living organisms to mix with the mud for building the structure.

When the construction of the hut was finished, there was some excess mud remaining; he took it all and piled it upon the roof, whereupon the hut immediately collapsed. For this reason, the Buddha established these precepts:

one is not permitted to privately construct a hut by felling large trees from the middle of the road; one is not permitted to use water containing living organisms to mix with the mud; and one is not permitted to pile mud onto the roof of a house.
This is called a "heavy regulation.

At that time, the Venerable Rāhula was staying at Nālagāpavana. There was a donor who had deep faith in the Triple Gem and, conceiving a heart of reverence for the Venerable Rāhula, built a private dwelling for him. Once the house was completed, he immediately invited Rāhula to take possession of it.
Rāhula enjoyed the use of it for some time, after which he left for other regions to teach and transform others.
The owner of the dwelling then gave this room as an offering to many people.
Later, when Rāhula returned and heard of this, he reported the matter in full detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha addressed Rāhula:
"Go to the donor's side and ask him:
'What faults have you seen in my body, speech, or mind?'"
The donor replied, "I see no fault.
Rāhula returned to the Buddha's presence and related the donor's words in full.

For this reason, the Buddha immediately assembled the bhikṣus and said: "There are some gifts that are given according to the Dharma, received according to the Dharma, and used according to the Dharma.
There are also some gifts that are given not according to the Dharma, received not according to the Dharma, and used not according to the Dharma."

If there is a donor who, having personally conceived the intention to build a dwelling to give to a single person, later transfers it as a gift to many people, this is called an unrighteous gift, an unrighteous acceptance, and an unrighteous use.

If someone, having personally intended to build a dwelling and give it to a single individual, later transfers it as a gift to the Saṃgha, this is called giving that is not in accordance with the Dharma, receiving that is not in accordance with the Dharma, and using that which is not in accordance with the Dharma.

If one with a specific intention builds a dwelling and offers it to a single person within a community, and that community later divides into two factions, and if one then diverts this dwelling to one faction, this is called an unrighteous gift, an unrighteous acceptance, and an unrighteous use.

If there is a donor who, of their own volition, constructs a dwelling to offer to a great multitude, yet later transfers it to a single person or transfers it to a large assembly, all such instances constitute an improper gift, an improper acceptance, and an improper use.
Regarding what is in accordance with the Dharma: if one gives to a single person, that one person enjoys it;
if one gives to many people, those many people enjoy it;
if one gives to the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha enjoys it.
If the Sangha is divided into two factions, and a gift is bestowed upon one side while that side makes use of it,
this is called "using in accordance with the Dharma.
This is called a "re-enactment of the rule."
These three points determine what constitutes an offense.
Furthermore, there are three points that determine what does not constitute an offense:
first, the circumstance; second, the original enactment; and third, the subsequent re-enactment.
The "condition" (pratyaya) is as explained above.

Regarding the "prohibition" (prajñapti): when one acts as was done before the precept was established, there is no offense; this is called the prohibition. Regarding the "re-prohibition" (punar-prajñapti):

if the Sangha points out a site for building a dwelling, and what is built conforms to the prescribed measurements and is free from obstacles or difficulties, or if one builds a stūpa or constructs a dwelling for the Sangha, there is no offense; this is called the re-prohibition.
In the city of Rājagṛha, there was a donor who built sixty rooms for the Saṃgha; none of these constituted an offense.
This is called a "repeated regulation.
These three cases are adjudicated as non-offenses.
To not transgress anything means to act in accordance with the Buddha’s teachings.
To transgress means to act in opposition to the Buddha’s teachings.
According to the dharma of a bhikṣu, that which the Buddha has permitted should be done, and that which the Buddha has not permitted should not be done.
As it was in the beginning, so it shall be in the middle and at the end.
What is meant by "Vinaya"?
Vinaya has five general meanings:
First, repentance; second, compliance; third, extinction; fourth, severance; fifth, relinquishment.
What is meant by "repentance"?
It refers to whatever has been transgressed within the seven categories of offenses, which should be repented of and eliminated.
Confession that can extinguish [transgressions] is called *vinaya*.
What is meant by "conformity"?

Conformity refers to the seven groups of followers who, in accordance with what the Tathāgata has prescribed and taught, accept and practice it without opposition; this is called *vinaya* of conformity.
What is meant by "extinction" (nirodha)?
That which can extinguish the seven types of disputes is called the Vinaya of Extinction.
What is meant by "severance" (cheda)?
That which can cause afflictions to be extinguished and not to arise is called *prahāṇa-vinaya* (the discipline of abandonment).
What is meant by "renunciation" (*pratinisarga*)?
There are two kinds of renunciation:
First is the relinquishing of what has been done; second is the relinquishing of the matter of views.
Regarding the relinquishing of what has been done, this refers to the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses.
Among these thirteen, in nine cases, the offense is completed as soon as the act is performed, and there is no need for admonition.

If one does not accept the four matters after three admonitions, the Saṃgha shall perform the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations), and the offense is established.
Once it is established, if one performs the *jñapti-tri-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and two proclamations) to repent, the matter is not rectified.
These thirteen are called the formal acts of relinquishment (*pratikṣepa-karman*).
Regarding "one who sees": it is as the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa said, "I have heard directly from the Buddha that the practice of sensual desire cannot obstruct the path."
Because one abandons this view, it is called "abandonment.
These two types are termed the *vinaya* of abandonment (*prahāṇa-vinaya*).
In total, there are two kinds:
There are two types: those that may be confessed and those that may not be confessed.

Those that may be confessed are: the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses for bhikṣus, the nineteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses for bhikṣuṇīs, and the six cases involving the threefold admonition; these involve formal legal procedures (*karmavācanā*) through which the offense can be removed, and are thus termed "confessable."
Among those matters that cannot be openly disclosed, there is one case where a nun may be formally admonished three times:
it is when a bhikṣu has committed an offense and the Saṃgha has performed a *karmavācanā* to expel him, yet a certain bhikṣuṇī constantly comes to assist him by speaking in his defense.
The bhikṣuṇīs admonish her, saying, "There is no need for assistance in this matter.

Even after being admonished up to three times, she does not desist. The Saṃgha then performs the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations). If she repents at the time of the third proclamation, her offense may still be removed; however, once the fourth proclamation is completed, it can no longer be removed. This is called "that which cannot be confessed."
Thus, for these four cases involving monks and seven involving nuns, there is no formal admonition.
This is called the *śamatha-vinaya* (settling of the dispute).
These five together are termed the meaning of *vinaya*.
"What constitutes an offense?
There are two kinds of offenses:
first, grave offenses; second, minor offenses."

Regarding "committing a grave offense": when one intends to commit an evil act, the fire of the afflictions becomes intense; it can burn the wholesome mind until it is extinguished, allowing the evil deed to be accomplished. This is the meaning of "burning."

Having committed an evil deed, when one later feels remorse, mental suffering arises; because the wholesome mind is so intense that it can extinguish the unwholesome mind, this is also called the meaning of "burning.

As for those who commit minor offenses, the afflictive mind that arises is slight; as they commit a minor transgression, their subtle wholesome mind is extinguished and cannot remain, which is called the meaning of "roasting."
When one later feels remorse and gives rise to a subtle mind of goodness that scorches a small mind of evil, this is also called the meaning of "scorching" (zhì).
What is meant by "transgression" (fàn)?
That which causes sentient beings to revolve in the three realms of existence is the meaning of transgression.
What further constitutes an offense?
To do that which was not permitted to be done is called an offense.
What is meant by "an offense"?
To transgress the precepts one upholds means that the fruits received from such transgression are not to be craved or delighted in; therefore, it is called "transgression.
Furthermore, why is it called "transgression"?
Any affliction by suffering or distress that touches and oppresses the body is all termed the meaning of "transgression."
To sever wholesome dharmas is the meaning of "transgression.

Furthermore, regarding what is called "transgression," the unwholesome actions committed by humans, the six heavens of the desire realm, the four dhyānas, and the four formless attainments—within the three realms—are all termed transgressions.
Furthermore, regarding what is called "offense": when a mind of anger manifests, it is termed an offense.
