Moreover, a mind defiled by afflictions (*kleśa*) is also termed an offense.
Furthermore, as for the meaning of "offense": when afflictions increase while within the path, this is the sense of an offense.
Furthermore, the fulfillment of afflictions is also termed "transgression.
Why are afflictions called transgressions?

It is like placing water in a vessel and lighting a fire beneath it; the overflowing fire of affliction causes the body and speech to become heedless and commit unwholesome karma—this is what is meant by "transgression."
Furthermore, regarding those who transgress: among the seven classes of offenses (*saptāpatti-skandha*), whatever should not be done, doing it is termed a transgression.
"Why is it called *pārājika*?
*Pārājika* means to break apart and disperse; therefore, it is called *pārājika*."
Furthermore, regarding *pārājika*: when one is wounded by another’s sword or spear and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is extinguished, it is called *pārājika*.
Within the Buddha-dharma, *pārājika* refers to contending with the afflictions (*kleśa*) and being harmed by evil; this is called *pārājika*.

Furthermore, regarding the *pārājika*: that which is abandoned by the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, abandoned by the four fruits of the śramaṇa, and abandoned by all wholesome dharmas—namely, ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—is called *pārājika*.
"Furthermore, 'pārājika' means that within the Vinaya, within the True Dharma, and within the dharma of a bhikṣu, one is cut off and extinguished, never to arise again; this is called pārājika."
The World-Honored One has said:
"There is a shore beyond called Nirvana.
Because one is unable to cross over and reach that shore, it is termed *pārājika*.
"Pārājika" means that just as when a person's head is cut off by another, they can never return to life;
being extinguished by evil, one no longer constitutes a bhikṣu—this is called pārājika.
The Venerable Kāśyapīya said:
"To commit the most grievous evil such that nothing further can be accomplished within the dharma of a bhikṣu is called *pārājika*.
Furthermore, *pārājika* is like a person who has committed a crime and is sentenced to death; there is no path to life again."
Having committed a *pārājika* offense, there is forever no path for repentance; one can never again practice within the dharma of a bhikṣu, hence it is called *pārājika*.
It is like a person wishing to reach the other shore who, due to folly, is deceived by others midway and loses the way to that shore.
Within the Buddha’s teaching, to be deceived by afflictions and lose the further shore of nirvāṇa is called "falling.
Among evils, sexual desire is the worst; taking what is not given is the worst;
taking human life is the worst; and claiming superhuman qualities is also the worst.
Diligent in what is unwholesome, yet most skillful at severing all virtues through expedient means—
this is called a *pārājika*. Though one may falsely wear the dharma-robes and sit in the ranks of the Saṃgha, [one is no longer a monk].
Because he is utterly separated from the Brahmā realm, he is called *pārājika*.
Receiving the alms of others to sustain his life, yet acting contrary to the path, he is no vessel for merit;
being a thief capable of plundering the kingdom, he is named *pārājika*.
"What is meant by *saṃghāvaśeṣa*?
As for *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, when an offense has been committed, it must be confessed before the Saṃgha; it may not be confessed before only one person, nor even before two or three people."
Confession before the assembly is called *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
All matters that must be confessed by a bhikṣu should be performed within the *saṃgha*; because the *saṃgha* acts on his behalf, it is named *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Furthermore, regarding the term *saṃghāvaśeṣa*: because a small remainder remains that has not been extinguished, it is called *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Moreover, "remainder" (*avaśeṣa*) is like a person who has been cut by another; because the throat remains, it is termed a "remainder."

It is like two men who have both entered a battle together; one has been killed by an opponent and his life has ceased, while the other has been wounded by an opponent and remains with his life-force not yet severed.
As for the one whose life is not yet severed, if he obtains a skilled physician and excellent medicine, he may recover; if he does not obtain them, he cannot recover.
It is likewise with those who have committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; there is still a principle by which it may be confessed.
If one obtains a pure assembly to perform the method for confessing and removing the offense according to the Dharma, this offense can be eliminated.
If there is no pure assembly, the offense cannot be extinguished;
this is called *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

As for the method of extinguishing the offense, one is instructed to undergo separate residence (*parivāsa*), perform the six-day practice (*mānatva*), and then perform the *ābhāṣya* (rehabilitation).
Having completed the *āpattipariśuddhi* (purification of the offense) through the *āvarhaṇa* (formal act of rehabilitation), one attains liberation from the point of transgression.
Having attained liberation and arisen [from the offense], one does not commit it again; this is called *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
"What is meant by *pāyattika*?
As for *pāyattika*, because the offense committed is slight, it is called *pāyattika*.
Furthermore, *pāyattika* refers to an offense that does not sever the roots of goodness; it is an offense concerning the branches and twigs, hence it is named *pāyattika*."
Furthermore, regarding the *pāyattika*: it is like one who has been struck with an axe; though his skin is slightly wounded, it does not reach the point of endangering his life.
The *pāyattika* offense is likewise: this offense inflicts only slight injury upon the locus of virtue, and is thus called *pāyattika*.
"What is meant by *pāṭidesanīya*?
As for *pāṭidesanīya*, one confesses immediately upon committing an offense; because one repeatedly commits offenses and repeatedly confesses them, it is called *pāṭidesanīya*."
Furthermore, it is called *pāṭidesanīya* because it is committed through forgetfulness or error, rather than intentionally;
therefore, it is named *pāṭidesanīya*. What is meant by *sthūlātyaya*?
Regarding *sthūlātyaya*: because it arises on the border of a grave offense (*sthūla-pāpaka*), it is called *sthūlātyaya*.
Furthermore, regarding *sthūlātyaya*: because one intends to commit a major offense but does not complete it, it is called *sthūlātyaya*.
Furthermore, regarding the *sthūlātyaya*: because it is a grave offense compared to the *duṣkṛta* of harsh speech, it is called *sthūla*.
First, eating human flesh is a *sthūlātyaya*;
second, keeping human skin is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Third, shaving the hair on the genitals or the armpits constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*;
fourth, using medicinal substances to irrigate the anus constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*;
fifth, keeping human hair in a *kṣipātra* (a bowl for refuse) constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*.
Sixth, practicing nakedness constitutes a sthūlātyaya;
seventh, keeping a stone bowl constitutes a sthūlātyaya;
eighth, angrily tearing one's robes constitutes a sthūlātyaya.
Ninth, destroying a dwelling out of anger is a *sthūlātyaya*;
tenth, destroying a stupa out of anger is a *sthūlātyaya*.
These are called *svabhāva-sthūlātyaya* (offenses by their very nature).
"Duskṛta (offense of wrong-doing) is termed 'evil action.
Violating the discipline of body and speech is termed 'evil action.
There are two kinds of evil speech:"
The first is false speech; the second is untimely speech. Regarding untimely speech:
when Śreṇika Bimbisāra’s son, Śakraka, maintained an impartial mind and offered medicine as alms to the Saṃgha, the group of six bhikṣus slandered him, saying:
"He gives the good portions to the elders and the inferior portions to us."
The donor replied,
"I shall go to the market and buy better medicine to give to the Venerable.
Because the group of six bhikṣus slandered others, this is called "evil speech" (pāruṣya).
To speak at an inappropriate time is called "untimely speech.
"That which should be consumed during the first watch of the night consists of two things: first, sugarcane juice; second, sugarcane juice mixed with water."
Furthermore, there are eight kinds of syrups:
first, mango syrup; second, jambu syrup; third, kola syrup; fourth, cudra syrup; fifth, moca syrup; sixth, śālmalī syrup; seventh, pālevata syrup; and eighth, grape syrup.
If the flavor and aroma of such fermented drinks have not changed, they may be drunk until the first watch of the night;
once they have changed, they must not be drunk.

Regarding "the two days and two nights [rule]": when one who has received full ordination (upasampadā) stays overnight with one who has not received full ordination, by the third night, the one who is fully ordained should rise and sit before the dawn light appears.

Furthermore, there are two nights associated with the concealment of offenses: if one who has committed an offense should confess it and undergo the *parivāsa* (probation) period, but is unable to remain in that separate residence due to fear or difficulty, the concealment for two nights is permitted.

Furthermore, there are two times associated with the practice of the Dharma: the first watch of the night and the last watch of the night, during which one should sit in meditation or walk in *caṅkrama* with uplifted diligence.

Why, then, is one not exhorted to practice during all three watches? Because during the middle watch—one period used for resting and refreshing oneself—it is therefore not possible to teach that one should practice throughout the entire night.
The reason for exhorting [the practice] of the first and last watches of the night is to ensure that one does not grow lax in the cultivation of the Path.
This is called "correspondence with the two periods.
Regarding "what should be done at night": during the night one may lie down in the open air, but not during the day.
When about to dawn, he returns to his room and lies down to sleep.
If, while walking in meditation during the night, he is unable to wear his full set of robes due to the heat, he may walk in meditation wearing only the *kāṣāya*.
If one is large-bodied, it is permissible not to wear the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (inner robe) or the *kaṣāya* (outer robe).
One may wear leather sandals to fetch water for others; however, if fetching water from the edge of a pond, this is permitted at night but not during the day.
"Regarding 'that which should be consumed before noon': from the appearance of the dawn light until midday, during this time one may eat what is appropriate without offense.
That which should be eaten at midday consists of the five kinds of primary foods (*maulabhakta*); it does not refer to other improper foods."
Regarding improper food, one may eat repeatedly before midday.
"The method for entering a village to eat before midday:
if there is no invitation from a donor, one may enter the village to beg for food without informing a neighboring seat; there is no fault."
If one who has accepted an invitation departs without informing his neighbor-sitter, he commits an offense. Why is this?

It is like the case of the Śākya son Upananda, who, while staying at the place where the invitation was received, did not inform his neighbor-sitter and departed in the morning for the location where the invitation had been accepted.
Later, they invited donors from another location, and having summoned Upananda as well as other bhikṣus, the bhikṣus waited for Upananda;
by the time he arrived, the proper hour had already passed, and they were unable to eat their midday meal.
For this reason, the Buddha established a rule:
"When a bhikṣu has been invited to a meal, he should inform his neighbor so that they may know.
During the morning hours, a sick bhikṣu is permitted to eat gruel.
Furthermore, if one must enter a village before midday, one should not inform the monk sitting beside them;
however, one may enter the village for the sake of the Buddha, for the Dharma, for the Sangha of the four quarters, for a stupa, or for the sick.
"When a co-practitioner disciple enters a village, he must inform his preceptor.
If a bhikṣu enters a village and sees a donor, he should inform his neighbor so that they may know."
"Regarding 'eating after [the meal]': having finished eating, one subsequently obtains more food.
If the time has not yet passed, one may eat by performing the *khalupaścādbhakti* (leftover-food) ritual; this is called 'eating after.
For one who is ill, there is no fault in eating repeatedly after the meal."
Regarding those who tend to the sick, whether the food is considered leftover or not, they may eat after the meal.
If there is an invitation from a donor (*dānapati*), one should inform a neighboring seat-mate;
if there is no invitation from a donor, there is no fault in not informing them.
If a bhikṣu is appropriate [to teach] by day but inappropriate by night, when instructing a bhikṣuṇī, he should teach her during the day and not at night.
"If a bhikṣuṇī receives the instruction and admonition..."
On the fifteenth day, she should inform the preceptor. If she is able to announce it to the Saṃgha immediately, the Bhikṣuṇī may perform the Poṣadha at dusk on the fifteenth day.
If the Saṃgha does not assemble during the day and she cannot announce it to the Saṃgha, she must announce it to the Saṃgha when the time for the Poṣadha arrives at dusk.

Once she has received the instruction, when the sixteenth day arrives, the bhikṣuṇī should receive the instruction from the instructor of bhikṣuṇīs; having received the instruction, she may immediately perform the poṣadha.

If on the fifteenth day the bhikṣuṇī goes among the great saṃgha to receive the instruction, she should request the instruction at the time the saṃgha assembles; she need not come again later to request it.
If a bhikṣuṇī has already received full ordination within the bhikṣuṇī saṃgha, she should then receive full ordination before the bhikṣu saṃgha during the daytime; she should not come at night.
"If a bhikṣuṇī obtains an extra bowl, she may give it away that very day or perform a formal act of purification (pariṣkāra-dāna); as long as the dawn has not yet appeared, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī obtains a utensil for use, its possession is permitted."

If one keeps one [vessel] from each of the sixteen types of vessels, or if the owner gives them away to others on that very day or performs a ritual purification (*pariśuddhi*), there is no offense until the appearance of the dawn light.

"Furthermore, there is that which corresponds to the daytime: if a bhikṣu delights in sitting in meditation and his place of residence has no resident preceptor, provided that he can travel back and forth to the preceptor’s dwelling within a single day, he may rely on him from afar without losing the status of formal reliance."

If two monasteries are situated such that one can travel between them and return within a single day, or if there is someone guarding the *saṃghārāma*, one may still rely on them from a distance without losing [the status of] formal dependence (*niśraya*).

If monks are at a place where they perform the *poṣadha* together and establish a great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), it is permitted to establish that great boundary even if it is as far as a day’s journey to and fro.
This is called the practice corresponding to the day.

"The practices to be performed during both day and night include: receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), the *poṣadha*, the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*), giving one's consent (*chanda*), giving the consent for purity (*śuddhachanda*), giving the invitation for criticism, undertaking the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), receiving the *kaṭhina* robe, and receiving the three robes so as not to be separated from them overnight; these are called the practices corresponding to day and night."
"Furthermore, there is a practice corresponding to two days and two nights:

a person who has received full ordination may stay overnight with one who has not received full ordination for two days and two nights; on the third night, the one who is fully ordained should rise and sit before the dawn light appears."

If a visiting bhikṣu arrives at another monastery and, having been offered and accepted a room and bedding, goes outside to stay overnight without informing the resident monks, then on the third night, before the appearance of the dawn light, it is well if he comes himself or sends someone to inform the residents; if he does not inform them until the dawn light appears, he incurs an offense.
"If a bhikṣu stays overnight twice within an army, and by the third night, before the appearance of the dawn light, if there is an opportunity, he may part from those he knows;
if there is no opportunity, he may simply depart outside the military camp, and if the dawn light appears [while he is thus outside], he does not commit an offense."
If one takes leave of an acquaintance and knows that they will not grant permission, one may depart directly without taking leave;
this is called the practice corresponding to two days and two nights.

"Regarding the rule of the three-night association: one who has received full ordination may stay in the same room for three nights with one who has not received full ordination; when the fourth night arrives and before the appearance of the dawn light, the one who has not received full ordination must go outside the boundary."
If one is unable to depart, those who have received full ordination (*upasampadā*) should go outside the boundary.
This is called the practice corresponding to three nights.
Furthermore, there is the practice corresponding to five days and five nights.

If a bhikṣu encounters the danger of bandits or the danger of military insurgents and is unable to carry his three robes with him, he may entrust his three robes to the house of a layperson who is an acquaintance for five days.
Until the appearance of the dawn on the sixth day, one should come to look at the robe and take hold of it with one's own hand.
If the sixth day passes until the appearance of the dawn, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If a bhikṣu acts with intimacy and takes another’s robe to wear it without informing them, and five days pass until the sixth day when the dawn appears, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu has his own three robes, he should inspect them by the fifth day to see whether they have been damaged by insects or rats.
If more than five days pass and the dawn of the sixth day appears, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This is called the practice corresponding to five nights.
Regarding the practice corresponding to six nights: if a bhikṣu stays apart from his robe overnight and reaches the dawn of the sixth day, he loses [the status of] the robe.
Furthermore, there is the practice of the six-night rite, which consists of performing the *mānatva* penance for six nights; this is called the "six-night associated rite.

Regarding the "seven-night associated rite": ghee, oil, fresh butter, honey, and black rock sugar may be stored by one who is ill for seven days; when the dawn appears on the eighth day, they must not be stored.

If a bhikṣu, during the summer retreat, is for the sake of the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, a stūpa, or illness, and so forth—on account of such various reasons—he may accept the seven-night rule (*saptarātra*).
The Venerable Sarvāstivādin said:
"If a bhikṣu has completed his formal acceptance of dependence (*niśraya*), he may request the seven-day rule to go outside the boundary."
"When the seven days are complete, he returns to the monastery and does not lose his formal dependence (*niśraya*).
This is called the "Dharma Corresponding to Seven Nights.
*Vinayamātṛkā Sūtra*, Scroll 7.
The Vinayamātṛkā Sūtra, Scroll Eight.
Translator’s name lost; currently appended to the Qin Records.
Regarding the "Dharma Corresponding to the Ten Nights": if a bhikṣu keeps an extra robe (*atirekacīvara*) and does not perform the ritual of *pariśuddhi* (purification) or bestow it as a gift...
If one keeps an extra bowl for more than ten days without performing the ritual of pure gift (*viśuddhi-pradāna*), it likewise constitutes an offense after ten days.
This is called the practice corresponding to ten nights.

"Regarding the practice corresponding to the half-month: one month prior to the summer retreat, one should seek a bathing robe; having obtained the robe, it must be worn for at least half a month, and during the summer retreat, one should bathe using it once every half-month."
If a bhikṣuṇī commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, the two assemblies of the Saṃgha shall gather, and she shall undergo the mānatva penance for half a month.
During that half-month, the bhikṣuṇī must request from the Saṃgha the instruction on the dharma of exhortation.
The two assemblies should wash [the robes] every half-month, and they should perform the *poṣadha* every half-month.

If a bhikṣu, during the summer retreat (*varṣā*), has a reason to go outside the boundary, he who travels a long distance should receive the "fifteen-day rule" (*pañcadaśarātra-dharma*) for the sake of maintaining the purity of his precepts; this is called the "Dharma Corresponding to the Half-Month."

Regarding the "One-Month Corresponding Rule": if a bhikṣu lacks one of his three robes and, having obtained the materials for a robe, he must cut, dye, sew, and formally accept it within one month. If more than one month passes, it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
After the *pravāraṇā*, one may stay apart from one's robes for one month.
During the final month of spring, one should request a bathing robe; the rule for the bathing robe is that it is six cubits long and two and a half cubits wide.

Regarding the matters to be performed during the summer retreat (*varṣā*), at the conclusion of the seven-day or fifteen-day period, one should request the procedure for accepting the *kāṭhina* robe for one month; on the sixteenth day of the seventh month, one should accept it.
If circumstances prevent one from doing so, one may receive [the precepts] until the fifteenth day of the eighth month; beyond that time, one may not receive them.
This is called the "Dharma Corresponding to One Month."
"Regarding the practice corresponding to two months: one does not shave the hair, and at the very latest, one must complete the full two months; it must not exceed this.
This is called the practice corresponding to two months."

Regarding the practice corresponding to the three months: when the three-month summer retreat has concluded, one should stay outside for one night; this is called the practice corresponding to the three months.
Regarding the practice corresponding to the four months: during the four months of summer, one uses the rain-bathing robe.
If a donor offers the Saṃgha medicinal substances for four months to be consumed, the Saṃgha should accept and use them, but must not exceed the four-month period.

If a follower of an external path comes to the monks seeking to go forth, they should be made to live separately for four months while their conduct is observed, to determine whether they have come with the intent of seeking out faults in the Saṃgha.
"Is he not a hypocrite seeking to leave the household life?
Is his mind and will harmonious and disciplined?
Having ascertained his conduct, only then shall you shave his hair and ordain him as a renunciant."
Furthermore, there is that which corresponds to four months: four months are winter, four months are spring, and four months are summer; this is called the Dharma corresponding to four months.

“Regarding the practice corresponding to five months: after the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, when five full months have passed and the *kaṭhina* robe has been relinquished, this is called the practice corresponding to five months.

Regarding the practice corresponding to twelve months: once one has received the full ordination (*upasampadā*) as a Great Way practitioner (*mahāyānika*), after completing the instruction on all the practices for Great Way practitioners within twelve months, only then may one receive the full ordination again; if the twelve months are not yet complete, one must not receive it.”
After a śrāmaṇera has received the full precepts (upasampadā), he may subsequently receive one more śrāmaṇera as a disciple.
A śrāmaṇerikā who has received the precepts must observe the śikṣamāṇā training for two years; she may not ordain another śrāmaṇerikā during that time.
Once a śikṣamāṇā has received full ordination, she may ordain śrāmaṇerīs.

The bhikṣuṇīs are also like the mahāsāṃghika monks: after having instructed her for twelve months in the rituals she ought to perform, if there is subsequently a śikṣamāṇā who wishes to receive full ordination, it is permitted to grant her full ordination.
This is called the Dharma corresponding to the twelve months.
The period for relying upon a teacher also concludes after these twelve months; one may receive reliance from a teacher, but one must not simultaneously receive reliance from two teachers at once.
"The practice corresponding to one year is the aforementioned practice corresponding to twelve months.
As for the practice corresponding to two years: if a girl who is eighteen years old is ordained as a śrāmaṇerikā, she may immediately receive the two-year training in the precepts as a śikṣamāṇā."

If a woman who is ten years old already has a husband, she may be ordained to leave the household life and receive the śrāmaṇerī precepts; after two full years have passed, she may be granted the śikṣamāṇā precepts.
Furthermore, after another two years have passed, one may receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
This is called the "practice corresponding to two years.

Regarding the "practice corresponding to three years": a monk of one year’s seniority may sit on the same bed as one of five years’ seniority; excluding those of three years’ seniority, this is called the "practice corresponding to three years."

"Regarding the Dharma of the Five-Year Correspondence: a bhikṣu who has completed five years of seniority must recite the Prātimokṣa so as to be proficient; he must also recite the one motion (jñapti), the one motion followed by one proclamation (jñapti-dvitīya), and the one motion followed by three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha) so that they are all mastered."
A bhikṣu who has not yet completed five years of ordination must not live apart from his formal reliance (niśraya).
The five ways of losing this reliance are as explained above.
This is called the practice corresponding to the five-year period.

"Regarding the six-year rule for associated items: a *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) must be kept for a full six years; if it exceeds this period or is less than six years old when it breaks, it should be given to others.
However, if one wears a patched robe (*saṃghāṭī*), one may keep it oneself; even if it does not break, one should continue to keep it oneself."

If a dwelling already exists but its walls on the four sides have not yet been roofed over, and after the Saṃgha has performed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) to appoint someone to complete the roofing, one who has resided within it for a full six years should return it to the Saṃgha; one must not exceed this period.
This is called the practice corresponding to six years.

Regarding the practice corresponding to ten years: when a bhikṣu has reached ten years of ordination, he may act as an upādhyāya to confer full ordination upon others, he may receive others as his attendants (niśraya), and he may accept śrāmaṇeras.
A ten-year-old girl who has a husband may receive the ten śrāmaṇerī precepts for two years and then receive the śikṣamāṇā precepts.
This is called the "Dharma of Correspondence with Ten Years."

"Regarding the rule concerning the twelve-year period: if a donor intends to build a dwelling for the Sangha, and the Sangha appoints a bhikṣu to oversee its construction, that bhikṣu may reside in the completed dwelling for twelve years; after which he must return it to the Sangha and may not remain there beyond that time."
This is called the practice corresponding to twelve years.
Regarding the practice corresponding to eighteen years: when a śrāmaṇerikā has reached the age of eighteen, she receives the śikṣamāṇā precepts.
This is called the procedure for those eighteen years of age.

Regarding the procedure for those twenty years of age: a girl who has received the śrāmaṇerī precepts and completed two years of training in the precepts may receive full ordination upon reaching twenty.
This is called the "Dharma of Correspondence for Twenty People.
Regarding the "Dharma of Correspondence for One Person": a folding chair (huchuang) may only be used by one person to sit upon; therefore, it is called the "Dharma of Correspondence for One Person."
Regarding the practice for two persons: a rope bed accommodates only two persons; this is called the practice for two persons.
Regarding the practice for three persons: a large bed accommodates only three persons; this is called the practice for three persons.
Regarding the rule for four persons: if a very large bed can accommodate four persons, this is called the rule for four persons.
Regarding the rule for five: these are the five types of formal meals.

Regarding the practice of the sevenfold association: at night, one must remain within forty-nine *dhanus* (arrows) of distance from one's robes—each *dhanu* being four *cubits*. This is called the practice of the sevenfold association.

Regarding the "eight-finger standard" (*aṣṭāṅgulapramāṇa*): the method for making a bed is such that all legs of the bed, excluding the upper portion inserted into the frame and leaving eight finger-breadths below, are called the eight-finger standard.
The tenfold concordant practice (*daśasaṃyukta-dharma*) refers to permitting the use of ten kinds of cloth materials to make robes; this is called the tenfold concordant practice.

The twentyfold concordant practice (*viṃśatisaṃyukta-dharma*) refers to the performance of the *āpattipratideśana* (expiation) by a community of twenty; this is called the twentyfold concordant practice.

"Regarding the 'dharma of single correspondence': at the time of receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), there is only one preceptor (*upādhyāya*); this is called the dharma of single correspondence. Regarding the 'dharma of double correspondence':
at the time of receiving full ordination, there are only two instructors (*ācārya*); this is called the dharma of double correspondence."

Regarding the three requisites (*trisaṃyuktadharma*): when receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), one must first prepare the three robes; if they are lacking, one cannot receive full ordination—this is called the three requisites.

Regarding the four requisites (*catuḥsaṃyuktadharma*): one receives full ordination through the formal procedure of a motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*)—this is called the four requisites.

Regarding the fivefold method of correspondence (*pañca-saṃyukta-dharma*): there are five kinds of obstacles that prevent one from receiving full ordination; these are called the fivefold method of correspondence. Regarding the sevenfold method of correspondence (*sapta-saṃyukta-dharma*):

one who has received the formal consent (*chanda*) speaks to one person, and in this manner it is passed on successively until the seventh person; all of them may receive the consent for purification. This is called the sevenfold method of correspondence.

Regarding the eightfold method of correspondence: if one possesses surplus material wealth, it should be made into a "pure gift" (śuddhadāna) with a width of four finger-breadths and a length of eight finger-breadths; this is called the eightfold method of correspondence.
Regarding the "method of tenfold correspondence": when one receives full ordination, it is received by means of ten persons; this is called the method of tenfold correspondence.
Regarding the "method of twentyfold correspondence": when one has reached the age of twenty and receives full ordination, this is called the method of twentyfold correspondence.
"Regarding the practice of a single round [of weaving]: when a bhikṣuṇī weaves one round of the warp-thread, this is called the practice of a single round.
Regarding the practice of two rounds: not weaving one round of the warp-thread and then weaving one round, this is called the practice of two rounds."
Regarding the method of threefold correspondence: one turn of woven cord and two turns of unwoven cord constitute what is called the method of threefold correspondence.
Regarding the method of fourfold correspondence: this refers to four *karṣāpaṇas*. In the country of India, sixteen copper coins constitute one *karṣāpaṇa*.
Regarding winter garments for warding off the cold, those of the highest quality may not exceed four *kārsāpaṇas* in cost; this is called the "practice of the four requisites.
As for the "practice of the five requisites," a bhikṣuṇī must possess the five robes in full to receive full ordination; this is called the "practice of the five requisites."
Regarding the sevenfold associated dharmas (*saptavidha-saṃprayukta-dharma*): these are the seven kinds of rice; this is called the sevenfold associated dharma.

Regarding the eightfold associated dharma: there was a donor who invited bhikṣuṇīs for a meal. When the bhikṣuṇīs departed, they arrived late; because the nuns there asked many questions regarding the sequence of seniority (*yavasa*), the time had already approached midday and they were unable to eat their fill.
Having heard this, the World-Honored One established a precept:
"From this day forward, when the community of bhikṣuṇīs assembles, it is permitted for eight senior nuns to take their seats in order, while the rest may sit according to their convenience."
Regarding the ten factors of correspondence: when a bhikṣu is endowed with ten qualities, the Saṃgha may, through formal ritual (karmavācanā), appoint him as a teacher of instruction for bhikṣuṇīs.
What are these ten?
First, the accomplishment of the *prātimokṣa* precepts;
second, extensive learning. As for "extensive learning," it means that one is proficient in both the words and the meanings of the Tripiṭaka through recitation; this constitutes extensive learning.
Third, they recite the *Bhikṣu-bhikṣuṇī-sūtra* three times.
Fourth, they constantly speak subtle and excellent words from their mouths, with compassion arising in their hearts, speaking clearly so that they are easily understood.
Fifth, his sense faculties are fully complete and his physical appearance is exceptionally distinguished, such that he is loved and respected by others.
Sixth, he is of noble lineage, whether a Kṣatriya, a householder, or a Brāhmaṇa.
Seventh, he possesses excellent eloquence, preaching the Dharma to the bhikṣuṇīs to instruct, benefit, and gladden them.
Eighth, he is held in high esteem by the bhikṣuṇīs.
Ninth, he is without fault regarding the three types of action (trikarma) toward the bhikṣuṇīs.
Tenth: if one has twenty years of seniority or more than twenty years of seniority, this is called the "dharma of ten-year correspondence.
As for the "dharma of twenty-year correspondence," it refers to those with twenty years of seniority.
"Regarding 'the single correspondence': a forest-dwelling bhikṣu stays alone in a certain place; on the day of the Saṃgha’s poṣadha, he reflects in his mind and speaks with his mouth:
'The Saṃgha performs the poṣadha today; I, too, perform the poṣadha.'"
Regarding the "Dharma of Mutual Correspondence": two bhikṣus speak to one another in turn, saying, "Venerable sir!
Today the Saṃgha performs the pure poṣadha; I too perform the pure poṣadha."
This is called the method of two-fold correspondence (*dvaya-saṃvāsa-dharma*).
Regarding the method of three-fold correspondence (*traya-saṃvāsa-dharma*): three persons also speak to one another in turn; this is called the method of three-fold correspondence.

Regarding the method of four-fold correspondence (*catuḥ-saṃvāsa-dharma*): one person makes a formal announcement (*jñapti*), and then the *poṣadha* is performed; this is called the method of four-fold correspondence.

Regarding the "fivefold formal procedure" (*pañcavargīya-karman*): in border regions where there is no Sangha, the full ordination may be received by five persons including a *vinayadhara*; this is called the fivefold formal procedure.
Regarding the "sevenfold formal procedure" (*saptavargīya-karman*): it refers to the seven methods for settling disputes; this is called the sevenfold formal procedure.
The eight factors of association refer to the eight respectful rules for bhikṣuṇīs; these are called the eight factors of association.
The ten factors of association refer to the ten dharmas that a bhikṣu must fulfill to be entitled to recite the Prātimokṣa; these are called the ten factors of association.
Regarding the "twentyfold formal act" (*vīsativagga kamma*), it is as explained above for the maiden.
The "onefold formal act" (*ekavagga kamma*) is when a single bhikṣu performs the *pravāraṇā*.
The "twofold formal act" (*duvīsativagga kamma*) is the method of mutual *pravāraṇā* between two bhikṣus.
The threefold correspondence and the fourfold correspondence both consist of performing the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to admonish) with one another in turn.

As for the fivefold correspondence, it refers to the case where five persons perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*) to appoint one person to conduct the *pravāraṇā*; this is called the fivefold correspondence.
Regarding the seven factors of association: the accomplishment of seven dharmas is called the seven factors of association.

Regarding the eight factors of association: when a layperson in white robes has deep faith in the Triple Gem yet accomplishes eight unrighteous acts, the Saṃgha performs the *pātra-āvarta* (turning-over of the bowl) karma against them;
once they have abandoned the eight unrighteous acts, the Saṃgha then performs the karma of restoring the bowl.
These are called the eight factors of correspondence.
Regarding the ten factors of correspondence: if one does not fulfill ten dharmas, one may not confer full ordination upon others; these are called the ten factors of correspondence.

Regarding the twenty-day rule for the requisite dharma: if a bhikṣu’s three robes are incomplete, he may strive with all his might to seek them out, and within twenty days, having finished making them—cutting, sewing, and receiving them—he must maintain them.
If it cannot be prepared, but can be prepared by the thirtieth day, one should cut, sew, and formally accept it.
If it cannot be prepared after the thirtieth day has passed, one should perform the ritual of pure giving (*śuddhaka-dāna*).
If one gives what is impure, one commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
Regarding "the first method of formal procedure": two bhikṣus live together, and one passes away.
The survivor thinks to himself:
"This property of the deceased bhikṣu should belong to me.
If this person immediately receives it, while the one who arrives later does not,
this is called the "single-correspondence dharma" (ekasaṃvāsika-dharma).

Regarding the second case concerning formal procedures (*sāmagrī-dharma*): when three persons are living together and one person passes away, the remaining two should speak to one another in turn, saying:
"Venerable sirs, please bear this in mind!"
"This property should belong to us.
In this manner, these two persons pass it on to one another; this is called the method of correspondence between two persons.

Regarding the method of correspondence between three persons: when four people live together and one of them passes away, the remaining three pass it on as described above; this is called the method of correspondence between three persons.

Regarding the *catuṣka-saṃvāsa-dharma*: when five persons live together and one passes away, the remaining four perform the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) to divide the property; this is called the *catuṣka-saṃvāsa-dharma*.

Regarding the procedure involving five persons (*pañcavargīya-karman*): when five persons perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*) to divide the belongings of a deceased bhikṣu, four persons perform a formal act to bestow them upon one person, and that one person then returns them to the community; only after this may they be divided together. This is called the procedure involving five persons.
Regarding the seven factors of association: the seven dharmas of reverence are called the seven factors of association.

Regarding the eight factors of association: when a bhikṣu is accomplished in eight dharmas, the Saṃgha should appoint him to inspire faith in the donors and to perform repentance; these are called the eight factors of association.

Regarding the "dharma of the tenfold correspondence": some say that when ten persons perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*), it is in accordance with the Dharma; whereas if nine or eleven persons perform it, it is not in accordance with the Dharma. This is called the dharma of the tenfold correspondence.
Regarding the *vīśativargakaraṇīya* (procedure requiring twenty): when twenty people draw lots, this is called the *vīśativargakaraṇīya*.

Regarding the *ekavargakaraṇīya* (procedure requiring one): if a bhikṣu living alone realizes he has committed an offense for which there is no place to confess, he should maintain it in his mind; later, upon seeing another bhikṣu, he should immediately confess it—this is called the *ekavargakaraṇīya*.

Regarding the method involving two factors: when a bhikṣu has committed an offense and confessed it to one person, if it is not thereby removed, he later goes before the assembly and confesses again; this is called the method involving two factors.

Regarding the practice involving three stages: if a bhikṣu has committed an offense and confesses it to two other bhikṣus, yet does not eliminate it, he later goes before the Saṃgha to perform further repentance; this is called the practice involving three stages.

Regarding the procedure involving four persons: if a bhikṣu commits an offense, he may have it removed by performing a formal act (*karmavācanā*) through confession before four persons; this is called the procedure involving four persons.
The fivefold method of practice consists of the five kinds of confession; this is called the fivefold method of practice.
The sevenfold method of practice refers to the seven dharmas by which a bhikṣu achieves the suspension of the recitation of the Prātimokṣa.
Regarding the eightfold corresponding dharmas: the Tathāgata saw eight kinds of faults; these are called the eightfold corresponding dharmas.
Regarding the tenfold corresponding dharmas: it is permitted to keep ten kinds of refuse-rag robes; these are called the tenfold corresponding dharmas.
Regarding the rule of twentyfold correspondence: if a bhikṣu wishes to make a new bedding, he should use twenty *liang* of wool to make it; this is called the rule of twentyfold correspondence.

"Those things associated with the morning meal are the five kinds of formal food, the nine kinds of secondary food, and whatever else is associated with the morning meal; these are called the dharmas associated with the morning meal."
Regarding those things associated with the first watch of the night: such as grape juice up to water-based drinks, these are called “dharmas associated with the first watch of the night.
Regarding those things associated with the seven-day period: the five kinds of medicine and other medicines, these are called “dharmas associated with the seven-day period.”

Regarding the dharmas corresponding to the duration of one's life: first, *śailēya*; second, *vijaka*; third, *mṛdvīkā*; fourth, *sālu*; fifth, *lōbhra*; sixth, *marica*; seventh, *śuṇṭhī*; eighth, *bibhītaka*; ninth, *śirīṣa*; tenth, *candana*; eleventh, *tintiḍīka*; twelfth, *kālōjīra*. There are many such as these; these are called the dharmas corresponding to the duration of one's life.

"Regarding 'being equipped with the requisites for maintaining life': the three robes, alms bowl, sitting mat, needle-case, water jar, and flask—such items as these required by a bhikṣu are called the method of being equipped with the requisites for maintaining life."
Regarding the alms bowl corresponding to human use: iron bowls, *sumana* bowls, and many others such as these are called the dharmas corresponding to human use.

Regarding the robe corresponding to human use: ten kinds of cloth materials, when dyed, stitched, and cut according to the Dharma, may be accepted and maintained; these are called the dharmas corresponding to human use.
Regarding the bedding requisites (*śayanāsana*), making them according to the prescribed measurements is called the practice corresponding to individuals.
Regarding the needle-cases and woolen tubes, as explained in the preceding text, these are called practices corresponding to individuals.
"Regarding the practice corresponding to alms-gathering: when gathering alms, one should accept food only until the bowl is level with the rim; one must not accept more than that.

When gathering robes, even if a donor offers a great abundance, one who lacks the three robes may take them, but must not take more than that. This is called the dharma of the practice corresponding to gathering robes."

At that time, the World-Honored One, having finished his almsround, returned to his dwelling. He took up his robes, folded them, and placed them in one spot; this is called the "Dharma of Correspondence regarding Robes" (*cīvara-saṃyukta-dharma*).

As for the "Correspondence regarding Reclining Utensils" (*śayanāsana-saṃyukta*), it is explained in detail in the *Śayanāsana-khaṇḍaka*; this is called the "Dharma of Correspondence regarding Reclining Utensils."
Regarding standard measurements: a *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (undergarment) that is four cubits long and one and a half cubits wide is called "of standard measurement.

As for bowls, robes, bedding, needle-cases, and rooms for traveling monks—all such items are called "of standard measurement" if they accord with what the Buddha has taught; those that do not accord with the Buddha’s words are called "not of standard measurement."
"Regarding those things associated with dyeing: when the robes of the bhikṣus had faded in color, the Buddha permitted them to use ten types of dyes for coloring.

The ten types of dyes are: first, clay; second, the bark of the *tāpa* tree; third, the bark of the *badara* tree; fourth, *naipāla*; fifth, *khaṇḍa*; sixth, the root of the walnut tree; seventh, the fruit of the *āmalaka*; eighth, the bark of the *khadira* tree; ninth, the bark of the *śiṃśapā* tree; and tenth, various combinations mixed together for use as dye."
Regarding those things that ought to be dyed, these are the ten kinds of colors.

This is the method for purifying a robe by means of three spots: first, using mud; second, using blue; and third, using an uneven color. By using these three types, one purifies the robe with three spots.

"Regarding 'correspondence with dignified deportment' (īryāpatha-sampanna): one's robes should be properly arranged, and so forth, up to not standing while defecating or urinating; this is called the dharma of correspondence with dignified deportment."
Regarding those who should be appointed: one appoints them by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* or a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.
First, one demarcates the impure ground; next, one demarcates the dwellings of the Saṃgha; and finally, one demarcates the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*).
Once the great boundary has been established, one should ask the Saṃgha:
"Where shall the pure kitchen be made?
The place approved by the Saṃgha shall be established as the pure kitchen.
After the place for the *poṣadha* has been demarcated, the final step is to demarcate the *acīvaramuṣitaka-sīmā* (the boundary where robes need not be kept with one).

When dissolving the boundaries, one first dissolves the *acīvaramuṣitaka-sīmā*, then dissolves the *poṣadha-sīmā*. Next, one dissolves the *saṃgha-śuddhikūṭi-sīmā* (the boundary for the Saṃgha’s pure kitchen), followed by the dissolution of the *mahāsīmā* (the great boundary), then the dissolution of the *vihāra-sīmā* (the boundary for the monastic quarters), and finally the dissolution of the *aviśuddhabhūmi-sīmā* (the impure ground boundary) used as a place for storing miscellaneous items.

Appointing a bhikṣu to instruct bhikṣuṇīs; appointing a monk to distribute voting tallies during the *pravāraṇā*; appointing one to manage affairs for the Saṃgha of the four directions; appointing one to divide the gruel and the morning meal according to the faith of a donor; even appointing one to prohibit the monastery’s laborers from begging at the homes of devout donors; appointing one to deal with those who are insane, deranged, or mentally disturbed; and appointing one to confer the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon a bhikṣuṇī—these and other cases not specifically enumerated above where a person is appointed to perform a *karmavācanā* are all termed "the procedure of appointing a person."
"Regarding 'correspondence with the site': if a stūpa or a robe is damaged, torn, or worn through, one should repair it or treat it with plaster; this is called correspondence with the site.
It also includes the dwelling place of the upādhyāya, the dwelling place of the ācārya, the dwelling place of the Saṃgha, and the place where the Saṃgha performs the poṣadha."
At that time, the World-Honored One established a *karmavācanā* for a sick bhikṣu to designate a pure ground as a place for preparing food.

If a visiting bhikṣu arrives, the resident of the monastery should inform him of the impure places, the monastic quarters, the area where the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) has been fixed, the pure kitchen, the place for the *poṣadha*, the area where robes need not be kept within the boundary (*acīvara-apahāra-sīmā*), and the place for drinking water; this is called the Dharma corresponding to the location.
"Regarding 'directional correspondence' (dig-yoga): if the preceptor and the community of monks follow their teacher toward a particular direction, this is called the 'location.

Furthermore, as for 'direction': when the Buddha was in the city of Rājagṛha, on the fifteenth day at the end of the month, the time for the recitation of the precepts, the community of monks all gathered together."
The Buddha asked, "From where have you come?
The bhikṣus described their respective locations; this is what is meant by "direction" (dis).
In the east there is the Rāhubhadra Stūpa; in the south there is a place named Daṇu; in the west there is a place named Śveta-rudra; and in the north there is a place named Anuprāptaviśa.
These four regions are the most remote frontiers; in these places, five persons including a *vinaya-dhara* may confer the full precepts (*upasampadā*).
This is called the "Dharma of Correspondence regarding Place.

Regarding the "Dharma of Correspondence regarding Country": in the country of Aparāntaka, five persons including a *vinaya-dhara* may receive the full precepts; in the country of Avanti, one is permitted to wash repeatedly due to the heat, and it is also allowed to wear leather sandals made of two or three layers of hide.
At that time, some bhikṣus who had spent the summer retreat in the Snowy Mountains arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling with their bodies chafed and worn.
Having heard of this, the Buddha said, "In such a land, I permit the wearing of fur-lined double robes."
There were two bhikṣus, one named Ukkaṭṭha and the other named Samandaka, who came to where the Buddha was and said:

"The various bhikṣus are of diverse natures and are renunciants from various countries; they use incorrect pronunciations to corrupt the meaning of the Buddha’s sūtras. We pray that the World-Honored One will allow us to use the *Cāndravyākaraṇa* treatise to rectify the meaning of the Buddha’s sūtras."
The Buddha said:

"In my Dharma, we do not prize flowery and ornate speech; rather, even if it is plain and simple, provided it does not lose its meaning, the essential thing is that it enables people to receive understanding."
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at Vaiśālī.
Because there was a famine and grain was expensive, almsfood was difficult to obtain; the bhikṣus therefore used their supernatural powers to travel to the kingdom of Kiṭāgiri to beg for food.
The people of that country despised and held in contempt the practitioners of the Way; they would place food on the ground rather than pass it through their hands.
Some bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"Although it is not received by hand, since the intention to give has already been completed, you may take and eat it.
This is called the rule corresponding to the country (*janapada-vinaya*).
"The rule corresponding to self-indulgence (*prātimokṣa-saṃvara*) is that a single person performs the recitation mentally and verbally."
Two, three, or four people may speak to one another in turn;
five people perform the *karmavācanā* for the *pravāraṇā*.
This is called the procedure corresponding to the *pravāraṇā*.
Regarding the "Dharma of Granting Consent in Accordance with the Pravāraṇā," there are five ways of granting consent:
first, "I grant my pravāraṇā";
second, "I [perform] the pravāraṇā myself."
Third, performing the *pravāraṇā* by means of gestures;
fourth, performing the *pravāraṇā* by means of facial expressions;
fifth, performing the *pravāraṇā* by means of vocal intonations.
If these five conditions are not fulfilled, it is not called the conferring of the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to criticize).
This is termed the "Dharma corresponding to *pravāraṇā*.
Regarding the "Dharma corresponding to the taking of the *pravāraṇā* consent": the Saṃgha appoints a person to take the consent.

Regarding the taking of consent (*chanda*): if there are obstacles such as the illness of one's parents, or obstacles regarding non-celibate conduct, or many such other obstacles, one should give it to another person to carry the consent away.
Regarding the procedure for giving consent (*chandadāna*), one says to the person who is carrying the consent:
"Venerable sir, please take note!
I, [name], today, while the Saṃgha performs the invitation (*pravāraṇā*), shall also perform the invitation; I give my pure consent to the Saṃgha."
This is called the dharma associated with the granting of consent (*chanda*).

If a monk who has received consent has not yet returned, and suddenly a great flood arises or there are dangers from lions, tigers, and wolves such that he cannot go to the *pravāraṇā*, then even if he performs the *pravāraṇā* outside the boundary, he still attains purity.
The one who departs also attains purification.
This is called the method for the *pravāraṇā* of those who have taken the consent (*chanda*).
Regarding the "correspondence with the *Prātimokṣa*": at that time, the Blessed One was in a quiet chamber and reflected thus:
"I now establish a rule for the bhikṣus: I permit you to assemble in one place to recite the Prātimokṣa precepts.
If I had not established this rule, how could newly ordained bhikṣus who wish to study the Prātimokṣa hear it?"
"What is it that should be cultivated and accumulated?
Then, at that time, the World-Honored One rose from his quiet chamber and addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, you should assemble in one place and recite the Prātimokṣa precepts."
When about to recite the precepts, one first makes this announcement:
"Venerable Sangha, listen!
If the time is right for the Sangha and the Sangha is willing to grant its attention, let the Sangha now assemble in one place to recite the Prātimokṣa precepts."
“Thus it is declared.
This is called the *Prātimokṣa-śīla-saṃprayukta-dharma* (The Dharma Corresponding to the Prātimokṣa Precepts).
Regarding that which is called “corresponding to the Prātimokṣa,” there are five concise expositions of the Prātimokṣa, the text of which is as previously stated.
Furthermore, there are those who speak of that which corresponds to the *prātimokṣa*; the text is as explained in the *Mātṛkā-sūtra*.
This is called the dharma corresponding to the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*).
Regarding that which corresponds to the *poṣadha*: even three persons may perform the *poṣadha* by speaking to one another in turn.
Regarding the *poṣadha* according to the Dharma: when there are four or more monks, one should first announce [the assembly] and then perform the *poṣadha*.
At the site of the *poṣadha*, the junior monk (*navakabhikṣu*) should sweep and sprinkle the ground; this is called the practice associated with the *poṣadha*.
Regarding "corresponding to desire," at that time the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"The purification (jñapti) should be proclaimed.
Once the purification has been proclaimed, the Saṃgha shall perform the poṣadha today."
"If a sick bhikṣu does not come, it is permitted to grant his consent (*chanda*) and dispatch someone to receive it on his behalf.
This is called the procedure corresponding to consent.
If there is a valid reason, one may grant consent; if there is no valid reason, one should go in person."
There are five ways of conveying the consent (*chanda*), as explained above.

Regarding "the correspondence with the person who conveys the consent": if the person conveying the consent encounters various difficulties and is unable to come, yet the conveyor of consent is pure and the Sangha is pure, this is called "correspondence with the person who conveys the consent."
"Regarding 'correspondence with purity' (pārisuddhi-saṃvattanika): if one who is ill is unable to come, they may declare their own purity; this is called the *poṣadha* corresponding with purity.
During the *pravāraṇā*, one may say, 'I give the desire for purity' (*pārisuddhi-icchā*); for other desires, one simply says 'I give my desire' (*icchā*), without mentioning purity."
This is called purity through the granting of consent (*chanda*).

Regarding the one who takes the consent, if there are obstacles and they are unable to go, this is called "purity through taking consent"; this is the method for the person taking consent to be in accordance with purity.
"The various rules explained above should be sought within such sūtras as the Bhikṣu-sūtra, the Bhikṣuṇī-sūtra, the Mātṛkā-sūtra, the Ekottarika-āgama, and the various Khandakas."
If it accords with the meaning of the Five Scriptures, you should uphold it and not abandon it;
if it does not accord with them, set it aside and do not practice it.

Furthermore, one should examine the Dharma according to five points: first, the object; second, the original enactment; third, the subsequent enactment; fourth, the summary; and fifth, the offense or non-offense. These essentials must correspond with the five types of scriptures.
In the Five Classics, one seeks [the meaning] by contrasting the *yuan* (provisional), the *zhi* (original enactment), and the *zhongzhi* (subsequent enactment).
What is meant by "general" (*zong*)?
That which refers to all bhikṣus collectively is called "general."
What is meant by "brief exposition"?
When the beginning, middle, and end are explained merely to make the meaning clear, it is called brief.
As for "extensive exposition," it is when a bhikṣu explains to another bhikṣu what he has understood, saying: "I have heard such a teaching from the Buddha."
Upon hearing this, one must neither reject what has been said nor immediately accept it. One should hold this understanding and compare it with the five collections of sūtras.
If it accords with the sūtras, one should say:
"What the Elder has said is excellent; you should receive and uphold it well, never letting it fall into abandonment, and should always explain it extensively to others in this way."
If what he says does not accord with the five scriptures, one should admonish him:
"Elder, what you have said should not be accepted or upheld, nor should it be widely proclaimed to others."
Furthermore, one seeks superior understanding.
This is called the first "extensive" [explanation].
As for the second "extensive," one says that one has heard it from the community of monks and also explains what one understands to others.
The hearer is also as described above; he neither rejects nor accepts it, but verifies it through the five experiences.
This is called the second broad [exposition].
As for the third broad exposition: if there is a bhikṣu who says that he heard it from three persons, and he also explains what he understands to other bhikṣus.
Regarding whether this hearer accepted or did not accept [the teaching], one should also verify it by examining the five divisions of the sūtras;
this is called the third "extensive" [explanation].
As for the fourth "extensive" [explanation]: furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who claims, "I heard such a teaching from two venerable bhikṣus," and he also explains his understanding to others.
Upon hearing whether that bhikṣu accepted or did not accept [the invitation], one should likewise verify it as described above.
This is called the fourth "extensive" [category].
There are two kinds of "extensive":
First is the extensive text, and second is the extensive meaning; these are called the four extensives.
Furthermore, the meanings of what is appropriate and what is inappropriate are briefly explained.

As for what is appropriate: the iron bowl, the clay bowl, the bowl from the country of Ujjayinī, the bowl from the country of Ujjāsika, the black bowl from the country of Vaiśālī, and the red bowl from the country of Śrāvastī.
Although there are six kinds of bowls, in reality there are only two: those made of iron and those made of clay; these are called "appropriate" (saṃyukta) bowls.

As for "inappropriate" (asaṃyukta) bowls, these include bowls made of sandalwood, śiṃśapā wood, stone, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, jade, and the seven precious jewels; these are called inappropriate. Therefore, one speaks of the appropriate and the inappropriate.
"This person is permitted; that person is not permitted.
One who is permitted is a bhikṣu who may keep an extra bowl for up to ten days.
One who is not permitted is a bhikṣuṇī who may not keep an extra bowl for more than one day."
This is called "inappropriate.
This refers to those for whom it is appropriate and those for whom it is inappropriate.

Regarding the number of people for whom it is appropriate and the number for whom it is inappropriate: if a bowl has been broken and exceeds five repairs, and one seeks a new bowl to receive and maintain, this must be received through a formal act of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a motion followed by one proclamation) among four persons; it is not permitted with three or fewer.
This is called "so many people are permitted" and "so many people are not permitted. Regarding the measure:
that which is equal in measure is permitted, and that which is unequal in measure is not permitted.
As for what is permitted: from one and a half *sheng* up to two and a half *sheng*, this is called permitted.
That which is improper refers to [a vessel] that is less than one and a half *śeṅ* or exceeds two and a half *śeṅ*; this is called "improper.
For this reason, it is said that [the measure] corresponds or does not correspond to the standard limit.
"Regarding 'this form should be associated with form' and 'should not be associated': that which is perfumed by form is associated; that which is not perfumed by form is not associated.
This is called the association and non-association of form."
"Sometimes it is appropriate and sometimes it is inappropriate. As for what is appropriate:

if one has been robbed by bandits, swept away by water, fallen and broken, or lost—if such a person is in this state, it is appropriate to speak to their parents, relatives, and kinsmen to seek [the object]; this is called 'appropriate. "
If it is not swept away by water, stolen by bandits, dropped on the ground, broken, or lost, yet one speaks to parents, relatives, and kinsmen to demand it back, this is called "inappropriate.
This is what is meant by "what is appropriate for a person" and "what is inappropriate."
"Regarding robes that are appropriate or inappropriate:
'appropriate' refers to the ten kinds of allowable robe-material.
'Inappropriate' refers to robes of superior color, brocade robes, white robes, and bearded robes; many such as these are all inappropriate."
This is called "inappropriate clothing.

Regarding the three robes, it is also inappropriate to wear only one robe while maintaining the practice; this extends even to wearing a *kambala* (woolen) garment with a fringe on the head, which is likewise inappropriate.
"There are times when one should speak and times when one should not.

If one is pursued by bandits, swept away by swift waters, or burned by fire, or if one has lost [the object], in such circumstances one may speak to one's parents, brothers, relatives, and kin; if it is not like this, one should not speak to seek it."
This is called "this is appropriate at this time; this is inappropriate at this time.

Regarding what is appropriate for the *saṃkakṣikā* (breast-cloth): it should be made no shorter than one span below the waist; the cloth must cover both breasts and extend to the armpits. This is called "appropriate."
Regarding what is "inappropriate": it is inappropriate to make [the robe] too short by exceeding the prescribed limits.

As for the undergarment (*nivāsana*), when lying down at night, it should cover the feet up to the throat; provided that it does not soil the outer clean robe, this constitutes the proper measurement.
The wound-covering cloth is four cubits long and two cubits wide;
the rain-bathing garment is two and a half spans long;
the body-cleansing towel is one span long and one span wide.
The face-cleansing cloth should be one cubit in length when rolled up and also one cubit in width when rolled up.
The eye-cleansing cloth should be one span in both length and width.
This is what is permitted and what is not permitted.
“Such a number of persons is appropriate; such a number of persons is inappropriate.
‘Appropriate’ refers to four persons or three persons; ‘inappropriate’ refers to two persons. This is called ‘such a number of persons is appropriate and such a number of persons is inappropriate.’”
Sometimes it is appropriate, and sometimes it is not.

"Appropriate" means that after the *pravāraṇā*, one may receive the *kāṭhina* robe during the course of one month; beyond this period, one may not receive it. This is called "sometimes appropriate, sometimes inappropriate."

There are forms that should be practiced and forms that should not be practiced: those permitted by the Buddha are to be practiced, and those not permitted by the Buddha are not to be practiced; this is called "there being forms that should be practiced and forms that should not be practiced."

There are measurements that should be observed and those that should not; regarding what should be observed, the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (undergarment) should extend three finger-widths above the ankle, and anything longer than this is improper. Therefore, these are called "proper" and "improper."
Regarding the rules for traveling: whether it be during the earlier or later *varṣā* (rainy season retreat), one should travel toward whichever location is favorable for the *varṣā*.
If there is a subsequent necessity at the site of the *varṣā*, one should also travel [to that place] by means of the seven-day leave (*saptarātra-anujñā*).
The month before and after the *varṣā* retreat should also be observed in this manner.

That which should not be practiced is as follows: during the summer, one should not request a seven-day leave without a valid reason; during the winter, one should not undertake travel without a valid reason.
This is called what should be practiced and what should not be practiced.
Regarding what is appropriate and inappropriate for a person: [a candidate] who is excessively tall or excessively short;
one who has various obstacles; or one whose preceptor and community of monks are incomplete.
This is called "inappropriate.
As for what is "appropriate": one who is neither too tall nor too short, has reached the age of twenty, is free from all obstacles, and has a pure and complete preceptor—this is called "appropriate."
Therefore, it is called "appropriate" (*yukta*) and "inappropriate" (*ayukta*).
Regarding the "appropriateness or inappropriateness of the site":

what is appropriate? When the Saṃgha has bestowed the ground according to the Dharma, when the location of the ground is free from all obstacles, and when the construction is made within the prescribed measurements—this is called "appropriate."

"Inappropriate" means that the Sangha has granted the site in a manner contrary to the Dharma; the location of the site is fraught with various difficulties; the construction exceeds the prescribed dimensions; and the requests are so numerous that they cause the donor to be subject to public reproach—this is called "inappropriate."

"This concerns what is permissible and impermissible regarding a dwelling. Regarding those who violate the *vinaya*, there are seven classes of offenses (*āpatti*) as set forth in the *Prātimokṣa*; for each of these seven classes of dharmas, one must investigate the specific conditions under which the offense was committed. Furthermore, one must investigate how this offense should be confessed so that it may be extinguished. Moreover, one should know at what time this offense arose—was it during the first watch of the night, the final watch of the night, or in between? Or did it arise during the second watch of the night? Furthermore, one must further investigate whether it was committed before a meal, after a meal, or during the daytime."
Regarding the offenses that arise, are they caused by persons or caused by dharmas?
An offense committed during the first watch of the night is, for example, the use of what should not be used.
An offense committed at night is, for example, a bhikṣu preaching the Dharma to a bhikṣuṇī.

Regarding the offense of staying for two nights: if one stays together with a person who has not received full ordination for more than two nights, and neither rises nor departs before the appearance of the dawn light, this is called an offense.
Regarding the offense committed before midday: if one washes the feet before midday and applies oil to the feet while entering a village, except in cases of illness, this constitutes an offense.

Regarding the offense of eating after [the proper time]: if one has first accepted an invitation for a midday meal and subsequently accepts another invitation elsewhere, yet departs without informing one's neighbor-monk, this is called an offense.
Regarding offenses during the day: if a bhikṣu lies down during the day in an open place with his side touching the ground, this is called an offense.
Furthermore, there is another offense during the day: to walk in meditation (caṅkrama) wearing only the saṃghāṭī robe without wearing the antaravāsaka and the saṃkakṣikā.

Furthermore, if a disciple takes food from his preceptor (upādhyāya) or teacher (ācārya) after they have already finished eating, or if he wears leather sandals while eating, this is called an offense committed during the day.
Regarding offenses arising from the Dharma: if one attains a state that transcends the human condition, one must not disclose it to laypeople.
If one speaks to a fellow renunciant who is known to be reliable and whose words do not contradict [the Dharma], one may speak to them; one should not speak to others.

Furthermore, there are those who commit offenses due to the Dharma: if one is teaching a scripture to another and they recite it together, if the teacher gives the first phrase while the listener takes up the subsequent phrase, such a person should not be taught the scripture.

Regarding "not reciting in unison": once the senior monk has finished reciting a preceding phrase, the junior monk should next recite the phrase just recited by the senior monk; it is not permitted for them to recite simultaneously.

One must not preach the Dharma to a woman for more than five or six words; one must not preach the Dharma to those who cover their shoulders or cover their heads. There are many such cases where one must not preach the Dharma; these are called offenses committed due to the Dharma.

Regarding those who receive precepts based on the transgressions of others: if the candidate is of excessive height or length, less than twenty years of age, possesses obstructing conditions (*āvaraṇa-dharma*), or if the preceptor and the monastic community are incomplete or impure; if the group receiving the precepts is unlawful, or if the precepts are received in mid-air, outside the boundary (*sīmā*), or if one bestows the precepts upon thirteen types of persons who are not fit to be Dharma-practitioners—then the recipient does not obtain the precepts.

All these are termed offenses committed due to causes. The offenses committed arise from six bases; one should investigate these six bases and perform repentance. There are offenses arising from the body but not from the mind or speech;

there are offenses arising from the speech but not from the body or mind; there are offenses arising from the mind but not from the body or speech; there are offenses arising from both body and mind; there are offenses arising from both mind and speech; there are offenses arising from body, speech, and mind; there are offenses arising from greed; there are offenses arising from hatred; and there are offenses arising from delusion.

There are offenses committed through the harm of physical and verbal ignorance; there are offenses committed through the harm of physical and verbal hatred; and there are offenses committed through the harm of physical and verbal greed.

There are offenses committed through the body rather than the mind or speech: the first *pārājika* offense and intentionally emitting semen by manipulating one's own organ; furthermore, there are offenses that are unwholesome (*akuśala*) and offenses that are neutral (*avyākṛta*), such as staying overnight separated from the three robes or intentionally striking others with a staff or the hand—all these are termed bodily offenses for a bhikṣu.

Regarding offenses arising from the mouth: the fourth *pārājika*; coarse and turbid speech with a mind of sexual desire toward a woman; speech with a mind of malice; praising oneself by saying, "I am to be honored through sexual desire"; making baseless accusations against another in two ways; disparaging another’s lineage or physical appearance; false speech and divisive speech—these and other such offenses committed through vocal karma are called offenses arising from vocal karma.

Regarding offenses arising from body and speech: the second *pārājika*, acting as a matchmaker for others, or engaging in sexual intercourse—these and others like them are called offenses of body and speech.

Regarding offenses arising from the mind: for example, among the thirty matters [of the *Śaikṣa-dharmas*], when gold or silver is given by a donor, although one does not physically grasp it with the hand, one mentally treats it as one's own and says to a *kappiya-kāraka*, "Hold this and place it in such-and-such a spot," rather than saying to the *kappiya-kāraka*, "Do as you see fit.
Likewise, if a bhikṣu sees another commit an offense and conceals it instead of confessing it to others, this constitutes an offense of the mind.
"Offenses arising from body and mind" refers to those offenses committed by body and mind as described above.
"Offenses arising from body, speech, and mind" refers to those offenses committed by body, speech, and mind as described above.

Offenses arising from desire include, for example, the first *pārājika*, intentionally emitting semen by manipulating one's own organ, bodily contact with a woman, and praising oneself. Such are these [offenses].
Offenses arising from hatred (*dveṣa*) include the third *pārājika* and the second *anuddhata-āpatti* (groundless accusation).
Offenses arising from delusion (*moha*) include cases such as when a bhikṣu is of evil character and refuses to accept admonition; all such instances are offenses arising from delusion.
Bodily greed refers to the first *pārājika* offense, bodily contact, intentional masturbation resulting in the emission of semen, and other such acts arising from bodily greed.
Verbal greed refers to coarse and turbid speech, praising oneself for the sake of sexual desire, and so forth; all such instances are termed verbal greed.
Regarding those who covet with body and speech: suppose there were a mother and son who both left the household life, and the son would regularly come to provide for his mother.
Both mother and son conceived a greedy desire, and the mother said to her son, "This is the very place from which you originally came; now that you return to look upon it, what fault could there be?"
The son followed his mother’s words and immediately committed an impure act.
This is what is called the greed of body and speech.
There are many such instances like these; I have merely described them briefly.

That which arises from bodily hatred includes personally severing another's life with one's own hands or striking them with a staff; furthermore, there are bhikṣus who dispute with laypeople and drain the water from their grain fields, causing the grain to die.
Such instances of hatred as these are called those arising from hatred of the body.
Those arising from hatred of speech are, for example, when a bhikṣu says to someone:
"Kill such-and-such a person for me."
If one sends a letter, there are many such instances; these are called those arising from verbal anger.

"Those arising from both bodily and verbal anger" refers to when, driven by a mind of anger, one harms or afflicts others through either body or speech; these are called those arising from both bodily and verbal anger.

That which arises from physical delusion: if a bhikṣu takes up bedding, mats, or sitting cloths and spreads them out in the open air, yet fails to put them away himself when departing, this is called that which arises from physical delusion.

That which arises from verbal delusion refers to a guest bhikṣu who, having received a dwelling and bedding from the Saṃgha, departs and stays away for two nights without coming back himself to inform [the Saṃgha], nor does he instruct another to come and inform them; this is called that which arises from verbal delusion.

That which arises from the delusion of body and speech refers to when one receives a dwelling, bed, or mat from the Saṃgha, yet upon departing, neither instructs others to put it away nor puts it away oneself; this is called arising from the delusion of body and speech.
"Regarding those harmed by lust for the body: there was a bhikṣu named Upasena who had been appointed by the Saṃgha to guard the monastery.
Later, a young girl came to the monastery, and he immediately seized her and committed sexual misconduct with her."
This girl died young, her faculties having failed.
