The bhikṣus were doubtful in their minds: "In which of these two cases does one commit an offense—by killing or by committing sexual misconduct?
They went to ask the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"One incurs guilt through the extreme of sexual misconduct.
This is called an offense committed by the harm of bodily greed.
Regarding those who commit offenses through being harmed by sensual desire of the mouth: at that time, a layperson was lying ill.
That man had a wife of upright and beautiful countenance, and a certain bhikṣu went to him to inquire after his illness, saying to the wife:
"You may engage in sexual intercourse with me."
The woman replied, "I have a husband;
I cannot act according to my own will.
The bhikṣu then preached the Dharma for the sake of the sick man, saying:
"If one commits evil deeds and remains in this world for a long time, one will suffer for those crimes for an even longer duration in future lives.
If one possesses merit, upon the end of life, one immediately receives celestial bliss.
What is the use of such a wretched existence?"
The sick person, on account of this, became weary of the body and sought death through such means.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha,
and the Buddha said:
"This person has committed a *pārājika* offense.
This is called an offense arising from what is craved by the mouth.
"That which is defiled and harmed by body and mouth" refers precisely to greed of body and mouth.
At that time, there was a laywoman named Subhaddā who said to the bhikṣu:
"If you engage in sexual desire with me, when the impure emission occurs, you should abandon it, rise, and depart; thus you will not commit an offense."
The bhikṣu then acted upon those words and engaged in sexual desire, believing he had committed no offense.
As this was repeated from one to another, the World-Honored One heard of it.
The Buddha said:
"This is an offense committed through the greed of body and speech.

Furthermore, regarding offenses committed through the greed of body and speech: there was a bhikṣu who conferred the precepts upon a disciple; once the ordination had been completed through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, he did not explain the characteristics of the precepts to him, but simply left and headed toward the monastery.
The disciple followed behind and saw his former wife;
he asked her, "What are you doing? She replied:
"The teacher will receive the full precepts here.
The wife immediately said, "The days of observing the precepts are long; since we have met by chance now, let us indulge in sexual desire together."
The husband then followed his wife’s words and committed the act of impurity together with her.
The reason this man committed the act of impurity was precisely because he did not recognize the characteristics of the precepts.
Upon hearing of this, the Buddha established the precept:
"From this day forward, once you have received the precepts, you must immediately explain the characteristics of the precepts to those who have received them so that they may understand.
This is called an offense committed through the greed of body and speech.

Regarding those harmed by physical ill-will: when one, driven by a mind of anger, personally takes the life of another with one's own hand, this is called an offense of physical harm committed through a mind of ill-will.
Regarding offenses of verbal harm through ill-will: when one dispatches a messenger to kill someone, this is called an offense of verbal harm committed through ill-will.
Regarding those harmed by physical or verbal anger: to kill with one's own body or to command another to kill with words—this is called an offense harmed by physical or verbal anger.
Regarding those harmed by physical delusion: if one takes another’s wood, fruit, or tree without informing the owner—this is called an offense harmed by physical delusion.
"Regarding offenses committed through foolishness of speech: if there is a bhikṣu who, seeing that the actions of another bhikṣu are improper, says:
'Venerable sir!
These actions are not in accordance with the Dharma; you need not perform them again.'"
He replied to the one who had admonished him, saying:
"I will not follow the words of the Venerable One.
I shall instead consult those who possess wisdom."
"This is called an offense committed through verbal folly.
Furthermore, there is another offense committed through verbal folly:
when the Saṃgha recites the precepts, one says, 'What is the use of reciting these minor rules?'"
This, too, is an offense committed through verbal folly.
Furthermore, there may be someone who, when the Saṃgha recites the precepts, speaks as follows:
"What you are saying, we have heard from others many times; why must it be repeated?"
"This is an offense committed through foolishness of speech.
As for an offense committed through foolishness of both body and speech: if two or three people instruct one person to kill, and that person who goes [to carry out the act] says:"
"Very well," he replied, and immediately went to kill him; this is called an offense committed through delusion of body and speech.
As for an unwholesome offense, it refers to an offense intentionally committed by an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), as well as an offense intentionally committed by one in training (*śaikṣa*).
What constitutes an offense that is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?

When an ordinary person acts unintentionally or through forgetfulness and error, or when a trainee (*śaikṣa*) or an Arhat acts through forgetfulness and error, this is called an indeterminate offense.
Regarding "confession through recollection": if one acts intentionally after knowing [the transgression], it is grave; if one acts out of ignorance or lack of understanding, it is light.
As for the grave offenses, they may be removed by confessing before a single person or before the Saṃgha.
As for minor offenses, they are cleared by mental reflection and verbal confession.
This constitutes the offense of *duṣkṛta* (wrong speech).
There is nothing unwholesome that does not constitute a *duṣkṛta*.
“*Duṣkṛta* (offenses of wrong-doing) are all termed *duṣkṛta* (evil actions).
Taking discarded rags from the corpse of a person who has not yet decomposed;
taking discarded rags from a corpse after having broken through a wall or barrier to bring the dead body outside.”

If there is clothing upon a fence, such as discarded rags (pāṃśukūla), and one takes it, all such acts are minor; they are removed by mental confession (*cittavijñapti*), for these are transgressions of the body.

If there is a transgression that cannot be confessed when the time for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) arrives, one should keep it in mind and confess it after the recitation of the precepts is finished.
Regarding those offenses committed through forgetfulness or error, they are extinguished by self-reproach in one's mind.
Those extinguished by self-reproach in the mind are those among the *śaikṣa* rules that were not intentionally committed.
As for those committed intentionally but of minor degree, repentance before a single person is called "light."

Regarding those committed intentionally: their intrinsic natures are *sthūlātyaya*, *pāyattika*, or *pratideśanīya*; these are called "middling offenses," for which one should repent before a single person.
The "heavy" offenses are the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, the *sthūlātyaya* bordering on *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, and the *sthūlātyaya* bordering on *pārājika*;
these are the heaviest among those requiring confession. The "inexpiable" offenses are the four grave *duṣkṛta*, *pāyattika*, and *sthūlātyaya*; these sins cannot be expiated.

"If bhikṣus are in dispute and wish to eliminate their offenses, they must first repent before those with whom they fought. Just as spreading grass over mud allows a person to walk across it without getting soiled, by repenting together in harmony, one covers evil and allows goodness to arise; only then should one repent for the specific transgression committed."
The *āpattipratideśana* (confession) is as explained above.
Regarding the *vinaya* for extinguishing strife and litigation: striking one another and using abusive language is what is termed "strife."
"Quarreling" (zheng) refers to mutual assistance within factions; this is called quarreling.
"Speaking" (yan) refers to bringing matters before the judicial officials; thus it is called speaking.
"Litigating" (song) refers to each party stating the facts and principles of right and wrong; this is called litigating.
There are three kinds of disputes:
wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
Furthermore, one should investigate what causes and conditions give rise to such contention.
How is it that through repentance one attains extinction [of the offense]?
Does this dispute arise in the first watch of the night, the middle watch, or the last watch?
Does it arise before the meal, after the meal, or between the two?
Does it arise because of two nights?
Does it arise because of the Dharma, or does it arise because of the person?

If it arises because of the first watch of the night, then regarding this "first-watch beverage," some say it is permissible to drink after the first watch has passed, while others say it is not; even down to matters of long and short durations that are contrary to the Dharma, various groups receive full ordination, with some saying they have obtained it and others saying they have not—on account of these matters, strife arises.
All such cases are offenses as described above.
In the Vinaya texts, it is said that there are six fundamental bases for these disputes, which are further divided into eighteen. What are the six?
First is malice; second is harmfulness; third is deceit and hypocrisy; fourth is stinginess and envy; fifth is the adherence to views; and sixth are the two extreme and false views.
Anger (*dveṣa*) is that which causes the facial complexion to change, making one terrifying to others.
Malicious harm (*vihethana*) is that which can injure others and cause them distress.
Deceit (*māyā-śāṭhya*) is when the mind is not true and one falsely fabricates empty matters; this is called deceit.
Regarding stinginess and envy: to covet things before one and be unwilling to give them to others is called stinginess (*mātsarya*).
To feel vexation upon seeing what others have obtained is called envy (*īrṣyā*).
Regarding the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*): to grasp one's own views as correct and the views of others as incorrect is called the clinging to views.
Regarding the extreme view (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*): to view continuity as eternal and cessation as annihilation is the extreme view.
Those with wrong views slander cause and effect;
this is said to arise from the six sense bases.
What are the eighteen kinds of discrimination?

From "arising above" based on what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, up to "speaking what is not the teaching," there are eighteen kinds of quarrels arising from above; these are called the collection of the roots of dispute.
This collection of quarrels is extinguished through two causes and conditions:
First, the person is present before one; second, one investigates the place from which it arose.
For example, the group of six bhikṣus were staying in Śrāvastī and went to bathe in the river Aḷavī; they took off their robes and placed them on the bank.

Later, when the bhikṣu Kālodāyin arrived, he took off his own robe and placed it upon the robes of the group-of-six (ṣaḍvargika) bhikṣus; failing to examine them carefully as he came out, he departed wearing the robes of the group-of-six bhikṣus.
The group of six monks slandered Kālodāyin for stealing a robe and performed a *karmavācanā* against him in private.
Kālodāyin felt doubt in his mind and went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"When you took the robe, with what kind of thought did you take it?
Kātyāyana replied,
"I took it with the thought that it was my own."
The Buddha said,
"If it is as you say, there is no offense of theft.
Thereupon, he established this precept:
"From this time forward, two conditions must be fulfilled:
first, the investigation of the cause; second, the presence of the person concerned. Only then shall the *vinaya* of cessation (*sammati-vinaya*) be enacted.
This is called the *vinaya* for the settling of disputes.

The Vinaya for the eradication of afflictions refers to this Vinaya which cuts off the proclivities (*anuśaya*), envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), and fetters associated with the paths of seeing and cultivation within the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm; this is called the Vinaya for the extinction of afflictions.
The meaning of "proclivity" (*anuśaya*) is that it follows after the practitioner and prevents them from cultivating goodness;
the meaning of "proclivity" is that what has been practiced for a long time is difficult to abandon;
the meaning of "proclivity" is that it can cause a person to sink into the evil realms.
The meaning of "proclivity" (*anuśaya*) is that which binds the practitioner within the cycle of birth and death;
it is the meaning of "proclivity" that it enables the person to receive a body in continuous succession;
it is the meaning of "proclivity" that it does not sever the afflictions (*kleśa*).
The meaning of "proclivity" (anuśaya) is enmity;
the meaning of "proclivity" is not relinquishing through skillful means;
the meaning of "proclivity" is the non-cessation of committing evil.

The ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are: the underlying tendency of views, the underlying tendency of doubt, the underlying tendency of adherence to precepts and rituals, the underlying tendency of sensual lust, the underlying tendency of ill will, the underlying tendency of lust for the realm of form, the underlying tendency of lust for the formless realm, the underlying tendency of ignorance, the underlying tendency of pride, and the underlying tendency of restlessness.

The fetters (paryavasthāna) are: the fetter of ignorance, the fetter of ill-will, the fetter of sloth, the fetter of torpor, the fetter of restlessness, the fetter of regret, the fetter of doubt, the fetter of attachment to one's own possessions, and the fetter of coveting the possessions of others.

From this arise strife, contention, and litigation; because of this, a harmful mind subsequently arises, which binds the practitioner and prevents liberation—this is the meaning of "entanglement" (*paryavasthāna*).

Furthermore, the entanglements are: the entanglement of the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi-paryavasthāna*), the entanglement of doubt (*vicikitsā-paryavasthāna*), the entanglement of attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa-paryavasthāna*), the entanglement of desire (*rāga-paryavasthāna*), the entanglement of ill-will (*pratigha-paryavasthāna*), the entanglement of stinginess (*mātsarya-paryavasthāna*), the entanglement of envy (*īrṣyā-paryavasthāna*), the entanglement of ignorance (*avidyā-paryavasthāna*), the entanglement of pride (*māna-paryavasthāna*), and the entanglement of restlessness (*auddhatya-paryavasthāna*).
These ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) are identical to the ten fetters (*saṃyojana*); therefore, they are called "envelopments.

They comprise twelve abodes subsumed under the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), twenty-two abodes in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and four abodes in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Among them, those to be abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*) are the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*).
What is abandoned through the path of cultivation?
By attenuating the greed, hatred, and ignorance of the desire realm, one attains the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*.
By completely severing the greed, hatred, and ignorance of the desire realm, one attains the fruit of *anāgāmin*.
Having severed the craving for the realms of form and formlessness and exhausted ignorance, one attains the fruit of arhatship.
One should investigate from where these arising afflictions originate.
Where does it cease?
As for the place of arising: at the place where the fetters (saṃyojana) arise, one gives rise to a mind of greedy attachment and defilement, which can produce all afflictions (kleśa).
What is the place where the fetters arise?
When the eye sees bodily forms, it gives rise to a mind of attachment, reckoning them as permanent and also reckoning them as a self; this extends even to the mind and mental objects (*dharmas*).

Regarding the six external sense objects, the six internal consciousnesses, the six internal contacts, the six feelings, the six cravings, the six perceptions, and the six thoughts—down to the five aggregates (*skandhas*), the twelve bases (*āyatanas*), and the four elements with their associated consciousnesses—one contemplates these as being the self and as being permanent.

Therefore, because one conceives of a self and permanence within the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements, one is able to give rise to all fetters and afflictions numbering five hundred; thus, they are called "all."
This is called the "aggregate of the place of origination.

Regarding the "aggregate of cessation," one conceives of faults within the phenomena that serve as the place of origination for the afflictions; seeing with the eye forms of the body, and so on up to mental objects, one contemplates them as impermanent and non-self. One contemplates the consciousness and its attendants as impermanent, suffering, a disease, an abscess, a poison, an arrow, the body, empty, and non-self.
Having performed this contemplation, one is able to sever all afflictions; this is called the locus for extinguishing the accumulation [of defilements].
"To sever afflictions, one must perform five kinds of contemplative practices:
the practice of impermanence, the practice of suffering, the practice of non-self, the dharma of cessation, and the practice of emptiness."
Regarding the practice of impermanence (*anicca*): that which does not abide for even a single moment, being subject to illness and decay, is called impermanence.
Regarding suffering (*dukkha*): like an abscess, like a disease, like an arrow piercing the heart, or like the arising of pain when an object is destroyed—this is called the practice of suffering.
Regarding emptiness (*śūnyatā*): one contemplates that "self" and "what belongs to self" are all like illusions or transformations and lack any real dharma; this is called emptiness.
Regarding the practice of non-self (*anātman*): one contemplates that all dharmas are devoid of a self.

The two aspects of impermanence (*anitya*) and suffering (*duḥkha*) collectively contemplate all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*). The two aspects of emptiness (*śūnya*) and non-self (*anātman*) universally contemplate both contaminated and uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*).
As for the meaning of "quiescence" (*śānta*), because it is devoid of the transformations of birth and death, it is called the "quiescent dharma."
Therefore, the practitioner should always bind the mind to the contemplation of the five practices.

As for the objects of contemplation, they include the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*), and the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). Furthermore, one should practice the contemplation of the six applications of mindfulness (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti-sthāna*), as well as the application of mindfulness to the dharma of cessation and the dharma-body, the application of mindfulness to *ānāpāna* (breath), and even the applications of mindfulness to the four immeasurable minds (*catvāry apramāṇāni*). From the perception of the impurity of food up to the perception of cessation, these should be understood in detail from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.

If one forms the perception of bones and the perception of decay, practicing the contemplation of impurity from the feet to the crown of the head up to the perception of dissolution, this is the objective sphere of the mind.

If one abides within the three emptinesses, employing whichever gateway of contemplation is appropriate to sever the fetters and latent tendencies, this is called abiding in the three gates of liberation.
When a practitioner dwells within the stages, they should contemplate six stages:

first, the stage of the contemplation of white bones; second, the stage of nature; third, the stage of the eight persons; fourth, the stage of thinness; fifth, the stage of freedom from desire; and sixth, the stage of having already accomplished—these are called the dwelling stages.
“There are six things to be abandoned through the vision of the truths:

first, the view of a self; second, doubt; third, attachment to precepts and rituals; fourth, desire directed toward evil destinies; fifth, hatred directed toward evil destinies; and sixth, delusion directed toward evil destinies.”
Those to be abandoned through the cultivation of the path (*bhāvanā-mārga*) are:
first, sensual attachment; second, aversion; third, attachment to the form realm; fourth, attachment to the formless realm; fifth, ignorance; sixth, pride; and seventh, restlessness.
By severing these seven afflictions, one attains the realization of the fruits: by severing the three fetters, one becomes a *srotāpanna*;
because sensual desire and ill will are attenuated, one becomes a *sakṛdāgāmin*;
and because sensual desire and ill will are severed, one becomes an *anāgāmin*.
Because all fetters (*saṃyojana*) have been exhausted, one is called an Arhat.
Therefore, it is said that by severing these [fetters], one attains the fruit. One distinguishes persons by means of their fruits:

because one has attained the fruit of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), one is called a Stream-enterer; because one has attained the fruit of Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), one is called a Once-returner; because one has attained the fruit of Non-returner (*anāgāmin*), one is called a Non-returner; and because one has attained the fruit of Arhatship, one is called an Arhat.
This is called the severing of the place of accumulation.

Regarding the full ordination (upasampadā) according to the Bhikṣu-vinaya, there are cases where it is appropriate and cases where it is not; even regarding the prescribed measurements, there are cases where it is appropriate and cases where it is not, or where it is permitted and where it is not permitted. It should be permitted when the measurements are observed; it is not permitted when they are not.
Regarding offenses and non-offenses: one who acts according to the Dharma does not commit an offense, while one who acts contrary to the Dharma commits an offense.
One should infer this according to the sequence [of the rules].
From the alms bowl down to the dwelling, what is appropriate and what is inappropriate should be understood as explained in the preceding text.

All those who have received full ordination should possess the following: a bowl bag, leather sandals, a needle case, a meditation belt, a *kāṣāya* robe, a hook-and-loop cord, a waistband, a tube for eye medicine, a vessel for medicinal incense and medicinal tools, a cap for the head, and a water-strainer.
Regarding such items as these, there are those that are permissible and those that are not; this is called the *vinaya* for bhikṣus.

As for the *vinaya* for bhikṣuṇīs, whether receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*) is permissible or not depends on the circumstances: if the measurements are correct, there is no offense; if they are incorrect, there is an offense. Furthermore, one must proceed in due order through the inspection of the alms bowl up to the dwelling quarters.

If bhikṣuṇīs obtain alms-bowls, they should accept and keep one on that very day; as for the others, they should either perform the ritual of pure giving (*viśuddha-dāna*) or give them away to others.

The same applies as previously explained regarding the *nivāsana* (lower robe) and the *saṃkakṣikā* (breast-covering robe); the same applies as previously explained regarding the wound-cloth (*vraṇapaṭṭa*) and the bathing robe (*snāna-vastra*).
Regarding robes up to dwellings, it is as explained in the Bhikṣu Sūtra.
A śikṣamāṇā may take food for herself; what she takes today she may eat tomorrow. All other matters are to be trained in according to the rules for the great bhikṣuṇīs.
This is called the *bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*.
Regarding the "partial *vinaya*": there are two hundred and fifty rules for *bhikṣus*, and five hundred rules for *bhikṣuṇīs*.
The śikṣamāṇā follows the same rules as a mahābhikṣuṇī, with the exception that she may take food for herself and, having taken it, keep it until the following day to eat;
the śrāmaṇerī, upāsaka, and upāsikā each have their own precepts, which constitute their respective vinaya.
This is called the *vinaya* of limited scope.

Regarding the *vinaya* of all circumstances: one should train in all pure precepts of conduct, pure precepts of mind, and pure precepts of wisdom; one should observe every subtle precept as if it were a grave one, until ultimately the *brahmacarya* and the *prātimokṣa* precepts are rendered completely pure.
All wholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind should be practiced in accordance with right view up to right concentration.
Laymen and laywomen should eliminate sexual misconduct, and so forth, distancing themselves from killing and wrong views; this is called the precept for the laity.
"Examine the gravity of the offense committed, its origin and conditions, and whether it is subject to extinction or not.
— *Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra*, Scroll 8.
